expansion: A committee for adapting this Directive to technical and scientific progress, referred to as ‘the Committee,’ is hereby established. This Committee shall be composed of representatives from each of the Member States, with the Commission appointing a representative to serve as its chairman. The purpose of the Committee is to ensure that the Directive remains up-to-date by incorporating relevant technical and scientific advancements.

The Commission is supported by a Committee responsible for adapting this Directive to scientific and technical progress. When this Article is referenced, Articles 5 and 7 of Decision 1999/468/EC apply, with the period specified in Article 5(6) set at three months. The Committee is tasked with adopting its own rules of procedure.

Every three years, Member States must provide the Commission with information on the implementation of this Directive through a sectoral report, which also includes other relevant Community Directives. This report is prepared based on a questionnaire or outline drafted by the Commission following the procedure in Article 6 of Directive 91/692/EEC. The questionnaire is sent to Member States six months before the reporting period begins, and the completed report must be submitted within nine months after the end of the three-year period. The initial report covers 1994 to 1996. Subsequently, the Commission will publish a Community report within nine months of receiving all Member States’ reports. If necessary, considering advances in medical knowledge and technology, the Commission will propose further measures to prevent and reduce asbestos pollution to protect human health and the environment.

Member States are required to enact the necessary laws, regulations, and administrative provisions to comply with this Directive by 31 December 1988 and must inform the Commission immediately upon doing so. For plants built or authorized before this date, provisions related to Articles 4 and 5 must be adopted and published by 30 June 1991 at the latest. Additionally, Member States must communicate the texts of their national laws adopted under this Directive to the Commission.

Finally, this Directive is addressed to the Member States, obliging them to implement its provisions accordingly.

The Directive sets out specific obligations for Member States regarding the handling and disposal of waste containing asbestos fibers or dust. Without prejudice to Directive 78/319/EEC, as last amended by the 1985 Act of Accession, Member States must ensure that during the transport and deposition of asbestos-containing waste, no asbestos fibers or dust are released into the air, and no liquids potentially containing asbestos fibers are spilled. Furthermore, when such waste is landfilled at licensed sites, it must be treated, packaged, or covered in a manner that prevents the release of asbestos particles into the environment, taking local conditions into account.

Member States are also permitted to introduce more stringent provisions than those in this Directive to better protect health and the environment, provided these comply with the Treaty’s conditions. To keep the Directive up to date with scientific and technical progress, a Committee composed of Member State representatives and chaired by the Commission has been established. This Committee oversees adaptations to the Directive, particularly regarding sampling and analysis methods, ensuring that limit values remain unchanged.

Every three years, Member States must report to the Commission on the Directive’s implementation, using a questionnaire or outline prepared by the Commission. These reports help monitor progress and inform any necessary further proposals to reduce asbestos pollution in light of medical and technological advances.

Finally, Member States were required to transpose the Directive into national law by 31 December 1988, with specific provisions related to certain plants to be adopted by 30 June 1991. They must also communicate the texts of these national provisions to the Commission. The Directive is addressed directly to the Member States, emphasizing their responsibility for compliance and enforcement.

For the purpose of this Directive, the national boatmasters' certificates for the carriage of goods and passengers by inland waterway, as referred to in Annex I, shall be subdivided into two groups:

- **Group A:** Boatmasters' certificates valid for waterways of a maritime character, as indicated in Annex II.

- **Group B:** Boatmasters' certificates valid for the other waterways in the Community, with the exception of the Rhine, the Lek, and the Waal.

This subdivision ensures that boatmasters are certified according to the specific nature of the waterways they navigate, distinguishing between maritime-character waterways and other inland waterways within the Community, excluding the Rhine, the Lek, and the Waal.

According to the requirements set forth, the 11 Member States are obligated to conduct ongoing surveillance of the conservation status of the natural habitats and species specified in Article 2. This surveillance must place special emphasis on priority natural habitat types and priority species, ensuring that these critical elements of biodiversity receive focused attention. The purpose of this monitoring is to assess the effectiveness of conservation measures, detect any negative trends, and inform necessary management actions. In addition to habitat monitoring, the protection of species involves implementing appropriate safeguards to prevent deterioration of their habitats, disturbance, or direct harm. This comprehensive approach helps maintain or restore favorable conservation status, contributing to the overall goal of preserving biodiversity within the Member States.

Under certain conditions, Member States may derogate from the strict protection provisions set out in Articles 12, 13, 14, and parts of Article 15 of the relevant legislation concerning species conservation. Such derogations are only permitted if there is no satisfactory alternative and if the derogation does not harm the maintenance of the species populations at a favorable conservation status within their natural range. The allowed grounds for derogation include: (a) protecting wild fauna, flora, and natural habitats; (b) preventing serious damage to crops, livestock, forests, fisheries, water, or other property; (c) safeguarding public health and safety or addressing other overriding public interests, including social, economic, or significant environmental benefits; (d) facilitating research, education, repopulation, reintroduction, and necessary breeding operations, including artificial propagation of plants; and (e) permitting, under strict supervision and on a selective and limited basis, the taking or keeping of certain specimens of species listed in Annex IV, within limits set by national authorities.

To ensure transparency and accountability, Member States must submit a report every two years to the Commission detailing the derogations applied. This report must follow a format established by the Committee and include specific information such as the species involved, reasons for derogation including risks and rejected alternatives, authorized methods for capture or killing and their justification, the circumstances and locations of derogations, the authorities responsible for overseeing and enforcing conditions, and the supervisory measures and outcomes. The Commission then reviews these reports and provides its opinion within 12 months, reporting back to the Committee accordingly.

The passage outlines the responsibilities of Member States and the Commission regarding research and scientific work in line with the objectives and obligations specified in the relevant articles. Specifically, Member States and the Commission are tasked with promoting the necessary research and scientific activities that support the goals established in Article 2 and fulfill the obligations mentioned in Article 11. To ensure effective coordination, they must exchange information related to research conducted both at the Member State level and at the Community level.

Special emphasis is placed on scientific work that is essential for implementing the provisions of Articles 4 and 10. Additionally, transboundary cooperative research between Member States is encouraged to enhance collaboration and address issues that cross national borders.

Regarding the procedure for amending the Annexes, while the passage does not provide explicit details, such amendments typically follow a formal process involving proposals by the Commission, consultations with Member States, and approval by the relevant legislative bodies to ensure that changes align with the overall objectives and legal framework of the Community.

In implementing the provisions of this Directive, Member States are required to take several key actions to ensure the effective conservation of wild fauna and flora. Firstly, they must assess the desirability of re-introducing species listed in Annex IV that are native to their territory, particularly when such re-introduction could aid in the species' conservation. This assessment should be thorough, incorporating investigations and experiences from other Member States or regions, to confirm that re-introduction will effectively help re-establish these species at a favorable conservation status. Importantly, any re-introduction efforts must be preceded by proper consultation with the public concerned.

Secondly, Member States must regulate the deliberate introduction of any non-native species into the wild within their territories. This regulation aims to prevent any negative impact on natural habitats within their natural range, as well as on the native wild fauna and flora. Where necessary, Member States may prohibit such introductions altogether. The outcomes of these assessments and regulatory measures must be communicated to the relevant committee for information.

Finally, Member States are encouraged to promote education and raise general awareness about the importance of protecting wild fauna and flora species, as well as conserving their habitats and natural environments. These efforts are essential to foster public understanding and support for biodiversity conservation initiatives.

Member States are required to implement measures ensuring that certain taxes applicable to road vehicles—specifically lorries, tractors, trailers, or semi-trailers—are either reduced or reimbursed when these vehicles are used in combined transport involving rail. This reduction or reimbursement can be granted either as a standard amount or proportionally based on the extent of the journeys undertaken by rail. The specific limits, conditions, and rules governing these reductions or reimbursements are to be determined by each Member State after consulting with the Commission.

The reductions or reimbursements must be provided by the Member State where the vehicles are registered, calculated on the basis of rail journeys carried out within that State. However, Member States have the discretion to extend these benefits to rail journeys that occur partially or entirely outside the State of registration.

Furthermore, vehicles used exclusively for road haulage in feeder or final delivery stages of combined transport may be exempted from these taxes, provided they are taxed separately, and this is without prejudice to any future reorganization of national commercial vehicle taxation systems at the Community level.

The provisions outlined address the treatment of airport slots during the COVID-19 pandemic, specifically in relation to Articles 8(2) and 10(2). Firstly, coordinators are instructed to consider slots allocated between 1 March 2020 and 24 October 2020 as having been operated by the air carriers to which they were originally assigned, effectively protecting carriers from losing their slot rights despite disruptions caused by the pandemic. Similarly, for slots allocated between 23 January 2020 and 29 February 2020 concerning flights between EU airports and those in the People’s Republic of China or Hong Kong, these slots are also deemed operated by the initially allocated carriers.

However, for slots dated after 8 April 2020, this protection applies only if the unused slots have been made available to coordinators for reallocation to other carriers, ensuring efficient use of available capacity. The European Commission is tasked with monitoring the situation continuously, using data from Eurocontrol and scientific evidence to assess the ongoing impact of COVID-19 on air traffic levels. Should the reduction in traffic persist, the Commission is empowered to amend the protected period through delegated acts, following the procedure in Article 12a.

Furthermore, the Commission must report its findings to the European Parliament and the Council by 15 September 2020 and act swiftly if necessary. In cases where urgent action is required due to prolonged effects of the pandemic on the air transport sector, the expedited procedure under Article 12b applies to the adoption of delegated acts. This framework aims to balance the need to maintain slot usage rights for carriers during unprecedented disruptions while allowing flexibility to adapt to evolving circumstances.

The procedure for handling complaints and rights of appeal under the relevant regulation is as follows:

1. Complaints concerning the application of Articles 7(2), 8, 8a, 10, and 14(1) to (4) and (6) must be submitted to the coordination committee, without prejudice to any rights of appeal available under national law. Upon receiving a complaint, the committee is required to consider the issue within one month and, if possible, propose solutions to the coordinator to resolve the problem. If the complaint remains unresolved after this process, the Member State responsible may arrange for mediation within an additional two-month period. This mediation can be conducted by a representative organization of air carriers or airports, or by another impartial third party.

2. To ensure coordinators can perform their duties effectively, Member States must implement appropriate measures under national law to protect coordinators from claims for damages related to their functions under this Regulation. Such protection does not apply in cases where the coordinator has acted with gross negligence or wilful misconduct.

The Regulation establishes specific provisions regarding relations with third countries in the context of the allocation and use of airport slots. If it appears that a third country does not provide Community air carriers with treatment comparable to that granted by the Regulation to air carriers from that country, or fails to grant de facto national treatment to Community air carriers, or offers more favorable treatment to air carriers from other third countries than to Community air carriers, the Commission is empowered to act. Following the procedure outlined in Article 13(2), the Commission may decide that one or more Member States should take appropriate measures. These measures can include the partial or complete suspension of the application of the Regulation concerning air carriers from the third country in question, aiming to address and remedy the discriminatory practices identified.

Furthermore, Member States have an obligation to keep the Commission informed about any significant legal or practical difficulties faced by Community air carriers in securing slots at airports located in third countries. This reporting ensures that the Commission remains aware of potential issues affecting fair access and can take necessary actions to uphold equitable treatment for Community air carriers internationally.

The Regulation will enter into force on the thirtieth day after its publication in the Official Journal of the European Communities. From that date onward, it shall be fully binding and directly applicable in all Member States, meaning that it must be applied in its entirety without the need for national implementing legislation.

The conditions for airport coordination under the relevant regulatory framework are as follows:

1. **Designation Authority and Principles**  
   A Member State is not obliged to designate any airport as schedules facilitated or coordinated except in accordance with the specific provisions outlined in the regulation. While a Member State may designate an airport as schedules facilitated, this must be done in a manner that respects the principles of transparency, neutrality, and non-discrimination. However, the designation of an airport as coordinated must strictly follow the conditions set out in paragraph 3.

2. **Capacity Analysis Requirement**  
   Before designating an airport as coordinated, the Member State responsible must ensure a thorough capacity analysis is conducted at airports without designation or those designated as schedules facilitated. This analysis should be performed by the airport managing body or another competent entity when deemed necessary by the Member State, or within six months following:  
   - A written request from air carriers representing more than half of the airport’s operations or from the airport managing body, if either party believes capacity is insufficient for current or planned operations during certain periods.  
   - A request from the Commission, especially if the airport is effectively accessible only to carriers with allocated slots or if new entrants face serious difficulties securing landing and takeoff opportunities.  

   The capacity analysis must use commonly recognized methods to identify any capacity shortfall, considering environmental constraints. It should evaluate potential solutions such as new or modified infrastructure, operational changes, or other measures, along with the expected timeframe for resolving capacity issues. The analysis and methodology must be shared with the requesting parties, other interested stakeholders upon request, and the Commission simultaneously. Updates to the analysis are required if significant changes occur or if paragraph 5 is invoked.

3. **Consultation and Designation Criteria**  
   Based on the capacity analysis, the Member State must consult with the airport managing body, regularly operating air carriers and their representatives, general aviation representatives, and air traffic control authorities regarding the airport’s capacity situation. If capacity problems persist for at least one scheduling period, the airport shall be designated as coordinated for the relevant periods only if:  
   - The capacity shortfall is severe enough that significant delays are unavoidable, and  
   - No short-term solutions exist to resolve these problems.  

   In exceptional circumstances, Member States may derogate from these criteria and designate airports as coordinated for the appropriate period. Once sufficient capacity is restored to meet actual or planned operations at a coordinated airport, the designation as fully coordinated shall be lifted.

The Member State responsible for a schedules facilitated or coordinated airport must appoint a qualified natural or legal person as the schedules facilitator or airport coordinator, respectively. This appointment is made after consulting regularly operating air carriers, their representative organizations, the airport managing body, and the coordination committee if one exists. The same facilitator or coordinator may serve multiple airports.

At a schedules facilitated airport, the schedules facilitator must operate independently, neutrally, transparently, and without discrimination, in accordance with the Regulation. At a coordinated airport, the coordinator’s independence must be ensured by functionally separating the coordinator from any single interested party, and the financing system must guarantee this independence. The coordinator must also act neutrally, transparently, and without discrimination.

Both the schedules facilitator and the coordinator participate in international scheduling conferences permitted by Community law. The schedules facilitator advises air carriers and recommends alternative arrival or departure times when congestion is anticipated. The coordinator is solely responsible for slot allocation, ensuring it follows the Regulation, and must provide for slot allocation outside office hours in emergencies.

The schedules facilitator monitors air carriers’ adherence to recommended schedules, while the coordinator monitors compliance with allocated slots. These checks are conducted in cooperation with the airport managing body and air traffic control authorities, considering relevant timing and airport parameters. The coordinator must submit an annual activity report to the Member States and the Commission upon request, detailing the application of specific Articles, complaints received, and resolution steps.

Schedules facilitators and coordinators collaborate to identify scheduling inconsistencies. Upon request, the coordinator must provide interested parties, especially coordination committee members or observers, with free access to detailed slot information, including historical slots, requested slots, allocated and outstanding slots, remaining available slots, and allocation criteria. This information must be available by the time of scheduling conferences and as needed thereafter, with summarised information provided on request, possibly for a cost-related fee.

Finally, where applicable and accepted, schedules facilitators, coordinators, and air carriers must apply relevant scheduling information standards, provided they comply with Community law.

At a coordinated airport, the Member State responsible must ensure the establishment of a coordination committee, which may serve more than one airport. This committee’s membership must include, at minimum, regularly operating air carriers and their representative organizations, the airport’s managing body, relevant air traffic control authorities, and representatives of general aviation users who regularly use the airport. The coordination committee has several key tasks: it advises or makes proposals to the coordinator and/or Member State on ways to increase or better utilize airport capacity (as defined in Article 3), sets coordination parameters (per Article 6), monitors the use of allocated slots, and develops local guidelines for slot allocation and monitoring, considering factors such as environmental concerns (Article 8(5)). Additionally, the committee addresses improvements to traffic conditions, serious issues faced by new entrants (Article 10(9)), and all matters related to airport capacity. It also mediates complaints regarding slot allocation as outlined in Article 11.

Member State representatives and the coordinator attend committee meetings as observers. The committee is responsible for drafting written rules of procedure that cover participation, elections, meeting frequency, and language use. Any committee member may propose local guidelines, which the committee discusses upon the coordinator’s request. Following these discussions, the committee submits a report to the Member State, detailing the various positions expressed within the committee.

The process of slot allocation involves several key steps to ensure the efficient and fair use of airport infrastructure for landing and take-off permissions during a given scheduling period:

1. **Allocation from Slot Pool:** A series of slots is allocated from the slot pool to applicant carriers, granting them permission to use the airport infrastructure for the requested scheduling period. Once this period expires, the slots must be returned to the slot pool as outlined in Article 10.

2. **Historic Use and Slot Retention:** If an air carrier has used a series of slots for scheduled or programmed non-scheduled services and can demonstrate to the coordinator that it has operated those slots for at least 80% of the allocated scheduling period (with coordinator approval), the carrier is entitled to retain the same series of slots for the next equivalent scheduling period, provided the request is made within the deadline specified in Article 7(1). This provision operates without prejudice to other relevant articles.

3. **Priority in Case of Conflicts:** When all slot requests cannot be fully accommodated, preference is given to commercial air services, especially scheduled and programmed non-scheduled services. Among competing requests within the same service category, priority is given to year-round operations.

4. **Re-timing of Slots:** Re-timing of slot series before allocating remaining slots to other carriers is permitted only for operational reasons or if it improves the timing relative to the initial request. Such changes require explicit confirmation from the coordinator before taking effect.

5. **Consideration of Additional Rules:** The coordinator must consider additional rules and guidelines established by the global or Community-wide air transport industry, as well as local guidelines approved by the relevant Member State or competent airport authority. These rules must not compromise the coordinator’s independence, must comply with Community law, and aim to improve airport capacity efficiency. The Member State communicates these rules to the Commission.

6. **Handling Unaccommodated Requests:** If a requested slot cannot be allocated, the coordinator must inform the air carrier of the reasons and suggest the nearest available alternative slot.

7. **Accommodation of Short-Notice Requests:** Beyond planned allocations, the coordinator strives to accommodate single slot requests made on short notice for all types of aviation, including general aviation. This is done using slots remaining in the pool after initial distribution and any slots available at short notice.

This structured approach ensures a transparent, fair, and efficient allocation of airport slots, balancing operational needs, historical usage, and regulatory compliance.

Mobile containers used for transporting petrol must be designed and operated to minimize the release of vapours, in accordance with specific regulatory requirements. Firstly, these containers are required to retain residual vapours after unloading petrol, preventing their escape into the atmosphere. When supplying petrol to service stations or terminals, mobile containers must also be capable of accepting and retaining return vapours from the storage facilities at these locations. For rail tankers, this requirement applies only if they supply petrol to service stations or terminals where vapour intermediate storage is used.

Except for vapour release through pressure relief valves, all vapours retained after unloading must remain within the container until the next petrol loading at a terminal. However, if the container is subsequently used to transport products other than petrol and vapour recovery or intermediate storage is not feasible, ventilation may be allowed in areas where emissions are unlikely to cause significant environmental or health issues.

Member States are responsible for ensuring that road tankers undergo regular vapour tightness testing and that vacuum and pressure relief valves on all mobile containers are periodically inspected to confirm proper operation.

These provisions apply immediately to new road tankers, rail tankers, and vessels from the date specified in Article 10. Existing rail tankers and vessels must comply within three years if loaded at terminals subject to certain requirements, and existing road tankers must comply when retrofitted for bottom loading as per Annex IV specifications.

An exception to these rules allows for vapour losses during measuring operations using dipsticks, applicable to existing mobile containers and new containers entering service within four years after the date in Article 10.

For the purposes of this Regulation, a ‘visa’ is defined as an authorization granted by, or a decision made by, a Member State that is necessary for entry into its territory. This authorization applies in cases where the individual intends to stay in that Member State, or in multiple Member States, for a period not exceeding three months in total. Additionally, a visa is required for transit through the territory or the airport transit zone of that Member State or several Member States.

For the purposes of this Directive, the term **‘system’** is defined as a formal arrangement involving three or more participants—excluding the system operator, possible settlement agents, central counterparties, clearing houses, or indirect participants—that operates under common rules and standardized procedures for clearing or executing transfer orders between participants. This arrangement may or may not involve a central counterparty. The system must be governed by the law of a Member State chosen by the participants, with the condition that at least one participant has its head office in that Member State. Furthermore, the system must be officially designated as such and notified to the European Securities and Markets Authority by the relevant Member State, which must be satisfied with the adequacy of the system’s rules.

Under certain conditions, a Member State may designate as a system a formal arrangement primarily executing transfer orders, even if it also executes orders related to other financial instruments to a limited extent, if such designation is justified on grounds of systemic risk. Additionally, on a case-by-case basis, a Member State may designate a formal arrangement between only two participants as a system, again excluding settlement agents, central counterparties, clearing houses, or indirect participants, if warranted by systemic risk considerations. Importantly, arrangements between interoperable systems do not themselves constitute a system.

Other key definitions include:

- **‘Institution’**: This encompasses credit institutions as defined in Directive 2006/48/EC, investment firms as defined in Directive 2004/39/EC (excluding certain entities), public authorities, publicly guaranteed undertakings, and undertakings outside the Community performing equivalent functions. Institutions are responsible for fulfilling financial obligations arising from transfer orders within a system. Under specific conditions, Member States may also consider certain participants in systems that only execute transfer orders and related payments as institutions, provided systemic risk justifies this.

- **‘Central counterparty’**: An entity interposed between institutions in a system, acting as the exclusive counterparty to these institutions regarding their transfer orders.

- **‘Settlement agent’**: An entity providing settlement accounts to institutions and/or central counterparties within systems, facilitating the settlement of transfer orders and potentially extending credit for settlement purposes.

- **‘Clearing house’**: An entity responsible for calculating net positions of institutions, central counterparties, and/or settlement agents.

For the purpose of this Regulation, several key terms are defined to ensure clarity and uniform application across participating Member States. Firstly, ‘participating Member States’ refers to those Member States listed in the table in the Annex. ‘Legal instruments’ encompass a broad range of documents with legal effect, including legislative and statutory provisions, administrative acts, judicial decisions, contracts, unilateral legal acts, and payment instruments other than banknotes and coins. The ‘conversion rate’ is the irrevocably fixed rate adopted by the Council for each participating Member State’s currency, as established under Article 123(4) of the Treaty. The ‘euro adoption date’ marks either the entry of a Member State into the third stage of economic and monetary union or the date when its derogation is lifted, depending on the circumstances outlined in Articles 121(3) and 122(2) of the Treaty. The ‘cash changeover date’ is the day when euro banknotes and coins become legal tender in a Member State. The ‘euro unit’ refers to the currency unit defined in the Treaty, while ‘national currency units’ denote the units of a Member State’s currency as defined the day before adopting the euro. The ‘transitional period’ is a maximum of three years starting at midnight on the euro adoption date and ending at midnight on the cash changeover date. The ‘phasing-out period’ is a maximum of one year beginning on the euro adoption date and applies only when the euro adoption and cash changeover dates coincide. To ‘redenominate’ means to change the unit in which outstanding debt is stated from the national currency to the euro without altering other terms of the debt, subject to national law. Finally, ‘credit institutions’ are defined according to Directive 2000/12/EC, excluding post office giro institutions, as specified in Article 2(3) of that Directive.

This Regulation shall enter into force on 1 January 1999. It is binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States, in accordance with the Treaty. However, its application is subject to the provisions set out in Protocols 11 and 12, as well as Article 109k(1) of the Treaty. This ensures that while the Regulation has uniform effect across the Union, certain specific conditions or exceptions outlined in these Protocols and Article are respected.

The rules governing the performance of acts under legal instruments denominated in either a national currency unit or the euro unit are as follows:

1. Acts specified in legal instruments that require the use of or are denominated in a national currency unit must be performed in that national currency unit. Similarly, acts under instruments stipulating the use of or denominated in the euro unit must be performed in euros.

2. However, these provisions are subject to any agreements made between the parties involved, allowing flexibility if the parties decide otherwise.

3. Regardless of the above, if an amount is denominated in either the euro unit or the national currency unit of a participating Member State and is payable within that Member State by crediting the creditor’s account, the debtor may pay in either currency. The creditor’s account will be credited in the currency denomination of the account, with any necessary currency conversion carried out at the official conversion rates.

4. Participating Member States have the authority to take necessary measures to redenominate outstanding debt issued by their general government from the national currency unit to the euro unit. This applies to debt issued under their own law, including bonds, securitized debt, and money market instruments. Issuers may also redenominate such debt unless the contract explicitly excludes redenomination. Additionally, Member States may change the unit of account in their operating procedures from the national currency unit to the euro unit for markets and systems involved in the regular exchange, clearing, and settlement of securities, commodities, and payments.

5. Any other provisions that impose the use of the euro unit must be adopted by participating Member States in accordance with timelines established by Community legislation.

6. National legal provisions that allow or require netting, set-off, or similar techniques apply to monetary obligations regardless of whether they are denominated in the euro unit or a national currency unit. Currency conversions in such cases are made using the official conversion rates.

In summary, while the default rule is to perform acts in the currency specified by the legal instrument, parties may agree otherwise, and Member States have specific rights to redenominate debt and adjust operational currency units in line with the transition to the euro. Payment flexibility and legal provisions for netting and set-off also accommodate currency conversions at official rates.

Member States may maintain or introduce tolls and/or user charges on the trans-European road network (TEN-T) or parts thereof only under specific conditions outlined in paragraphs 2 to 12 of the relevant Directive. This framework respects the right of Member States, consistent with the Treaty, to apply tolls or user charges on roads outside the TEN-T, including parallel or competing roads, or on vehicle categories not defined as ‘vehicles’ on the TEN-T, provided such charges do not discriminate against international traffic or distort competition between operators.

When tolls or user charges are applied only to parts of the TEN-T, exemptions on other parts—due to factors like isolation, low congestion or pollution, or to facilitate new tolling arrangements—must not discriminate against international traffic. Member States may limit tolls/user charges to vehicles with a maximum permissible laden weight of 12 tonnes or more; if tolls are extended to lighter vehicles, the Directive’s provisions fully apply. From 2012 onwards, tolls/user charges should apply to all vehicles, though derogations are allowed if extending tolls to vehicles under 12 tonnes would significantly disrupt traffic flow, environment, noise, congestion, health, or if administrative costs exceed 30% of additional revenue.

Tolls and user charges cannot be imposed simultaneously on the same vehicle category for a single road section, but tolls may coexist with user charges levied for bridges, tunnels, or mountain passes. Charges must not discriminate based on haulier nationality, establishment country, vehicle registration, or transport origin/destination. Reduced rates or exemptions may be granted for vehicles exempt from recording equipment requirements or under specific conditions, with discount schemes capped at 13% of the toll paid by equivalent vehicles and subject to Commission approval.

Collection and payment of tolls/user charges must minimize traffic hindrance and avoid mandatory border checks, with payment facilities available 24/7 at major outlets and using common payment methods. Systems requiring on-board units must provide these units under reasonable terms. User charges, including administrative costs, must not exceed maximum rates set out in Annex II and should be proportional to infrastructure use duration. Tolls are based on recovering infrastructure costs, including construction, operation, maintenance, development, and possibly a market-based return on capital.

Member States may vary toll rates to address environmental damage, congestion, infrastructure wear, optimize infrastructure use, or promote road safety, provided variations are proportionate, transparent, non-discriminatory, not designed to generate extra revenue (with any unintended revenue balanced within two years), and respect maximum flexibility thresholds.

In determining the levels of weighted average tolls to be charged on a given infrastructure network or a clearly defined part thereof, Member States must consider the various costs outlined in Article 7(9). These costs should specifically relate to the network segment subject to tolling and the vehicles liable to pay the tolls. However, Member States retain the discretion to recover these costs fully, partially, or not at all through toll revenues.

Tolls must be set in accordance with Article 7 and the cost considerations described above. For new tolling schemes introduced after 10 June 2008, excluding concession tolls, Member States are required to calculate costs using a methodology based on the core calculation principles detailed in Annex III. In the case of new concession tolls established after this date, the maximum toll level must not exceed the amount that would result from applying the Annex III methodology. This equivalence is assessed over a suitably long reference period that reflects the nature of the concession contract. Tolling arrangements already in place as of 10 June 2008, or those for which tenders or negotiation responses were received before that date, are exempt from these requirements as long as they remain unchanged.

Member States must notify the European Commission at least four months before implementing new tolling arrangements. For non-concession tolls, this notification must include the unit values and parameters used in cost calculations, detailed information on the vehicles covered, the geographic scope of the tolled network or its part, and the percentage of costs intended to be recovered. For concession tolls, the notification must include the concession contracts or any significant amendments, as well as the base case underpinning the concession notice, which should detail estimated costs (per Article 7(9)), forecasted traffic by vehicle type, proposed toll levels, and the geographic extent of the concession network.

Additionally, Member States must inform the Commission at least four months in advance about new tolling arrangements on parallel roads that might divert traffic from the trans-European road network or compete directly with tolled sections of that network. This information should cover the geographic scope, vehicles affected, proposed toll levels, and the rationale behind the toll setting.

Upon receiving the required information, the Commission has four months to issue an opinion on whether the obligations have been met for tolling arrangements subject to the methodology requirements. For tolls on parallel roads, the Commission may also provide an opinion on proportionality, transparency, and potential impacts on competition within the internal market and the free movement of goods. The provision outlined in 7b clarifies that the Directive does not restrict the ability of Member States to implement tolls and/or user charges for infrastructure use. Specifically, Member States retain the freedom to introduce such systems as a means to ensure appropriate compensation for the costs associated with infrastructure provision and maintenance. This freedom is exercised without prejudice to Articles 87 and 88 of the Treaty, which govern state aid and competition rules within the European Union. Therefore, while Member States can charge users to recover infrastructure costs, they must do so in a manner consistent with the broader legal framework aimed at preventing distortions of competition and ensuring fair treatment across the internal market.

The Commission is tasked with promoting dialogue and the exchange of technical expertise among Member States to support the effective implementation of this Directive, with particular emphasis on Annex III. To ensure the Directive remains current and effective, the Commission will update and clarify Annexes 0, III, and IV to reflect technical advancements. Additionally, Annexes I and II will be revised to account for inflation. These updates and clarifications will be carried out following the procedure outlined in Article 9c(3).

The Commission shall be assisted by a Committee to facilitate its functions. In matters where reference is made to this paragraph, Articles 3 and 7 of Decision 1999/468/EC shall apply, taking into account the provisions of Article 8 of the same Decision. Additionally, when reference is made to this paragraph, Articles 5 and 7 of Decision 1999/468/EC shall also apply, with due regard to Article 8. Notably, the period specified in Article 5(6) of Decision 1999/468/EC is set at three months. Furthermore, the Committee is responsible for adopting its own rules of procedure to govern its operations.

For the purpose of this Regulation, several key definitions are established to clarify the scope and application of aid-related measures:

(a) **‘Aid’** refers to any measure that meets all the criteria set out in Article 92(1) of the Treaty.

(b) **‘Existing aid’** encompasses various categories of aid that were in place before or authorized under specific conditions:
   - (i) Aid schemes and individual aid that existed prior to the entry into force of the Treaty in the respective Member States and remain applicable thereafter, subject to certain provisions in the Acts of Accession for Austria, Finland, Sweden, and several Central and Eastern European countries.
   - (ii) Aid schemes and individual aid authorized by the Commission or the Council.
   - (iii) Aid deemed authorized under Article 4(6) of this Regulation or under prior procedures consistent with this Regulation.
   - (iv) Aid considered existing pursuant to Article 15.
   - (v) Aid that was not originally considered aid when put into effect but later became so due to developments in the common market, without changes made by the Member State. However, measures that become aid following the liberalization of an activity under Community law are not regarded as existing aid after the liberalization date.

(c) **‘New aid’** means all aid, including aid schemes and individual aid, that does not qualify as existing aid, including any modifications to existing aid.

(d) **‘Aid scheme’** is any act that allows, without further implementing measures, the awarding of individual aid to undertakings defined generally and abstractly within the act, or any act enabling aid not linked to a specific project to be granted to one or more undertakings for an indefinite period or amount.

(e) **‘Individual aid’** refers to aid not awarded on the basis of an aid scheme, as well as notifiable awards of aid under an aid scheme.

(f) **‘Unlawful aid’** is new aid implemented in violation of Article 93(3) of the Treaty.

(g) **‘Misuse of aid’** means aid used by the beneficiary contrary to a decision made under Article 4(3) or Article 7(3) or (4) of this Regulation.

(h) **‘Interested party’** includes any Member State or any person, undertaking, or association of undertakings whose interests may be affected by the granting of aid, notably the aid beneficiary, competing undertakings, and trade associations.

Article 10 addresses the procedures the Commission follows when it possesses information regarding alleged unlawful aid. Firstly, the Commission is obligated to examine such information promptly, regardless of its source. If the initial examination indicates the need for further details, the Commission may formally request additional information from the Member State concerned. In doing so, the provisions set out in Article 2(2) and Article 5(1) and (2) apply mutatis mutandis, ensuring consistency in the procedural framework. Should the Member State fail to provide the requested information within the prescribed timeframe, even after a reminder under Article 5(2), or if the information supplied is incomplete, the Commission will issue a formal decision known as an ‘information injunction.’ This decision explicitly states the information required and sets a deadline for its submission, thereby compelling the Member State to comply and facilitating the Commission’s investigation into the alleged unlawful aid.

The rights of interested parties in the context of Commission decisions and investigations are clearly defined to ensure transparency and participation. Firstly, any interested party has the right to submit comments following a Commission decision to initiate a formal investigation procedure, as stipulated in Article 6. Those who submit comments, as well as any beneficiaries of individual aid, must be provided with a copy of the Commission’s decision pursuant to Article 7. Secondly, interested parties may notify the Commission of any alleged unlawful aid or misuse of aid. If the Commission finds that the information provided is insufficient to form a view on the case, it must inform the interested party accordingly. Should the Commission make a decision related to the information supplied, a copy of that decision must be sent to the interested party. Lastly, any interested party has the right to request and obtain copies of decisions made under Articles 4 and 7, Article 10(3), and Article 11. These provisions collectively ensure that interested parties are kept informed and can actively participate in the oversight and enforcement of aid regulations.

Article 27 grants the Commission the authority to adopt implementing provisions related to various procedural and technical aspects necessary for the effective application of the regulation. Specifically, acting in accordance with the procedure established in Article 29, the Commission can determine the form, content, and other details of notifications and annual reports. Additionally, the Commission is empowered to specify details regarding time-limits, including how they are calculated, as well as to set the interest rate mentioned in Article 14(2). This delegation of power ensures that the practical and administrative elements of the regulation can be updated and clarified through implementing acts, facilitating consistent and efficient enforcement.

The Commission may close the formal investigation procedure by adopting one of several types of decisions, as outlined in the relevant legal provisions. First, if the Commission determines that the notified measure does not constitute state aid—potentially after modifications by the Member State concerned—it will record this finding through a decision. Second, if the Commission finds that any doubts regarding the compatibility of the notified aid with the common market have been resolved, again possibly following modifications, it will issue a positive decision confirming the aid’s compatibility and specifying the Treaty exception applied. Third, the Commission may issue a conditional decision, attaching conditions and obligations to ensure the aid remains compatible and compliance can be monitored. Fourth, if the Commission concludes that the notified aid is incompatible with the common market, it will adopt a negative decision prohibiting the aid from being put into effect.

Decisions under these categories are to be made as soon as doubts have been removed, with the Commission aiming to adopt a decision within 18 months from the opening of the investigation procedure. This period can be extended by mutual agreement with the Member State. If the 18-month period expires and the Member State requests a decision, the Commission must decide within two months based on the information available. Should the information be insufficient to establish compatibility, the Commission may issue a negative decision. This framework ensures clarity and timeliness in concluding formal investigations into state aid measures.

The Regulation establishes a Community-fleet capacity policy applicable to inland waterway vessels used for transporting goods between two or more points within Member States. This policy, effective from 29 April 1999 for a maximum of four years, governs the conditions under which new vessel capacities may be introduced.

**Scope and Application:**  
The Regulation applies to cargo-carrying vessels and pusher craft that provide transport services either on their own account or for hire, and which are either registered in a Member State or operated by an undertaking established in a Member State. An "undertaking" is defined broadly as any natural or legal person engaged in economic activity, whether industrial or non-industrial.

**Exemptions:**  
Certain vessels are exempt from the Regulation, including those operating solely on national waterways not connected to other Community waterways, vessels restricted by size to national waterways (captive vessels) that do not compete with regulated vessels, vessels operating exclusively on the Danube up to Kelheim, pusher craft with motive power under 300 kW, sea-going inland waterway vessels and ship-borne barges on voyages including sea crossings, vessels used only for storage at the same location, dredging equipment not used for goods carriage, ferries, and vessels providing non-profit public services. Additionally, Member States may exclude vessels under 450 tonnes deadweight tonnage from the Regulation’s scope, notifying the Commission accordingly.

Member States with inland waterways linked to others and fleets exceeding 100,000 tonnes must establish an Inland Waterways Fund, administered by competent authorities with involvement from national inland waterway carrier organizations. Each Fund includes a reserve fund with separate accounts for dry cargo carriers, tanker vessels, and pusher craft. The reserve is financed by surplus funds from previous structural improvement schemes, special contributions, and resources available during serious market disturbances. The Fund supports market stabilization measures and structural improvements at the Community level, with mutual financial support between Funds to ensure equal treatment of carriers.

The Regulation establishes that each Member State whose inland waterways connect with those of another Member State and whose fleet tonnage exceeds 100,000 tonnes—referred to as "the Member State concerned"—must establish an Inland Waterways Fund ("the Fund") under its national legislation and using its own administrative resources. The competent authorities of these Member States are responsible for administering the Fund, and they must involve national organizations representing inland waterway carriers in this administration.

Each Fund must maintain a reserve fund divided into three separate accounts for dry cargo carriers, tanker vessels, and pusher craft. This reserve fund is financed by surplus funds from structural improvement schemes up to 28 April 1999 (which consist solely of industry contributions), special contributions as outlined in Article 4, and financial resources available in case of serious market disturbances as per Article 7 of Directive 96/75/EC.

The reserve fund can be used for suitable measures related to market disturbances and improvement measures organized at the Community level, following procedures defined in the Regulation. Additionally, the reserve fund may be used for measures under Article 8 if unanimously requested by inland waterway transport organizations, provided these measures are actions at the Community level.

Mutual financial support between the Funds is mandated regarding the separate accounts, ensuring equal treatment for all carriers regardless of the Fund to which their vessel belongs. Until the new Fund is established, Member States continue to administer the Fund set up under the previous Regulation (EEC) No 1101/89.

Regarding vessel operations, the Regulation introduces an "old-for-new" rule: vessels covered by the Regulation, whether newly constructed, imported, or leaving specified waterways, may only be brought into service if the owner either scraps an equivalent tonnage without receiving a scrapping premium or pays a special contribution into the relevant Fund. The ratio between old and new tonnage is set by the Commission and is gradually reduced to zero by 29 April 2003, after which the rule becomes a standby mechanism, reactivated only during serious market disturbances.

Owners have the choice to pay the special contribution or scrap old tonnage either when ordering or importing the new vessel or when bringing it into service, with specific conditions on timing and documentation. Certain vessels withdrawn from the market for non-commercial purposes may count as compensatory tonnage if permitted by the Member State and communicated to the Commission.
