The procedure for committee involvement in implementing measures under this Directive is outlined as follows:

1. The Commission is supported by the European Securities Committee, established under Article 1 of Decision 2001/528/EC.

2. When reference is made to this paragraph, the procedural rules set out in Articles 5 and 7 of Decision 1999/468/EC apply, taking into account the provisions of Article 8 of the same Decision. However, any implementing measures adopted under this procedure must not alter the essential provisions of the Directive. Additionally, the time period specified in Article 5(6) of Decision 1999/468/EC is fixed at three months.

2a. In cases where this paragraph is referenced, Articles 5a(1) to (4) and Article 7 of Decision 1999/468/EC also apply, again considering the provisions of Article 8.

3. The Commission is required to conduct a review of the provisions related to its implementing powers by 31 December 2010 and subsequently at least every three years. This review involves presenting a report to both the European Parliament and the Council on how these powers are functioning. The report must specifically assess whether amendments to the Directive are necessary to ensure that the scope of the Commission’s implementing powers remains appropriate. Any conclusion regarding the need for amendments must be supported by a detailed explanation. If amendments are deemed necessary, the report should be accompanied by a legislative proposal to modify the provisions granting implementing powers to the Commission.

This Regulation sets out harmonised measures aimed at the intra-Community control and monitoring of specific substances that are commonly used in the illicit manufacture of narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances. Its primary objective is to prevent the diversion of these substances from legitimate channels to illegal drug production. By establishing uniform rules across Member States, the Regulation seeks to enhance cooperation and ensure effective tracking and oversight of these precursor chemicals throughout the internal market, thereby contributing to the fight against drug trafficking and related criminal activities.

According to the regulation, each year the competent authorities in every Member State are required to provide the Commission with comprehensive information regarding the implementation of monitoring measures related to trade in both scheduled and non-scheduled substances. This communication is particularly focused on substances that are commonly used in the illicit manufacture of narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances, as well as on the methods employed for diversion and illegal production. The purpose of this annual reporting is to allow for any necessary adjustments to the monitoring arrangements to enhance their effectiveness. Subsequently, the Commission compiles a summary of all such communications and submits it to the International Narcotics Control Board. This submission is carried out in accordance with Article 12(12) of the United Nations Convention and is done in consultation with the Member States, ensuring coordinated international oversight and control.

The procedure involving the Committee is established as follows:

1. The Commission is to be assisted by the Committee established under Article 30 of Council Regulation (EC) No 111/2005. This Committee plays a consultative role in the implementation of the relevant measures.

2. When reference is made to this paragraph, the procedural rules set out in Articles 4 and 7 of Decision 1999/468/EC apply, with due consideration to the provisions of Article 8 of the same Decision. Notably, the time limit specified in Article 4(3) of Decision 1999/468/EC is extended to three months for the purposes of this procedure.

3. Additionally, when this paragraph is invoked, Articles 5a(1) to (4) and Article 7 of Decision 1999/468/EC are applicable, again taking into account the stipulations of Article 8. These provisions govern the detailed steps and conditions under which the Committee operates in assisting the Commission.

The customer declaration requirements for the supply of scheduled substances under the relevant regulations are as follows:

1. Any operator established within the Community who supplies a customer with a scheduled substance classified under category 1 or 2 of Annex I must obtain a declaration from the customer specifying the exact use or uses of the scheduled substance. This declaration must be provided separately for each scheduled substance and must follow the model outlined in point 1 of Annex III. For legal entities, the declaration must be made on official headed notepaper.

2. Instead of obtaining a declaration for each individual transaction, an operator who regularly supplies a customer with a category 2 scheduled substance may accept a single declaration covering multiple transactions over a period not exceeding one year. This is allowed only if the operator is confident that: (a) the customer has been supplied with the substance at least three times in the previous 12 months; (b) there is no reason to suspect the substance will be used illicitly; and (c) the quantities ordered align with the customer’s usual consumption. This declaration must conform to the model in point 2 of Annex III and, for legal persons, be on headed notepaper.

3. For scheduled substances of category 1, the operator must stamp and date a copy of the customer’s declaration, certifying it as a true copy of the original. This certified copy must always accompany category 1 substances during transport within the Community and must be presented upon request to authorities responsible for vehicle content inspections during transport operations.

To promote effective cooperation among competent authorities, operators, and the chemical industry—especially concerning non-scheduled substances—the Commission is tasked with developing and regularly updating guidelines. These guidelines, prepared following the procedure outlined in Article 15(2), are designed to assist the chemical industry in managing relevant issues. Specifically, the guidelines will include: (a) clear instructions on how to identify and report suspicious transactions; (b) a frequently updated list of non-scheduled substances to help the industry voluntarily monitor trade activities involving these substances; and (c) any additional information considered useful to support these objectives. Furthermore, competent authorities are responsible for ensuring that both the guidelines and the list of non-scheduled substances are disseminated regularly and through channels they deem appropriate, aligning with the overall goals of the guidelines.

The regulation establishes a comprehensive framework for the role and functioning of immigration liaison officers (ILOs) posted by Member States to third countries or international organizations. Each Member State is required to ensure that its ILOs maintain direct contacts with competent authorities and relevant organizations in the host country to facilitate and expedite the collection and exchange of information related to illegal immigration.

ILOs are tasked with gathering information at both operational and strategic levels on various critical issues, including the flows and routes of illegal immigrants, their methods of operation (such as transport means and involvement of intermediaries), activities of criminal organizations involved in smuggling, incidents that may affect immigration flows, methods of document forgery, and ways to assist host countries in preventing illegal immigration and facilitating the return of illegal immigrants. They also collect information on relevant legislation and legal practices, as well as data transmitted through early warning systems.

Furthermore, ILOs have the authority to assist in identifying third-country nationals and facilitating their return to their countries of origin. Their activities must comply with national laws, including data protection provisions, and any agreements with host countries or international organizations.

Member States must promptly inform each other, the Council, and the Commission about the secondment of ILOs, including their duties, and notify intentions regarding secondments to third countries to enable cooperative agreements. ILOs posted in the same countries or regions are to form local or regional cooperation networks to regularly meet, exchange information and experiences, coordinate positions, attend joint training, organize information sessions for diplomatic staff, adopt common approaches to information collection and reporting, contribute to biannual activity reports, and establish contacts with similar networks in host and neighboring countries.

The European Commission representatives may participate in these network meetings, and the Member State holding the Council Presidency is responsible for initiating such meetings. Member States may also agree bilaterally or multilaterally for ILOs to represent the interests of multiple Member States or share tasks.

By the end of each semester, the Presidency or acting Presidency Member State must prepare reports on the activities of ILO networks and the situation in host countries concerning illegal immigration. These reports, following a Commission-established format, inform evaluations and annual reports on common policies addressing illegal immigration, smuggling, trafficking, border control, and return procedures. The Commission may propose recommendations based on these evaluations.

The regulation establishes a comprehensive framework for the deployment and cooperation of immigration liaison officers among EU Member States. According to Article 3, Member States are required to promptly and systematically inform each other, as well as the Council and the European Commission, about the secondment of immigration liaison officers, including detailed descriptions of their duties. The Commission compiles this information and shares it with the Council and Member States. Furthermore, Member States must notify others of their plans to second officers to third countries, enabling interested Member States to pursue cooperative agreements regarding such secondments, as outlined in Article 5.

Article 4 emphasizes the importance of creating local or regional cooperation networks among immigration liaison officers posted to the same third countries or regions. These networks are tasked with regular meetings, information exchange, coordination of positions in dealings with commercial carriers, joint training, and organizing sessions for diplomatic and consular staff. They are also responsible for adopting common methods for collecting and reporting strategically relevant information, contributing to biannual activity reports, and establishing contacts with similar networks in host and neighboring countries. The European Commission representatives may participate in these meetings, although meetings can proceed without them if operational needs dictate. The Member State holding the Council Presidency, or the acting Presidency if unrepresented locally, is responsible for initiating these meetings.

Article 5 allows Member States to enter bilateral or multilateral agreements whereby immigration liaison officers posted by one Member State may also represent the interests of others or share specific tasks among themselves, enhancing cooperation and resource efficiency.

Under Article 6, the Member State holding the Council Presidency or the acting Presidency must prepare a biannual report on the activities of immigration liaison officer networks and the situation in the host country concerning illegal immigration. These reports follow a Commission-established format and serve as a basis for an evaluation report at the end of each Presidency, which the Commission drafts and submits to the Council. The Commission also incorporates a factual summary of these reports into its annual report on common policies addressing illegal immigration, smuggling, trafficking, border control, and return of illegal residents, and may propose recommendations to the Council.

The regulation respects existing consular cooperation provisions as stated in Article 7 and came into force on 5 January 2004, binding all Member States directly under the Treaty establishing the European Community (Article 8). This framework ensures coordinated, transparent, and effective collaboration among Member States in managing immigration liaison officers abroad, thereby strengthening the EU’s collective response to illegal immigration and related challenges.

According to the regulation, the Member State holding the Presidency of the Council of the European Union, or if that Member State is not represented in a given country or region, the Member State serving as acting Presidency, is required to prepare a report by the end of each semester. This report must cover the activities of immigration liaison officers' networks in which it has representation, as well as the situation in the host country concerning illegal immigration. These reports are to be submitted to both the Council and the Commission.

The reports must follow a model and format established by the Commission to ensure consistency and comparability. They serve as a crucial source of information for the preparation of an evaluation report at the end of each Presidency. This evaluation report, drafted by the Commission and submitted to the Council, assesses the situation in every third country where Member States' immigration liaison officers are posted.

Furthermore, the Commission uses these reports to include a factual summary in its annual report on the development of a common policy addressing illegal immigration, smuggling and trafficking of human beings, external border management, and the return of illegal residents. When presenting its evaluation to the Council, the Commission may also propose recommendations or measures it considers appropriate.

This regulatory framework ensures systematic monitoring and evaluation of immigration liaison officers' activities and the broader context of illegal immigration, facilitating coordinated EU action and policy development. The regulation entered into force on 5 January 2004 and is binding and directly applicable in all Member States.

The Regulation referenced clarifies that it does not affect the provisions related to consular cooperation at the local level, as outlined in the Common Consular Instructions on visas applicable to diplomatic missions and consular posts. According to Article 8, this Regulation came into force on 5 January 2004 and is binding in its entirety, being directly applicable in all Member States pursuant to the Treaty establishing the European Community. The Regulation was adopted in Brussels on 19 February 2004, under the authority of the Council President, M. McDowell. The document also includes references to various Official Journal publications that provide further legal context and related legislative acts.

The Regulation in question is set to enter into force on 5 January 2004. It is established that this Regulation shall be binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States, in accordance with the Treaty establishing the European Community. The formal adoption of this Regulation took place in Brussels on 19 February 2004.

Article 13 outlines the acceptable methods for serving the document instituting proceedings, or an equivalent document, on the debtor, ensuring proof of receipt. Service may be effected by:

(a) Personal service accompanied by an acknowledgement of receipt signed by the debtor, which includes the date of receipt.

(b) Personal service confirmed by a document signed by the competent person who carried out the service, stating that the debtor has either received the document or refused to receive it without legal justification, along with the date of service.

(c) Postal service, evidenced by an acknowledgement of receipt signed and returned by the debtor, including the date of receipt.

(d) Electronic service, such as by fax or e-mail, supported by an acknowledgement of receipt signed and returned by the debtor, including the date of receipt.

Furthermore, any summons to a court hearing may be served on the debtor either in accordance with the methods described above or orally during a previous court hearing on the same claim, with such oral service recorded in the minutes of that hearing. This ensures that the debtor has been properly informed of the proceedings with verifiable proof of receipt.

Article 19 sets out the minimum standards for granting a review of a judgment certified as a European Enforcement Order in exceptional cases. According to this provision, beyond the general rules established in Articles 13 to 18, a debtor has the right to request a review of the judgment under the law of the Member State of origin only if certain conditions are met.

Firstly, the debtor must have been served with the document instituting the proceedings (or an equivalent document) or, where applicable, the summons to a court hearing by one of the methods specified in Article 14. However, the service must have been effected so late that the debtor did not have sufficient time to prepare a defense, and this delay must not be attributable to any fault on the debtor’s part.

Secondly, the debtor may also seek a review if they were prevented from objecting to the claim due to force majeure or other extraordinary circumstances, again without any fault on their part. In such cases, the debtor must act promptly to exercise this right.

Importantly, Article 19 clarifies that these conditions represent minimum standards. Member States retain the discretion to allow access to a review of the judgment under more favorable or generous conditions than those outlined in paragraph 1. This ensures a degree of flexibility in protecting the rights of debtors across different jurisdictions within the European Union.

Article 21 addresses the refusal of enforcement of a judgment certified as a European Enforcement Order (EEO). According to this provision, enforcement must be refused by the competent court in the Member State where enforcement is sought if the debtor applies for such refusal and the judgment is found to be irreconcilable with an earlier judgment issued either in another Member State or in a third country. This refusal applies only if three conditions are met: (a) the earlier judgment concerns the same cause of action and involves the same parties; (b) the earlier judgment was rendered in the Member State where enforcement is requested or meets the criteria for recognition in that Member State; and (c) the irreconcilability between the two judgments was not, and could not have been, raised as an objection during the original court proceedings in the Member State of origin. Importantly, Article 21(2) clarifies that the substance of the judgment or its certification as an EEO cannot be reviewed by the court in the Member State of enforcement, ensuring that only procedural or formal grounds, such as irreconcilability with an earlier judgment, can justify refusal of enforcement.

This Regulation shall enter into force on 21 January 2005. It will apply from 21 October 2005, except for Articles 30, 31, and 32, which shall apply from 21 January 2005. The Regulation is binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States in accordance with the Treaty establishing the European Community.

For the purposes of this Regulation, the following definitions shall apply:

1. **‘Judgment’**: Any judgment given by a court or tribunal of a Member State, regardless of its title, including a decree, order, decision, or writ of execution, as well as the determination of costs or expenses by an officer of the court.

2. **‘Claim’**: A claim for payment of a specific sum of money that has fallen due or for which the due date is indicated in the judgment, court settlement, or authentic instrument.

3. **‘Authentic instrument’**:  
   (a) A document which has been formally drawn up or registered as an authentic instrument, and the authenticity of which:  
   (i) relates to the signature and the content of the instrument; and  
   (ii) has been established by a public authority or other authority empowered for that purpose by the Member State in which it originates; or  
   (b) An arrangement relating to maintenance obligations concluded with administrative authorities or authenticated by them.

4. **‘Member State of origin’**: The Member State in which the judgment has been given, the court settlement has been approved or concluded, or the authentic instrument has been drawn up or registered, and is to be certified as a European Enforcement Order.

The use of acoustic deterrent devices under Article 2(1) must adhere to the technical specifications and conditions of use outlined in Annex II. However, Member States may, as an exception, permit the temporary use of devices that do not meet these specifications if there is sufficient documented evidence demonstrating their effectiveness in reducing incidental catches of cetaceans. Such authorisations are limited to a maximum duration of two years. Furthermore, Member States are required to notify the Commission of any authorisations granted under this derogation within two months of issuance, providing detailed technical and scientific information about the device and its impact on cetacean bycatch.

According to the provisions outlined, the Commission is required to submit an overall assessment and review of the operation of the Regulation within one year after Member States have submitted their second annual report. This assessment is based on the information gathered through the application of Article 6 and the evaluation conducted by the Scientific, Technical and Economic Committee for Fisheries on the reports provided by the Member States. The Commission’s report must specifically address how the Regulation has been applied across different types of vessels and geographic areas, evaluate the quality of data obtained from observer schemes, and assess the effectiveness of pilot projects implemented under the Regulation. Furthermore, the report may include relevant proposals to improve the Regulation’s implementation. An updated version of this report is to be prepared following the submission of the fourth annual report by Member States, ensuring ongoing review and refinement of the Regulation based on the latest available data and assessments.

According to the provisions outlined, adaptation to technical progress and the provision of additional technical guidance are governed by specific procedures under Regulation (EC) No 2371/2002. Firstly, operational and technical guidance related to the tasks of observers, as specified in Article 6, along with detailed rules concerning reporting requirements also set out in Article 6, shall be adopted following the management procedure established in Article 30(2) of the Regulation. Secondly, any amendments to Annex II that are necessary to align it with technical and scientific progress must be adopted in accordance with the regulatory procedure described in Article 30(3) of the same Regulation. These measures ensure that technical guidance and regulatory frameworks remain up-to-date and effective in response to evolving scientific and technical developments.

The Centre is committed to proactive communication regarding its activities within its mission areas. Before making any communications, it provides prior information to the Member States and the Commission to ensure transparency and coordination. Its goal is to deliver objective, reliable, and easily accessible information promptly to the public and all interested parties about the outcomes of its work. To facilitate this, the Centre makes information available to the general public, including through a dedicated website, and publishes its opinions as outlined in Article 6.

Furthermore, the Centre works closely with the Member States and the Commission to ensure coherence in risk communication related to health threats. This collaboration helps maintain consistent messaging and effective dissemination of information. Additionally, the Centre cooperates as appropriate with competent bodies within the Member States and other stakeholders to support public information campaigns, thereby enhancing the reach and impact of its communications.

The Management Board is composed of one member designated by each Member State, two members designated by the European Parliament, and three members representing and appointed by the Commission. Members are appointed to ensure the highest standards of competence and a broad range of relevant expertise, with alternates appointed by the same procedure to represent members in their absence. Each member serves a four-year term, which can be extended.

The Board is responsible for adopting the Centre’s internal rules based on proposals from the director, and these rules are made public. It elects a Chair from among its members for a renewable two-year term. The Board meets at least twice a year, either at the Chair’s invitation or upon request by at least one-third of its members, and it adopts its own Rules of Procedure.

Key responsibilities of the Management Board include exercising disciplinary authority over the director, including appointment and dismissal; ensuring the Centre fulfills its mission and tasks as set out in the Regulation, supported by independent external evaluations every five years; compiling and publishing a list of competent bodies; adopting the Centre’s annual and multiannual work programmes aligned with Community legislative and policy priorities; and adopting the general report on the Centre’s activities each year by 30 March.

Financially, the Board adopts the Centre’s financial rules after consulting the Commission, adhering to the relevant EU financial regulations unless specific exceptions are approved by the Commission. The Board also unanimously determines the rules governing the Centre’s languages, balancing internal operations and external communication to ensure broad access and participation.

The director participates in Board meetings without voting rights and provides the secretariat for the Board.

For the purposes of this Regulation, the following definitions apply:

(a) **‘Competent body’** refers to any structure, institute, agent, or other scientific entity recognized by the authorities of Member States as providing independent scientific and technical advice or capacity for action in the field of the prevention and control of human disease.

(b) **‘Prevention and control of human disease’** means the range of measures undertaken by competent public health authorities within Member States aimed at preventing and halting the spread of disease.

(c) **‘Dedicated surveillance network’** denotes any specific network focused on diseases or particular health issues, selected for epidemiological surveillance, and involving accredited structures and authorities of the Member States.

(d) **‘Communicable diseases’** are the categories of diseases listed in the Annex to Decision No 2119/98/EC.

(e) **‘Health threat’** signifies any condition, agent, or incident that may cause ill health, either directly or indirectly.

(f) **‘Epidemiological surveillance’** carries the meaning ascribed to it in Decision No 2119/98/EC.

(g) **‘Community network’** also holds the meaning ascribed to it in Decision No 2119/98/EC.

(h) **‘Early warning and response system’** means the network established in accordance with Decision No 2119/98/EC for the prevention and control of communicable diseases. This system is formed by maintaining permanent communication between the Commission and the competent public health authorities in each Member State through appropriate means specified in Commission Decision 2000/57/EC of 22 December 1999.

Article 185 of the Financial Regulation governs the application of financial rules related to the discharge of the Centre’s budget, as well as its audits and accounting procedures. Specifically, this article ensures that all financial activities carried out by the Centre comply with established standards for budget execution, transparency, and accountability. It mandates that the Centre’s budget must be managed in accordance with the principles and procedures set forth in the Financial Regulation, including proper recording of transactions, adherence to approved appropriations, and timely reporting. Furthermore, Article 185 requires that audits be conducted to verify the accuracy and legality of the Centre’s financial operations, thereby safeguarding public funds and promoting sound financial management. In summary, the application of Article 185 ensures that the Centre’s budget discharge, audits, and accounting rules are consistently aligned with the overarching financial governance framework.

The Centre plays a crucial role in providing scientific and technical assistance and training to Member States, the Commission, and other Community agencies. It offers expertise in developing, regularly reviewing, and updating preparedness plans, as well as in formulating intervention strategies within its mission areas. Upon request from the Commission, Member States, third countries, or international organizations—especially the WHO—the Centre may deliver scientific or technical support grounded in evidence-based science and technology. This assistance can include helping to develop technical guidelines on best practices and protective measures against human health threats, offering expert advice, and mobilizing and coordinating investigation teams. All responses are provided within the Centre’s financial capacity and mandate.

Requests for assistance must include an agreed deadline, ensuring timely and coordinated responses. If the Centre’s financial resources are insufficient to address a request, it will evaluate the situation and seek alternative solutions, potentially involving other Community mechanisms. The Centre is also responsible for promptly informing Member States and the Commission about any such requests and its intended actions, maintaining transparency within the Community network established by Decision No 2119/98/EC.

Furthermore, the Centre supports and coordinates training programs aimed at equipping Member States and the Commission with adequately trained specialists, particularly in epidemiological surveillance and field investigations. This training ensures that there is sufficient capacity to define and implement effective health measures to control disease outbreaks, thereby strengthening overall public health preparedness and response capabilities.

Back data relating to the first quarter of 2000 onwards must be transmitted by 31 December 2004. In cases where exact data is unavailable, it is acceptable to provide the information using a best-estimate approach to ensure timely and reasonable reporting. This allows for the inclusion of historical data while accommodating any gaps or uncertainties in the records.

The prohibitions outlined in Article 2 do not apply in certain specific circumstances as detailed below:

(a) Technical assistance, financing, and financial assistance related to arms and related materiel are permitted when intended solely to support the United Nations Operation in Côte d’Ivoire (UNOCI) and the French forces supporting it.

(b) Technical assistance related to non-lethal military equipment intended exclusively for humanitarian or protective use is allowed, including equipment for EU, UN, African Union, and ECOWAS crisis management operations, provided such activities have prior approval from the Sanctions Committee.

(c) Financing or financial assistance related to non-lethal military equipment intended solely for humanitarian or protective use, including for EU, UN, African Union, and ECOWAS crisis management operations, is also exempted.

(d) Technical assistance related to arms and related materiel intended solely to support or be used in restructuring defense and security forces under paragraph 3(f) of the Linas-Marcoussis Agreement is permitted, subject to prior approval by the Sanctions Committee.

(e) Financing or financial assistance related to arms and related materiel for the restructuring of defense and security forces as per the Linas-Marcoussis Agreement is similarly allowed.

(f) Temporary sales, supplies, or exports of arms and related materiel to forces of a State acting in accordance with international law to facilitate the evacuation of its nationals or those under its consular responsibility in Côte d’Ivoire are permitted, provided these activities are notified in advance to the Sanctions Committee.

All authorizations for these activities, including those requiring Sanctions Committee approval or notification, must be obtained through the competent authority of the Member State where the service provider is established or the exporting Member State, as listed in Annex II. Importantly, no authorizations will be granted retroactively for activities that have already occurred.

This Regulation shall apply in several specific contexts to ensure comprehensive coverage within and related to the Community. Firstly, it applies within the territory of the Community, including its airspace, thereby covering all activities and entities operating on land and in the skies under Community jurisdiction. Secondly, the Regulation extends to any aircraft or vessel under the jurisdiction of a Member State, regardless of their location, ensuring that these modes of transport comply with the established rules. Thirdly, it applies to any person who is a national of a Member State, whether they are inside or outside the territory of the Community, thus maintaining regulatory reach over its citizens globally. Additionally, the Regulation covers any legal person, entity, or body incorporated or constituted under the law of a Member State, ensuring that organizations formed under Member State laws are subject to its provisions. Finally, it applies to any legal person, entity, or body conducting business within the Community, thereby encompassing foreign entities operating within the Community’s market. Together, these provisions establish a broad and effective scope for the Regulation’s application.

The procedure for the Balance of Payments Committee (the Committee) is established to assist the Commission in its functions. According to the rules, the Committee operates under the framework set out in Decision 1999/468/EC. Specifically, Articles 5 and 7 of that Decision apply to the Committee’s procedures, with consideration given to the provisions of Article 8. The time limit for the examination period under Article 5(6) is extended to three months. Additionally, when relevant, Articles 5a(1) to (4) and Article 7 of Decision 1999/468/EC also govern the Committee’s operations, again taking into account Article 8. Furthermore, the European Central Bank (ECB) is permitted to attend the Committee’s meetings in the capacity of an observer, allowing it to participate without voting rights. This structure ensures that the Committee functions within a clear legal framework while facilitating cooperation between the Commission and the ECB.

Member States are required to submit data on balance of payments, international trade in services, and foreign direct investment to the Commission (Eurostat) as specified in Annex I. The data must conform to the definitions provided in Annex II. Additionally, the submission of this data must adhere to the deadlines outlined in Annex I to ensure timely and consistent reporting.

The quality of data transmitted by Member States is governed by specific criteria and reporting obligations to ensure consistency and reliability. Firstly, Member States are required to take all reasonable measures they deem necessary to guarantee that the data they transmit meets common quality standards. These standards are established by the Commission, which also defines the content and frequency of the quality reports that Member States must submit. These quality reports provide detailed information on the quality of the transmitted data.

The Commission, with the support of the Balance of Payments Committee, evaluates the quality of the data based on these reports. This evaluation is then communicated to the European Parliament for informational purposes. Additionally, any significant methodological or other changes that could affect the data must be reported by Member States to the Commission within three months of their implementation. The Commission, in turn, informs the European Parliament and other Member States about such changes. The procedures for updating the common quality standards and reporting requirements follow a regulatory process with scrutiny, ensuring that amendments are carefully considered and implemented.

The statistics to be produced shall be organized and transmitted to the Commission (Eurostat) according to five distinct data flows. These data flows include: (a) balance of payments euro indicators, which provide key summary measures of a country’s external economic transactions; (b) balance of payments quarterly statistics, offering detailed quarterly data on cross-border economic activities; (c) international trade in services, covering the exchange of services between residents and non-residents; (d) foreign direct investment (FDI) flows, reflecting the movement of investment capital across borders within a given period; and (e) FDI positions, representing the stock of foreign direct investment held at a specific point in time. The precise definitions, formats, and requirements for these data flows are further detailed in Annex I, ensuring standardized and consistent reporting to Eurostat.

According to the regulation, the Commission, through Eurostat, is responsible for disseminating the Community statistics produced under its provisions. This dissemination must occur with a frequency that aligns closely with the periodicity outlined in Annex I of the regulation. By adhering to this schedule, Eurostat ensures that statistical data is made available to stakeholders in a timely and consistent manner, supporting transparency and informed decision-making within the Community.

Member States are required to transmit quarterly non-financial accounts by institutional sector to the Commission, as detailed in the Annex, with the exception of items P.1, P.2, D.42, D.43, D.44, D.45, and B.4G in the initial phase. The Commission will establish a timetable for the transmission of these excluded items and may decide to require a breakdown of the transactions by counterpart sector. Such decisions, which amend non-essential elements of the Regulation, will be adopted following the regulatory procedure with scrutiny outlined in Article 8(3), and only after the Commission has reported to the European Parliament and the Council on the Regulation’s implementation pursuant to Article 9.

The quarterly data specified must be submitted to the Commission no later than 90 calendar days after the end of the relevant quarter. However, during a transitional period of three years from the Regulation’s entry into force, this deadline is extended to 95 calendar days. Any revisions to data from previous quarters must be transmitted simultaneously. The Commission holds the authority to adjust the transmission deadline by up to five days, following the regulatory procedure with scrutiny.

The first transmission of quarterly data pertains to the third quarter of 2005 and must be delivered by 3 January 2006. This initial submission must also include back data covering the periods from the first quarter of 1999.

Article 11 of the Regulation sets out the notification and consultation requirements for Member State authorities regarding decisions on authorisation applications. Firstly, authorities listed in Annex I must notify all other Member State authorities and the Commission, also listed in that Annex, whenever they dismiss an application for authorisation or annul a previously granted authorisation. This notification must occur within 30 days of the decision date.

Secondly, if a competent authority receives a new application involving an essentially identical import, export, or supply of technical assistance transaction to one that was dismissed by another authority within the past three years, it is required to consult that authority before granting authorisation. 

Thirdly, if after such consultation the competent authority decides to grant the authorisation, it must immediately inform all authorities listed in Annex I of its decision, providing reasons and any supporting information.

Finally, a refusal to grant authorisation based solely on a national prohibition under Article 7(1) does not count as a dismissal of an application for the purposes of the notification requirement in paragraph 1.

This Regulation applies specifically to certain defined territories. Firstly, it covers the customs territory of the Community as outlined in Regulation (EEC) No 2913/92. In addition to this, the Regulation extends to include the Spanish territories of Ceuta and Melilla, as well as the German territory of Helgoland. For the purposes of this Regulation, Ceuta, Helgoland, and Melilla are to be regarded as integral parts of the customs territory of the Community, ensuring that the rules and provisions set forth apply uniformly across these areas.

The export of goods that serve no practical purpose other than for capital punishment or for torture and other cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment, as specified in Annex II, is strictly prohibited regardless of the origin of the equipment. Additionally, providing technical assistance related to these goods, whether paid or unpaid, from within the customs territory of the Community to any person, entity, or body in a third country is also forbidden. However, an exception to this prohibition exists: the competent authority may grant authorization for the export of such goods and the supply of related technical assistance if it can be clearly demonstrated that the goods will be used exclusively for public display in a museum, highlighting their historical significance.

The import of goods listed in Annex II is strictly prohibited regardless of their origin. This prohibition extends not only to the physical importation of such goods but also to the acceptance of any related technical assistance supplied from third countries, whether paid or unpaid, by any person, entity, or body within the customs territory of the Community. However, an exception to this rule exists: the competent authority may grant authorization for the import of these goods and the provision of related technical assistance if it is clearly demonstrated that the goods will be used exclusively for public display in a museum within the Member State of destination, highlighting their historic significance.

When granting export authorisations for goods listed in Annex III, the competent authority must evaluate each application individually, considering all relevant factors. A key criterion is whether a similar application has been rejected by another Member State within the past three years. Importantly, authorisations must be denied if there are reasonable grounds to believe that the exported goods could be used for torture or other cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment, including judicial corporal punishment, by law enforcement or any other entity in a third country. In making this determination, the authority should consider international court judgments, findings from UN bodies, the Council of Europe, and the EU, as well as reports from the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and the UN Special Rapporteur on Torture. Additionally, national court rulings, civil society reports, and information about export restrictions imposed by the destination country may also inform the decision. This comprehensive approach ensures that export authorisations are granted responsibly and in line with human rights considerations.

According to the regulations on reaching required catch percentages, any quantities of living aquatic resources caught in excess of the permitted percentages specified in Annexes II and III must not be landed. Instead, these excess catches are to be returned to the sea prior to each landing. However, there is an important exception: if during a fishing voyage a vessel departs from any of the groups of subdivisions listed in Annexes II and III, the vessel must ensure that the minimum percentage of target species, as defined in those annexes for that geographical area, is met and retained on board within two hours of leaving the area. This rule ensures compliance with catch composition requirements while allowing some operational flexibility during fishing trips.

The conditions for the use of fishing gear are clearly defined to ensure compliance with geographical and temporal restrictions, as well as to regulate the readiness of gear on board vessels. 

1. **Stowage of Prohibited Gear:** Any fishing gear that is not allowed to be used within a certain geographical area or during a specific period must be stowed in a way that it is not ready for use in the prohibited area or during the prohibited time. Additionally, reserve gear must be stored separately and also in a manner that it is not ready for immediate use.

2. **Definition of Gear Not Ready for Use:** Fishing gear is considered not ready for use under the following conditions:
   - For trawls, Danish seines, and similar gears (except pair trawl):
     - The trawl boards must be secured to the inner or outer side of the bulwark or the gallows.
     - Sweep lines or warps must be unshackled from the trawl boards or weights.
   - For pair trawl:
     - The wing tip weights must be unshackled and stowed away.
   - For lines, gillnets, entangling nets, and trammel nets:
     - Nets must be stowed under a lashed cover.
     - Lines and hooks must be kept in closed boxes.
   - For purse seines:
     - The main or bottom wire must be unshackled from the seine.

3. **Restriction When Targeting Cod:** As an exception to the general rule on stowage, if any gear is used for which cod (Gadus morhua) is defined as a target species according to Annexes II or III, no other type of gear shall be kept on board the vessel.

These conditions ensure that fishing activities are conducted responsibly, preventing unauthorized use of gear and supporting sustainable fishing practices.

According to the regulations, a fish is considered undersized if its length is less than the minimum size specified for its species and geographical area as outlined in Annex IV. To determine the size of a fish accurately, the measurement must be taken from the tip of the snout, with the mouth closed, straight to the extreme end of the tail fin. This standardized method ensures consistent assessment of fish sizes in compliance with the specified minimum size limits.

According to the regulations on retention of undersized fish, undersized fish must not be retained on board, transhipped, landed, transported, stored, sold, displayed, or offered for sale. Instead, they must be returned immediately to the sea. However, there is an exception for fish other than those listed as target species in Annex II for mesh size categories ‘smaller than 16 mm’ or ‘16 to 31 mm’ when caught using trawls, Danish seines, or similar gears with mesh sizes less than 32 mm, or with purse seines. In these cases, the prohibition on retention does not apply, provided that the undersized fish are not sorted and are not sold, displayed, or offered for sale for human consumption.

The regulation establishes specific requirements regarding target species and minimum mesh sizes for fishing activities within the subdivisions listed in Annex I. Firstly, the permissible ranges of mesh sizes for each target species are defined in Annex II for fishing with trawls, Danish seines, and similar gears, and in Annex III for fishing with gillnets, entangling nets, and trammel nets. It is mandatory that no part of the fishing gear or nets have a mesh size smaller than the minimum mesh size specified within these ranges.

Furthermore, the minimum percentage of the target species among the living aquatic resources retained on board is also specified for each geographic subdivision and mesh size range in Annex II and Annex III. This ensures that the catch composition aligns with sustainable fishing practices.

When dredges are carried on board during any fishing voyage, retention and landing of any living aquatic resources are prohibited unless at least 85% of the live weight consists of molluscs and/or Furcellaria lumbricalis, emphasizing the protection of non-target species.

The use of gillnets or entangling nets with mesh sizes smaller than those specified in Annex III is prohibited within any subdivision. Similarly, the use of trammel nets is regulated such that the largest mesh sizes must correspond to categories in Annex III unless the smallest mesh size is less than 16 mm. In cases where the smallest mesh size is below 16 mm, all larger meshes must comply with the categories set out in Annex III.

Finally, landings are prohibited for any fishing voyage if the catch retained on board from the subdivisions listed in Annex I does not comply with the mesh size and species composition conditions established in Annex II or Annex III. This comprehensive framework ensures that fishing practices are regulated to protect target species and maintain sustainable fisheries.

The audit report must contain several key elements to ensure clarity and compliance with statutory requirements. Firstly, it should include an introduction that identifies the financial statements subject to the statutory audit and specifies the financial reporting framework applied in their preparation. Secondly, the report must describe the scope of the statutory audit, at a minimum identifying the auditing standards followed during the audit process.

Central to the audit report is the audit opinion, which can be unqualified, qualified, or adverse. This opinion must clearly state whether the annual financial statements present a true and fair view in accordance with the relevant financial reporting framework and, where applicable, whether they comply with statutory requirements. If the auditor is unable to express an opinion, the report should include a disclaimer of opinion.

Additionally, the report may include references to any matters the auditor wishes to emphasize without qualifying the audit opinion. It must also contain the opinion and statement as required by Article 34(1) of Directive 2013/34/EU concerning annual and consolidated financial statements and related reports.

The audit report must be signed and dated by the statutory auditor. If an audit firm conducts the audit, the report should bear the signature of at least one statutory auditor responsible for the audit on behalf of the firm. In exceptional cases, Member States may allow withholding the public disclosure of signatures if revealing them poses a significant threat to personal security; however, the names must still be known to the relevant authorities.

For consolidated financial statements, the audit report must meet the same requirements. When reporting on the consistency between the management report and the financial statements, the auditor must consider both the consolidated financial statements and the consolidated management report. If the parent undertaking’s annual financial statements are attached to the consolidated financial statements, the audit reports may be combined accordingly.

The 32 principles of public oversight establish a comprehensive framework to ensure effective supervision of statutory auditors and audit firms. Member States are required to organize a robust public oversight system that applies to all statutory auditors and audit firms without exception. This system must be governed primarily by non-practitioners who possess relevant expertise in statutory audit, although a minority of practitioners may participate in governance through an independent and transparent nomination process.

The public oversight system holds ultimate responsibility for key functions including the approval and registration of auditors and audit firms, the adoption of professional ethics standards, internal quality control, auditing standards, as well as continuing education, quality assurance, and disciplinary procedures. It is empowered to conduct investigations and take necessary actions to uphold audit quality and integrity.

Transparency is a fundamental principle of the oversight system, which must publish annual work programmes and activity reports to maintain public trust. Additionally, the system must be adequately and securely funded, ensuring financial independence free from undue influence by the auditors or audit firms it oversees. Together, these principles create a structured, transparent, and accountable public oversight framework that supports the integrity and reliability of statutory audits.

Under the regulatory framework governing statutory audits, Member States are required to establish clear rules regarding the dismissal and resignation of statutory auditors or audit firms. Specifically, statutory auditors or audit firms may only be dismissed on proper grounds, ensuring that such actions are justified and not arbitrary. Importantly, differences in opinion related to accounting treatments or audit procedures do not constitute valid reasons for dismissal, thereby protecting auditors from being removed due to professional disagreements.

Furthermore, both the audited entity and the statutory auditor or audit firm have an obligation to notify the relevant public oversight authority or authorities in the event of a dismissal or resignation during the auditor’s term of appointment. This notification must include an adequate explanation of the reasons behind the dismissal or resignation. These provisions aim to promote transparency and accountability in the audit process, safeguarding the integrity of statutory audits and maintaining public trust.

Article 47 addresses the cooperation between Member States and competent authorities from third countries regarding the transfer of audit working papers and other documents held by statutory auditors or audit firms. Under this provision, Member States may permit such transfers to third-country authorities only under specific conditions to ensure proper oversight, data protection, and reciprocity.

Firstly, the documents eligible for transfer must relate to audits of companies that have issued securities in the third country or belong to groups issuing consolidated accounts there. Transfers must occur through the home competent authorities of the Member States and only upon request from the third country’s competent authorities. Additionally, the third country’s authorities must meet adequacy requirements assessed and declared by the European Commission, ensuring they provide protections equivalent to those required under EU law. Working arrangements based on reciprocity must be established between the involved authorities, and any transfer of personal data must comply with the data protection rules set out in Directive 95/46/EC.

These working arrangements must guarantee that requests for documents are justified, that recipients are bound by professional secrecy, and that the documents are used solely for public oversight, quality assurance, or investigations with standards equivalent to those in the EU. Requests can be refused if providing the documents would harm the sovereignty, security, or public order of the EU or the Member State, or if judicial proceedings on the same matter are already underway in the Member State.

The Commission plays a key role in assessing the adequacy of third countries’ authorities and adopting related decisions through regulatory procedures, ensuring uniform application across Member States. In exceptional cases, Member States may allow direct transfers of audit documents from auditors or audit firms to third-country authorities, provided investigations have been initiated, reciprocal access is granted, the home authority is informed in advance, and all other conditions, including those on data protection and professional secrecy, are met.

Finally, Member States are required to communicate the working arrangements established under these provisions to the Commission, facilitating transparency and coordination in international audit cooperation.

The Commission shall be assisted by a committee (referred to as the Committee) in carrying out its tasks. When reference is made to the Committee procedure, Articles 5 and 7 of Decision 1999/468/EC apply, with due regard to Article 8 of the same Decision. Notably, the period specified in Article 5(6) of Decision 1999/468/EC is set at three months. Additionally, Articles 5a(1) to (4) and Article 7 of Decision 1999/468/EC also apply in this context, again considering the provisions of Article 8.

Furthermore, the Commission is required to review the provisions concerning its implementing powers by 31 December 2010 and subsequently at least every three years. This review involves presenting a report to both the European Parliament and the Council on how these powers are functioning. The report must specifically assess whether there is a need for the Commission to propose amendments to the Directive to ensure that the scope of the implementing powers is appropriate. Any conclusion regarding the necessity of amendments must be supported by a detailed statement of reasons. If deemed necessary, the report should be accompanied by a legislative proposal to amend the provisions that confer implementing powers on the Commission.

Member States are required to ensure that manufacturers design appliances so that waste batteries and accumulators can be easily removed. Appliances containing batteries or accumulators must include instructions that clearly explain how to safely remove these components. Additionally, when appropriate, the instructions should inform the end-user about the specific type of battery or accumulator incorporated in the appliance. However, these requirements do not apply in cases where a permanent connection between the appliance and the battery or accumulator is necessary to maintain safety, performance, medical functions, data integrity, or continuous power supply.

According to the regulations governing the export of waste batteries and accumulators, treatment and recycling may be carried out either outside the Member State concerned or outside the European Community, provided that all shipments comply with Council Regulation (EEC) No 259/93 of 1 February 1993. This regulation supervises and controls the shipment of waste within, into, and out of the European Community to ensure proper handling.

When waste batteries and accumulators are exported outside the Community, such shipments must also adhere to Council Regulation (EC) No 1420/1999, which establishes common rules and procedures for shipments to certain non-OECD countries, as well as Commission Regulation (EC) No 1547/1999, which specifies control procedures for shipments to countries not covered by the OECD Decision C(92)39 final. Importantly, these exported waste batteries and accumulators will only be counted towards fulfilling the obligations and efficiency targets set out in Annex III of the Directive if there is credible evidence that the recycling operations abroad meet conditions equivalent to those required by the Directive.

Furthermore, detailed rules for implementing these provisions, including criteria for assessing whether the conditions abroad are equivalent, will be established. These implementing measures, which serve to amend non-essential elements of the Directive by supplementing it, will be adopted following the regulatory procedure with scrutiny as outlined in Article 24(3) of the Directive.

According to the labelling requirements set out for batteries, accumulators, and battery packs, Member States must ensure that all such products are appropriately marked with the symbol shown in Annex II. Additionally, by 26 September 2009, the capacity of all portable and automotive batteries and accumulators must be indicated on them in a visible, legible, and indelible manner. Detailed rules for implementing this capacity indication, including harmonised methods for determining capacity and its proper use, were to be established by 26 March 2009 through measures adopted via the regulatory procedure with scrutiny as per Article 24(3).

Batteries, accumulators, and button cells containing more than 0.0005% mercury (Hg), 0.002% cadmium (Cd), or 0.004% lead (Pb) must also be marked with the chemical symbol of the respective heavy metal. This symbol must be printed beneath the Annex II symbol and cover at least one-quarter of its size.

The Annex II symbol itself must cover at least 3% of the area of the largest side of the battery, accumulator, or battery pack, with a maximum size of 5 × 5 cm. For cylindrical cells, the symbol must cover at least 1.5% of the surface area, also with a maximum size of 5 × 5 cm. If the battery or accumulator is so small that the symbol would be less than 0.5 × 0.5 cm, marking on the battery is not required; instead, a symbol of at least 1 × 1 cm must be printed on the packaging.

All symbols must be printed visibly, legibly, and indelibly. Exemptions from these labelling requirements may be granted through measures adopted following the regulatory procedure with scrutiny as outlined in Article 24(3).

According to the Directive, Member States are required to submit a national implementation report to the Commission every three years, with the first report covering the period up to 26 September 2012. These reports must be prepared based on a questionnaire or outline established through the procedure outlined in Article 24(2), which is to be provided to Member States six months before the start of the reporting period. The reports should include information on measures taken to encourage developments that affect the environmental impact of batteries and accumulators. Specifically, Member States must report on efforts such as voluntary reductions by producers of heavy metals and hazardous substances in batteries, new recycling and treatment techniques, participation of economic operators in environmental management schemes, relevant research activities, and initiatives promoting waste prevention. The completed reports must be submitted to the Commission no later than nine months after the end of each three-year period, with the first report due by 26 June 2013. Subsequently, the Commission is responsible for publishing a comprehensive report on the Directive’s implementation, its environmental impact, and its effects on the internal market within nine months of receiving the Member States’ reports.

Article 24 outlines the committee procedure related to the Commission's activities. Firstly, the Commission is to be assisted by the Committee established under Article 18 of Directive 2006/12/EC. When this Article is referenced, the procedural rules set out in Articles 5 and 7 of Decision 1999/468/EC apply, with consideration given to the provisions of Article 8 of the same Decision. Notably, the time period specified in Article 5(6) of Decision 1999/468/EC is adjusted to three months for the purposes of this procedure. Furthermore, when reference is made to paragraph 3 of Article 24, Articles 5a(1) to (4) and Article 7 of Decision 1999/468/EC apply, again taking into account the provisions of Article 8. This framework ensures that the Commission's actions are supported and regulated through established committee procedures and decision-making rules.

According to the provisions established after consultation with the VAT Committee, each Member State of the European Union is permitted to apply a reduced value-added tax (VAT) rate to the supply of natural gas, electricity, or district heating. This measure allows Member States to lower the tax burden on these essential energy sources, potentially making them more affordable for consumers and businesses. The decision to implement a reduced VAT rate is at the discretion of each Member State, provided it aligns with the guidelines and conditions set forth by the EU VAT Directive and follows the recommendations of the VAT Committee. This flexibility aims to support energy accessibility and affordability while maintaining a harmonized approach to VAT across the Union.

The term ‘supply of goods’ primarily refers to the transfer of the right to dispose of tangible property as an owner. Beyond this basic definition, certain specific transactions are also considered supplies of goods. These include: (a) the transfer of ownership of property by order of a public authority or under legal mandate, provided compensation is paid; (b) the actual delivery of goods under contracts for hire over a fixed period or sales on deferred payment terms, where ownership is expected to pass upon final payment; and (c) the transfer of goods under contracts where commission is payable on purchase or sale. Additionally, Member States have the discretion to classify the handing over of certain construction works as a supply of goods.

Member States are required to exempt certain transactions from VAT as outlined in the following provisions:

1. The supply of goods that are dispatched or transported to a destination outside the Community by or on behalf of the vendor is exempt from VAT.

2. Similarly, the supply of goods dispatched or transported to a destination outside the Community by or on behalf of a customer who is not established within the Member State’s territory is exempt, except in cases where the goods are transported by the customer themselves for the equipping, fuelling, and provisioning of pleasure boats, private aircraft, or any other means of transport intended for private use.

3. Supplies of goods to approved bodies that export these goods outside the Community as part of their humanitarian, charitable, or teaching activities are also exempt from VAT.

4. Services consisting of work on movable property that has been acquired or imported for the purpose of undergoing such work within the Community, and which is then dispatched or transported out of the Community by the supplier, the customer (if not established within the territory), or on behalf of either party, are exempt.

5. Additionally, supplies of services—including transport and ancillary transactions—directly connected with the exportation or importation of goods covered by specific Articles (Article 61 and Article 157(1)(a)) are exempt, except for services already exempted under Articles 132 and 135.

Furthermore, the exemption related to supplies to approved bodies (point (c)) may be implemented through a refund of the VAT, allowing these bodies to recover VAT paid on such transactions.

Article 151 outlines specific exemptions from VAT that Member States must apply to certain transactions. These exemptions cover supplies of goods or services under diplomatic and consular arrangements, ensuring that such transactions are not subject to VAT. Additionally, supplies made to key European institutions—such as the European Community, the European Atomic Energy Community, the European Central Bank, the European Investment Bank, and other bodies established by the Communities under the Protocol of 8 April 1965—are exempt, provided these do not distort competition and comply with the relevant protocols and agreements.

Further exemptions apply to supplies made to international bodies recognized by the host Member State’s public authorities, as well as to their members, within the limits set by international conventions or headquarters agreements. Supplies intended for the armed forces of NATO member states, including civilian staff and their messes or canteens, are also exempt when these forces participate in common defense efforts. This exemption applies both within a Member State party to the North Atlantic Treaty and when supplying armed forces of other NATO states stationed there.

Moreover, supplies to the armed forces of the United Kingdom stationed in Cyprus under the Treaty of Establishment of 1960 are exempt, covering goods and services for the use of these forces, their civilian staff, and their messes or canteens.

Until common tax rules are adopted, these exemptions are subject to limitations imposed by the host Member State. In situations where goods are not transported out of the Member State where the supply occurs, or in the case of services, the VAT exemption may be implemented through a refund mechanism. This ensures that the intended beneficiaries of these exemptions are not unduly burdened by VAT, while maintaining compliance with national tax regulations.

According to the provisions outlined, Member States have the discretion to exempt certain transactions involving warehousing arrangements. Specifically, they may exempt the importation of goods that are intended to be placed under warehousing arrangements other than customs warehousing. Similarly, they may exempt the supply of goods within their territory that are also intended to be placed under such non-customs warehousing arrangements. However, there is a clear restriction regarding the use of warehousing arrangements other than customs warehousing: Member States are not permitted to establish these alternative warehousing arrangements for goods that are not subject to excise duty if those goods are intended to be supplied at the retail stage. This ensures that non-excise goods destined for retail supply cannot benefit from warehousing schemes outside the customs warehousing framework.

According to the provisions outlined, Member States have the option, after consulting the VAT Committee, to exempt certain transactions carried out by or intended for a taxable person, provided these do not exceed the value of that person's exports during the previous 12 months. Specifically, this exemption can apply to: (a) intra-Community acquisitions of goods made by the taxable person, as well as imports and supplies of goods to that person, when these goods are intended for export from the Community either in their original form or after processing; and (b) supplies of services that are connected to the taxable person's export business.

Furthermore, if a Member State chooses to apply this exemption, it must also extend the exemption—again after consulting the VAT Committee—to transactions related to supplies made by the taxable person under the conditions set out in Article 138. This extension is limited to an amount equal to the value of such supplies carried out by the taxable person during the preceding 12 months, in accordance with the same conditions. This framework allows Member States to facilitate export-related activities by reducing VAT burdens on certain transactions linked to export operations.

According to the provisions outlined in Article 26, paragraph 1, certain transactions are to be treated as a supply of services for consideration under VAT law. Specifically, this includes: (a) the use of goods that form part of the assets of a business for private purposes by a taxable person or their staff, or more broadly, for any purposes other than those related to the business itself, in cases where the VAT on such goods was wholly or partly deductible; and (b) the supply of services performed free of charge by a taxable person for their own private use, that of their staff, or generally for non-business purposes. These transactions are considered taxable supplies because they represent a benefit derived from business assets or services for non-business use, which would otherwise escape VAT.

Furthermore, paragraph 2 allows Member States the flexibility to derogate from the rule established in paragraph 1. However, any such derogation must not result in distortion of competition within the internal market. This means that while Member States can choose not to treat these transactions as taxable supplies in certain circumstances, they must ensure that this does not create unfair advantages or competitive imbalances between businesses operating in different Member States.

For the purposes of this Chapter, several key definitions are established to clarify the scope and application of the rules concerning second-hand goods, works of art, collectors' items, and antiques. 

1. **Second-hand goods** are defined as movable tangible property suitable for further use either as they are or after repair. This category explicitly excludes works of art, collectors' items, antiques, and precious metals or stones as defined by Member States.

2. **Works of art**, **collectors' items**, and **antiques** are defined by reference to specific lists found in Annex IX, Parts A, B, and C respectively. However, Member States are not obliged to classify certain objects listed in points (5), (6), or (7) of Annex IX, Part A as works of art.

3. A **taxable dealer** is any taxable person who, in the course of their economic activity and with the intention of resale, purchases, applies for business purposes, or imports second-hand goods, works of art, collectors' items, or antiques. This includes those acting on their own behalf or on behalf of another person under a commission-based contract.

4. An **organiser of a sale by public auction** is a taxable person who offers goods for sale by public auction during their economic activity, aiming to transfer ownership to the highest bidder.

5. The **principal of an organiser of a sale by public auction** is the person who provides goods to the organiser under a commission-based contract. Such contracts must stipulate that the organiser conducts the auction and transfers the goods in their own name but on behalf of the principal, ensuring clarity in the legal and commercial relationship during the auction process.

These definitions provide a structured framework for the treatment and regulation of these categories of goods and the roles of various economic actors involved in their trade within the Community.

Article 318 outlines provisions allowing Member States, after consulting the VAT Committee, to simplify the tax collection process for supplies of goods subject to the margin scheme. Specifically, Member States may decide that for certain transactions or categories of taxable dealers, the taxable amount is determined on a per tax period basis, coinciding with the submission of the VAT return as per Article 250. When such a provision is applied, the taxable amount for supplies subject to the same VAT rate is calculated as the total profit margin earned by the taxable dealer during that period, minus the VAT attributable to that margin.

The total profit margin is defined as the difference between two key figures within the tax period: (a) the total value of supplies of goods subject to the margin scheme, meaning the aggregate selling prices of those goods, and (b) the total value of purchases of such goods, referring to the aggregate purchase prices as specified in Article 314. This calculation ensures that the taxable amount reflects the actual margin realized by the dealer.

Furthermore, Member States are required to implement measures to prevent taxable dealers benefiting from unjustified advantages or suffering unjustified harm as a result of applying this simplified margin scheme method. This safeguard aims to maintain fairness and integrity in the VAT system while facilitating administrative ease.

The place of supply of goods, as an exception to the general rule in Article 32, is determined based on the location of the goods at the time when their dispatch or transport to the customer ends, rather than where the dispatch or transport begins. This applies under specific conditions: first, the supply must be made to a taxable person, a non-taxable legal person whose intra-Community acquisitions are exempt from VAT under Article 3(1), or any other non-taxable person; second, the goods supplied must not be new means of transport nor goods supplied after assembly or installation by or on behalf of the supplier, whether or not a trial run has been conducted. Furthermore, if the goods are dispatched or transported from a third territory or country and are imported by the supplier into a Member State different from the place where the dispatch or transport to the customer ends, the place of supply is considered to be the Member State where the goods were imported. This ensures clarity in VAT treatment when goods cross borders within or outside the EU before reaching the customer.

The provisions outlined specify conditions under which Article 33 does not apply to the supply of goods dispatched or transported entirely to the same Member State, which is also the Member State where the transport ends. Specifically, this exemption applies if the goods are not subject to excise duty, and the total value of such supplies within that Member State does not exceed EUR 100,000 (or the equivalent in national currency) in the current calendar year, as well as did not exceed this threshold in the previous calendar year.

Furthermore, the Member State where the goods are located at the end of their transport may reduce this threshold to EUR 35,000 if it believes that the higher threshold could cause serious competition distortions. Should a Member State choose to apply this lower threshold, it must inform the competent authorities in the Member State where the dispatch or transport begins.

The European Commission is tasked with reporting to the Council on the operation of this special EUR 35,000 threshold and may propose adjustments if necessary.

Additionally, the Member State where the goods are located at the start of their dispatch or transport must allow taxable persons who qualify under these conditions the option to apply the place of supply rules as per Article 33. The Member States involved are responsible for establishing detailed rules for exercising this option, which must cover a minimum period of two calendar years.

For the purposes of this Directive, and without prejudice to other Community provisions, ‘investment gold’ is defined as follows: (1) gold in the form of bars or wafers with weights accepted by the bullion markets, having a purity of at least 995 thousandths, regardless of whether they are represented by securities; (2) gold coins with a purity of at least 900 thousandths, minted after the year 1800, which are or have been legal tender in their country of origin, and are typically sold at a price not exceeding the open market value of the gold content by more than 80%. Additionally, Member States have the option to exclude from this special scheme small bars or wafers weighing 1 gram or less. Furthermore, for the purposes of this Directive, the coins described in point (2) are not considered to be sold for numismatic interest.

Articles 33 and 34 do not apply to supplies of second-hand goods, works of art, collectors' items, or antiques, as defined in points (1) to (4) of Article 311(1). Additionally, these articles are not applicable to supplies of second-hand means of transport, as defined in Article 327(3). Instead, such supplies are subject to VAT under the relevant special arrangements established for these categories.
