Confidentiality and data protection are fundamental principles governing the handling of information during investigations. Information transmitted or obtained in the course of external investigations must be safeguarded according to the relevant provisions to ensure its protection. Similarly, information arising from internal investigations is subject to professional secrecy and benefits from the protections established by the rules applicable to the Union institutions.

The institutions, bodies, offices, or agencies involved are responsible for maintaining the confidentiality of investigations conducted by the Office, while also respecting the legitimate rights of the individuals concerned. In cases where judicial proceedings have been initiated, all applicable national rules governing such proceedings must be strictly observed.

To oversee data protection matters, the Office may appoint a Data Protection Officer in line with Article 24 of Regulation (EC) No 45/2001. Furthermore, the Director-General is tasked with ensuring that any information released to the public is presented in a neutral and impartial manner. Such disclosures must uphold the confidentiality of ongoing investigations and comply with the principles outlined in this Article and Article 9(1).

In accordance with the Staff Regulations, Office staff are prohibited from unauthorized disclosure of information obtained during their duties, except when such information is already public or publicly accessible. This obligation of confidentiality continues to bind staff even after they have left the service, underscoring the enduring commitment to data protection and confidentiality.

The Supervisory Committee plays a crucial role in overseeing the Office’s investigative function to ensure its independence and proper exercise of powers as established by the Regulation. It regularly monitors how investigations are conducted, focusing particularly on procedural guarantees and the length of investigations, based on information provided by the Director-General. The Committee issues opinions and recommendations regarding the Office’s investigative priorities, resource needs, and investigation durations. These opinions can be initiated by the Committee itself, requested by the Director-General, or by other EU institutions, bodies, offices, or agencies, without interfering with ongoing investigations. Copies of such opinions are shared with the requesting entities. In justified cases, the Committee may request additional information, including reports on closed investigations, again without disrupting active inquiries.

The Committee consists of five independent members with senior judicial, investigative, or comparable experience relevant to the Office’s activities. These members are appointed jointly by the European Parliament, the Council, and the Commission, with a reserve list maintained to fill any vacancies arising from resignation, death, or incapacity. Members serve a non-renewable five-year term, with staggered replacements (three members replaced first, then two) to maintain continuity and expertise. Members remain in office until successors are appointed. If a member no longer meets the required conditions or is found guilty of serious misconduct, they may be removed by common agreement of the appointing institutions.

Members receive daily allowances and reimbursement for expenses according to Commission rules. They must act independently, without seeking or accepting instructions from any government or EU institution. The Committee appoints its own chair and adopts rules of procedure, which are submitted for information to the European Parliament, Council, Commission, and European Data Protection Supervisor. Meetings are convened by the chair or the Director-General, with at least ten meetings held annually. Decisions are made by majority vote, and the Office provides the Committee’s secretariat in close cooperation.

Annually, the Supervisory Committee produces at least one report detailing its activities, including assessments of the Office’s independence, procedural safeguards, and investigation durations. These reports are sent to the European Parliament, Council, Commission, and Court of Auditors. Additionally, the Committee may submit reports on investigation outcomes and subsequent actions to these institutions.

The total appropriations allocated for the Office, encompassing the Supervisory Committee and its secretariat, are to be recorded under a distinct budget line within the general budget of the European Union, specifically under the section pertaining to the Commission. These appropriations must be detailed comprehensively in an Annex attached to that section of the budget. Furthermore, the establishment plan for the Office, which includes the secretariat of the Supervisory Committee, shall be incorporated as an annex to the overall establishment plan of the Commission. This ensures clear financial and organizational integration of the Office within the Commission’s budgetary and administrative framework.

This Regulation shall enter into force on the first day of the month following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union. Regarding transitional provisions, Article 15(3) will govern the duration of the term of office for members of the Supervisory Committee who are in office at the time this Regulation takes effect. Immediately after the Regulation enters into force, the President of the European Parliament will select by lot two members of the Supervisory Committee whose terms will end after 36 months, as a derogation from the usual provisions of Article 15(3). These two outgoing members will be replaced automatically by two new members appointed for a five-year term, based on the order of names listed in Article 1(2) of Decision 2012/45/EU, Euratom, which concerns the appointment of Supervisory Committee members of the European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF). The new appointees will be the first two individuals named on that list. Additionally, the third sentence of Article 17(1) will apply to the term of office of the Director-General who is in office at the date this Regulation enters into force.

Article 198 outlines the measures that customs authorities must take regarding the disposal of goods under certain circumstances. The customs authorities are empowered to take necessary actions, including confiscation, sale, or destruction of goods, in the following cases:

1. When obligations under customs legislation related to the introduction of non-Union goods into the customs territory of the Union have not been fulfilled, or when goods have been withheld from customs supervision.

2. When goods cannot be released due to specific reasons, such as:
   - The examination of goods could not be undertaken or continued within the prescribed period due to reasons attributable to the declarant.
   - Required documents for placing goods under or releasing them for the requested customs procedure have not been provided.
   - Payments or guarantees related to import or export duties have not been made or provided within the prescribed timeframe.
   - The goods are subject to prohibitions or restrictions.

3. When goods have not been removed within a reasonable period after their release.

4. When, after release, goods are found not to have fulfilled the conditions for that release.

5. When goods are abandoned to the State in accordance with Article 199.

Furthermore, non-Union goods that have been abandoned to the State, seized, or confiscated are considered to be under the customs warehousing procedure. These goods must be recorded either by the customs warehousing operator or by the customs authorities if they hold the goods. If such goods are already subject to a customs declaration, the records must reference this declaration, which the customs authorities will invalidate.

Regarding the costs of these measures, they are to be borne as follows:

- For failure to fulfill obligations or withholding goods from customs supervision (point a), by the person required to fulfill those obligations or who withheld the goods.
- For cases where goods cannot be released due to reasons related to the declarant or failure to remove goods timely (points b and c), by the declarant.
- For goods not fulfilling release conditions after release (point d), by the person responsible for complying with those conditions.
- For goods abandoned to the State (point e), by the person who abandons the goods.

In summary, customs authorities have clear powers to dispose of goods under various circumstances to ensure compliance with customs legislation, and the financial responsibility for these measures lies with the parties responsible for the non-compliance or abandonment.

The customs territory of the Union encompasses the territories of its Member States, including their territorial waters, internal waters, and airspace, with certain specific exceptions. It includes the entire territories of countries such as Belgium, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Estonia, Ireland, Greece, Croatia, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Hungary, Malta, Austria, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovenia, Slovakia, Finland, and Sweden. However, some Member States have territorial exclusions: Denmark’s customs territory excludes the Faroe Islands and Greenland; Germany excludes the Island of Heligoland and Büsingen; Spain excludes Ceuta and Melilla; France excludes its overseas countries and territories governed by Part Four of the TFEU; Italy excludes the municipalities of Livigno and Campione d'Italia and certain national waters of Lake Lugano.

Additionally, the customs territory includes the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland along with the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man. Beyond the territories of Member States, certain external territories are also considered part of the Union’s customs territory based on international agreements. These include the territory of Monaco, as defined by the Customs Convention signed in Paris in 1963, and the United Kingdom Sovereign Base Areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia in Cyprus, as established by the 1960 Treaty concerning the Establishment of the Republic of Cyprus. These inclusions ensure a comprehensive customs area facilitating trade and regulatory uniformity across the Union and its associated territories.

Article 50 outlines the conferral of implementing powers to the European Commission regarding customs controls within the Union. 

1. The Commission is empowered to adopt implementing acts to ensure the uniform application of customs controls. These measures include the exchange of risk information and risk analysis results, establishing common risk criteria and standards, defining control measures, and identifying priority control areas as specified in Article 46(3). The adoption of these implementing acts follows the examination procedure set out in Article 285(4). However, in cases of imperative urgency—where rapid updates to the common risk management framework are necessary to respond to evolving risks—the Commission may adopt immediately applicable implementing acts under the urgent procedure described in Article 285(5). When the committee’s opinion is sought via written procedure, Article 285(6) applies.

2. Additionally, the Commission determines, through implementing acts, the specific ports or airports where customs controls and formalities apply to certain categories of cabin and hold baggage, in accordance with Article 49. These categories include:

   (a) Baggage of persons:
   - Taking flights on aircraft arriving from a non-Union airport that stop over at a Union airport before continuing to another Union airport.
   - Taking flights on aircraft that stop over at a Union airport before continuing to a non-Union airport.
   - Using maritime services on vessels with successive legs involving non-Union ports.
   - Traveling on board pleasure craft and tourist or business aircraft.

   (b) Baggage:
   - Arriving at a Union airport on an aircraft from a non-Union airport and transferred to another aircraft for an intra-Union flight.
   - Loaded at a Union airport onto an aircraft for an intra-Union flight, then transferred at another Union airport to an aircraft destined for a non-Union airport.

Through these provisions, the Commission ensures a harmonized and responsive customs control system across the Union’s external and internal borders.

The primary method for customs valuation of imported goods is based on the transaction value, which refers to the price actually paid or payable for the goods when sold for export to the customs territory of the Union, with necessary adjustments. This price includes the total payment made or to be made by the buyer to the seller, or to a third party for the seller’s benefit, encompassing all payments required as a condition of sale.

For the transaction value to be accepted as the customs value, several conditions must be met:

1. There must be no restrictions on the buyer’s disposal or use of the goods, except for certain allowable restrictions such as those imposed by law or public authorities within the Union, limitations on the geographical area where the goods may be resold, or restrictions that do not significantly affect the customs value.

2. The sale or price must not be subject to any condition or consideration for which a value cannot be determined in relation to the goods being valued.

3. No part of the proceeds from any subsequent resale, disposal, or use of the goods by the buyer should directly or indirectly benefit the seller, unless an appropriate adjustment to the value can be made.

4. The buyer and seller must not be related parties, or if they are related, the relationship must not have influenced the price.

When all these criteria are fulfilled, the transaction value serves as the primary and preferred basis for customs valuation.

In determining the customs value under Article 70, the price actually paid or payable for the imported goods must be supplemented by certain elements when these costs are incurred by the buyer but are not included in the price. These elements include:

(a) Commissions and brokerage fees, except buying commissions; the cost of containers that are treated as one with the goods for customs purposes; and the cost of packing, including both labor and materials.

(b) The value, apportioned as appropriate, of goods and services supplied directly or indirectly by the buyer free of charge or at a reduced cost for use in connection with the production and sale for export of the imported goods, to the extent that such value is not already included in the price. This includes materials, components, parts incorporated into the goods; tools, dies, molds used in production; materials consumed in production; and engineering, development, artwork, design work, plans, and sketches undertaken outside the Union necessary for production.

(c) Royalties and license fees related to the goods being valued that the buyer must pay, directly or indirectly, as a condition of sale, if these are not included in the price.

(d) The value of any part of the proceeds from any subsequent resale, disposal, or use of the imported goods that accrues directly or indirectly to the seller.

(e) Costs up to the place where the goods enter the customs territory of the Union, including the cost of transport and insurance of the imported goods, as well as loading and handling charges associated with their transport.

Additions to the price actually paid or payable must be based solely on objective and quantifiable data. No other additions beyond those specified in this Article are permitted in determining the customs value.

The application of this Regulation is triggered by a specific condition related to the combined maximum annual ship recycling output of facilities listed in the European List. Specifically, the Regulation shall come into effect from the earlier of two possible dates, with the caveat that it cannot apply before 31 December 2015. One of these dates is defined as six months after the total maximum annual ship recycling capacity of the ship recycling facilities included in the European List reaches or exceeds 2.5 million light displacement tonnes (LDT). This means that once the combined capacity of these approved facilities hits this threshold, a six-month period begins, after which the Regulation becomes applicable—provided this date is not earlier than 31 December 2015. The other date, not detailed here, would be the alternative trigger for the Regulation’s application, with the earliest possible enforcement date firmly set at the end of 2015.

The reduction of direct payments to farmers is governed by specific rules aimed at limiting excessive subsidies. Member States are required to reduce the amount of direct payments granted to a farmer by at least 5% on the portion of payments exceeding EUR 150,000 in any given calendar year. Before applying this reduction, Member States may deduct from the total payment the salaries linked to agricultural activities that the farmer actually paid and declared in the previous year, including related taxes and social contributions. If no recent salary data is available, the most recent data should be used.

However, if a Member State chooses to grant redistributive payments to farmers and allocates more than 5% of its annual national ceiling for this purpose, it may opt not to apply the reduction rule. Similarly, if the application of maximum limits on redistributive payments prevents the use of more than 5% of the national ceiling, the Member State may also decide not to apply the reduction.

To prevent abuse, no advantage shall be given to farmers who have artificially created conditions after 18 October 2011 to avoid these payment reductions. In cases involving legal persons or groups of persons, Member States may apply the reduction at the level of individual members, provided national law recognizes these members as having rights and obligations similar to individual farmers and that they have contributed to strengthening the agricultural structures concerned.

Finally, Member States are obligated to notify the European Commission by 1 August 2014 about their decisions regarding these reductions and provide estimates of the expected reduction amounts for the years 2015 to 2019.

The Single Area Payment Scheme (SAPS) as applied by Member States in 2014 under Chapter 2 of Title V of Regulation (EC) No 73/2009 may be continued until 31 December 2020 at the latest, provided the Member State notifies the European Commission of its decision and the intended end date by 1 August 2014. During the period of SAPS application, most provisions of Sections 1, 2, and 3 of the relevant Chapter do not apply to these Member States, except for specific provisions including the second subparagraph of Article 23(1), Article 23(6), and Articles 32(2) to (6).

The SAPS payment is granted annually per eligible hectare declared by farmers, in line with point (a) of the first subparagraph of Article 72(1) of Regulation (EU) No 1306/2013. The payment amount is calculated each year by dividing the annual financial envelope allocated to the scheme by the total number of eligible hectares declared in the Member State.

From 1 January 2018 at the latest, Member States opting to apply Article 38 of the Regulation may use up to 20% of their annual financial envelope to differentiate the payment per hectare. This differentiation must consider the support granted in 2014 under various schemes specified in Regulation (EC) No 73/2009, including points (a), (b), and (c) of Article 68(1) and Articles 126, 127, and 129. Cyprus has the option to differentiate aid based on sector-specific financial envelopes outlined in Annex XVIIa of Regulation (EC) No 73/2009, adjusted for any aid granted under Article 37 of the current Regulation. When differentiating payments, and if the redistributive payment under Article 41 is not applied, Member States must fully account for support granted in 2014 under Article 125a of Regulation (EC) No 73/2009.

The European Commission is responsible for adopting implementing acts that set the annual national ceiling for SAPS for each Member State. This ceiling is determined by deducting ceilings fixed under Articles 42, 47, 49, 51, and 53 from the national ceiling established in Annex II. These implementing acts follow the examination procedure outlined in Article 71(2).

The regulation on permanent grassland sets out specific obligations for Member States to protect environmentally sensitive permanent grasslands, particularly those located within areas covered by Directives 92/43/EEC (Habitats Directive) or 2009/147/EC (Birds Directive), including peatlands and wetlands. Member States are required to designate these sensitive permanent grasslands to ensure their strict protection, which is essential for meeting the environmental objectives of these Directives. Additionally, Member States have the discretion to designate further sensitive permanent grassland areas outside these Directive-covered zones, especially those on carbon-rich soils, to enhance environmental protection.

Farmers are prohibited from converting or ploughing permanent grassland in these designated areas to preserve their ecological value. To maintain the overall extent of permanent grassland, Member States must ensure that the ratio of permanent grassland to total agricultural area declared by farmers does not decrease by more than 5% compared to a reference ratio established in 2015. This reference ratio is calculated based on permanent grassland areas declared in 2012 (or 2013 for Croatia) and 2015, relative to the total agricultural area declared in 2015.

If the ratio of permanent grassland falls by more than 5% at national, regional, or sub-regional levels, Member States are obliged to impose reconversion requirements at the farm (holding) level. This means farmers who have converted permanent grassland to other land uses in the past must restore it to permanent grassland. However, this obligation does not apply if the decrease is due to environmentally compatible afforestation, excluding plantations such as short rotation coppice, Christmas trees, or fast-growing trees for energy production.

The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts to provide detailed rules on maintaining permanent grassland, including reconversion procedures, obligations at holding level, adjustments to the reference ratio, and frameworks for designating additional sensitive areas. It also establishes methods for calculating the permanent grassland ratio and defines the relevant historical period for reconversion obligations. Furthermore, the Commission will adopt implementing acts to set limits related to the maintenance of permanent grassland, following the appropriate examination procedures.

In summary, this regulatory framework aims to safeguard permanent grasslands due to their environmental importance, ensuring their extent is maintained and that any loss beyond a defined threshold triggers restoration measures, thereby contributing to biodiversity conservation and climate objectives within the EU agricultural policy.

The general rules governing the payment for young farmers under the basic payment scheme or the single area payment scheme are as follows:

1. Member States are required to grant an annual payment to young farmers who qualify for payments under the basic or single area payment schemes. This payment is specifically aimed at supporting young farmers.

2. A "young farmer" is defined as a natural person who is either setting up an agricultural holding for the first time as the head of the holding or has done so within the five years prior to their first application under the relevant payment schemes. Additionally, the young farmer must be no older than 40 years in the year of application.

3. Member States may impose additional objective and non-discriminatory eligibility criteria related to skills or training for young farmers applying for this payment.

4. The payment is granted annually upon activation of payment entitlements or, in Member States applying specific provisions, upon declaration of eligible hectares by the farmer. This is subject to financial discipline rules and reductions as stipulated in related regulations.

5. The payment is granted for a maximum of five years per farmer. This period is adjusted by subtracting the number of years elapsed between the farmer’s initial setup and their first application for the young farmer payment.

6. For Member States not applying certain area-based declarations, the payment amount is calculated by multiplying the number of activated entitlements by 25% of either the average value of the farmer’s payment entitlements or a fixed amount derived from the national ceiling and eligible hectares declared in 2015.

The national ceilings for each Member State and each year represent the total value of all allocated payment entitlements, including those from the national reserve or regional reserves, as well as ceilings established under Articles 42, 47, 49, 51, and 53. These ceilings are specified in Annex II of the regulation. If a Member State opts to use the provision in Article 22(2), it may exceed its national ceiling by the amount calculated according to that article for the relevant year.

For Member States applying the single area payment scheme, a derogation applies: their national ceiling for each year, which includes ceilings fixed under Articles 36, 42, 47, 49, 51, and 53, is also set out in Annex II.

Furthermore, to reflect changes in the total maximum amounts of direct payments—such as those arising from decisions made by Member States under Article 136a of Regulation (EC) No 73/2009, Article 14 of this Regulation, or the application of Article 20(2)—the European Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts. These acts, pursuant to Article 70 of the Regulation, allow the Commission to adjust the national ceilings listed in Annex II accordingly.

The Flexibility Instrument is designed to provide additional financing within a given financial year for specific expenditures that cannot be covered under the existing ceilings of one or more other budget headings. For each year, the maximum amount available through the Flexibility Instrument is capped at EUR 471 million, based on 2011 prices. If the full amount allocated for a particular year is not used, the unused funds can be carried forward and utilized up to three years later (year n+3). When using these carried-over funds, the oldest unused amounts from previous years must be applied first. However, any portion of the annual amount from year n that remains unused by the end of year n+3 will expire and no longer be available.

The Global margin for commitments for growth and employment, particularly youth employment, refers to the unused budgetary margins left below the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) ceilings for commitment appropriations during the years 2014 to 2017. These remaining margins collectively form a Global MFF Margin, which is reserved to be made available in addition to the established MFF ceilings for the years 2016 to 2020. The purpose of this margin is to support policy objectives focused on promoting growth and employment, with a special emphasis on youth employment.

Each year, the European Commission is responsible for calculating the amount available within this Global MFF Margin as part of the technical adjustment process outlined in Article 6. Subsequently, the European Parliament and the Council have the authority to mobilize all or part of this margin during the budgetary procedure, in accordance with Article 314 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU). This mechanism ensures that any unused budgetary capacity from previous years can be effectively redirected to enhance initiatives aimed at fostering economic growth and addressing youth unemployment within the EU.

The European Parliament, the Council, and the Commission are required to comply with the annual expenditure ceilings established in the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) during each budgetary procedure and throughout the implementation of the budget for the relevant year. Specifically, the sub-ceiling for Heading 2, as detailed in the Annex, is set without affecting the flexibility between the two pillars of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP). Any adjustments to the ceiling applicable to Pillar I of the CAP, resulting from transfers between the European Agricultural Fund for Rural Development and direct payments, must be specified in the relevant legal act, with the MFF being correspondingly updated through the technical adjustment mechanism outlined in Article 6(1) of the Regulation.

To maintain flexibility within the MFF and facilitate a smooth budgetary process, special instruments described in Articles 9 to 15 are established. These instruments allow commitment appropriations to be entered into the budget beyond the ceilings of the relevant MFF headings when necessary. Such cases include the use of resources from the Emergency Aid Reserve, the European Union Solidarity Fund, the Flexibility Instrument, the European Globalisation Adjustment Fund, the Contingency Margin, specific flexibility measures aimed at addressing youth unemployment and enhancing research, and the global margin for commitments supporting growth and employment, particularly youth employment. These provisions are in accordance with Council Regulation (EC) No 2012/2002, Regulation (EC) No 1927/2006, and the Interinstitutional Agreement between the European Parliament, the Council, and the Commission.

Furthermore, when a guarantee for a loan covered by the Union’s general budget under Regulation (EC) No 332/2002 or Regulation (EU) No 407/2010 needs to be activated, this guarantee is considered additional to the ceilings established in the MFF and does not count against them.

Each year, prior to the budgetary procedure for the following year (year n+1), the European Commission is required to perform a series of technical adjustments to the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF). These adjustments include: (a) revaluing the ceilings and overall figures for appropriations for commitments and payments at the prices of year n+1; (b) calculating the margin available under the own-resources ceiling as established by Decision 2007/436/EC, Euratom; (c) determining the absolute amount of the Contingency Margin outlined in Article 13; (d) calculating the global margin for payments as provided in Article 5; and (e) calculating the global margin for commitments as set out in Article 14.

The Commission bases these technical adjustments on a fixed deflator of 2% per year, ensuring consistency in the application of price changes. Once completed, the Commission communicates the results of these adjustments along with the underlying economic forecasts to both the European Parliament and the Council.

Importantly, aside from the provisions in Articles 7 and 8, no further technical adjustments are permitted for the year in question, neither during that year nor as retrospective corrections in subsequent years. This ensures stability and predictability in the financial planning process.

The Connecting Europe Facility (CEF) aims to facilitate the preparation and implementation of projects of common interest within the framework of the trans-European networks policy, focusing on the transport, telecommunications, and energy sectors. Its primary goal is to support the development and construction of new infrastructures and services, as well as the upgrading of existing ones, with a particular emphasis on addressing missing links in the transport sector. The CEF prioritizes projects that offer European added value and significant societal benefits but lack sufficient market financing.

The general objectives of the CEF across these sectors are threefold:

1. **Contributing to smart, sustainable, and inclusive growth** in line with the Europe 2020 Strategy by developing modern, high-performing trans-European networks. These networks are designed to accommodate future traffic flows, thereby enhancing the Union’s global competitiveness, promoting economic, social, and territorial cohesion within the internal market, and fostering an investment-friendly environment. This is achieved through a combination of financial instruments and direct Union support, leveraging synergies across sectors. Success in this objective is measured by the volume of private, public, or public-private partnership investments mobilized, with a particular focus on maximizing the efficient use of public funds.

2. **Supporting the Union’s sustainable development targets**, including achieving at least a 20% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions compared to 1990 levels, improving energy efficiency by 20%, and increasing the share of renewable energy to 20% by 2020. These efforts contribute to the EU’s mid- and long-term decarbonisation goals while promoting solidarity among Member States.

Through these objectives, the CEF plays a crucial role in advancing integrated, sustainable, and resilient infrastructure networks that underpin the EU’s economic growth and environmental commitments.

The Connecting Europe Facility (CEF) aims to contribute to specific sectoral objectives in transport, energy, and telecommunications, complementing its general objectives.

1. **Transport Sector Objectives**  
CEF supports projects of common interest identified under Regulation (EU) No 1315/2013, focusing on three main goals:

   (a) **Removing bottlenecks and enhancing rail interoperability**, bridging missing links, and improving cross-border sections. Success is measured by indicators such as the number of new or improved cross-border connections, kilometres of railway adapted to the European nominal gauge and equipped with ERTMS, removed bottlenecks and increased capacity sections across transport modes, length of inland waterways by class, and upgraded railway network length per regulatory requirements.

   (b) **Ensuring sustainable and efficient transport systems** to prepare for future transport flows and enable decarbonisation through innovative low-carbon and energy-efficient technologies, while optimizing safety. This is measured by the number of alternative fuel supply points on the TEN-T core road network, the number of inland and maritime ports equipped with such supply points, and reductions in road casualties.

   (c) **Optimising integration and interconnection of transport modes** and enhancing interoperability of transport services, ensuring accessibility of infrastructure. Indicators include the number of multimodal logistic platforms connected to railways, improved rail-road terminals and port connections via motorways of the sea, kilometres of inland waterways fitted with River Information Services (RIS), and deployment levels of SESAR, VTMIS, and Intelligent Transport Systems (ITS) for roads.

These indicators do not apply to Member States lacking rail or inland waterway networks and are not used as selection or eligibility criteria. Budget allocation among these objectives follows indicative percentages with limited deviation allowed.

Under Article 196 of Regulation (EU) No 1308/2013 and as provided in Article 198 of the same Regulation, the European Commission is empowered to adopt implementing acts to fix export refunds. These refunds can be set at regular intervals for products listed in Article 196(1), or through tendering procedures specifically for cereals, rice, sugar, and milk and milk products. The adoption of these implementing acts follows the examination procedure outlined in Article 15(2) of the relevant Regulation.

When determining the level of export refunds for a product, the Commission considers several factors. These include the current and anticipated prices and availability of the product both within the Union market and on the global market. The objectives of the common market organisation are also taken into account, aiming to maintain market equilibrium and support the natural development of prices and trade. Additionally, the Commission seeks to prevent disturbances that could cause prolonged imbalances between supply and demand in the Union market.

Other considerations include the economic viability of the proposed exports, compliance with limits set by international agreements, and balancing the use of Union-produced basic products in processed goods for export against the use of third-country products under processing arrangements. The Commission also evaluates the most favorable marketing and transport costs from Union markets to export points and onward to destination countries, as well as demand within the Union market. For specific sectors such as pigmeat, eggs, and poultrymeat, the price difference between Union and world markets is assessed relative to the feed grain input required for production.

To respond swiftly to rapidly changing market conditions, the Commission may adjust the amount of export refunds through implementing acts without following the examination procedure, either on its own initiative or upon request from a Member State.

However, Articles 7 to 12 are set to apply only until the end of the 2016/17 marketing year for sugar, which concludes on 30 September 2017. The Regulation is binding in its entirety and is directly applicable in all Member States.

The public intervention prices for various agricultural products are established with specific guidelines as follows:

1. The level of the public intervention price is set according to the type of product and the method of buying-in:
   (a) For common wheat, durum wheat, barley, maize, paddy rice, and skimmed milk powder, the intervention price shall be equal to the respective reference threshold specified in Article 7 of Regulation (EU) No 1308/2013 when buying-in occurs at a fixed price. In cases where buying-in is conducted by tendering, the price shall not exceed the respective reference threshold.
   (b) For butter, the intervention price shall be set at 90% of the reference threshold outlined in Article 7 of Regulation (EU) No 1308/2013 for fixed price buying-in, and shall not exceed 90% of that threshold when buying-in is by tendering.
   (c) For beef and veal, the intervention price shall not exceed the level indicated in point (c) of Article 13(1) of Regulation (EU) No 1308/2013.

2. The public intervention prices for common wheat, durum wheat, barley, maize, and paddy rice mentioned above shall be adjusted upwards or downwards based on the main quality criteria relevant to each product.

3. The European Commission is responsible for adopting implementing acts that specify the exact increases or reductions to the public intervention prices for these products, in accordance with the conditions set out in the regulation. These implementing acts are to be adopted following the examination procedure described in Article 15(2).

In summary, public intervention prices are carefully regulated to align with reference thresholds, adjusted for product quality, and formally established through Commission implementing acts to ensure transparency and consistency in the agricultural market.

Under the rules governing public intervention buying-in prices and quantitative limitations, the following provisions apply:

1. When public intervention is open pursuant to point (a) of Article 13(1) of Regulation (EU) No 1308/2013, buying-in must be conducted at the fixed price specified in Article 2 of the Regulation. The quantities bought in must not exceed the following limits for each period defined in Article 12 of the same Regulation:
   - Common wheat: 3 million tonnes
   - Butter: 50,000 tonnes
   - Skimmed milk powder: 109,000 tonnes

   However, as a derogation for the year 2016, the quantitative limits for butter and skimmed milk powder were doubled to 100,000 tonnes and 218,000 tonnes respectively. Additionally, any volumes bought in under tendering procedures ongoing as of 19 April 2016 are excluded from these limits.

2. For quantities exceeding these limits for common wheat, butter, and skimmed milk powder, as well as for durum wheat, barley, maize, paddy rice, and beef and veal, buying-in must be carried out through a tendering procedure. This procedure determines the maximum buying-in price, which cannot exceed the relevant level set out in Article 2(1) of the Regulation and is established by implementing acts.

3. In special and justified cases, the Commission may adopt implementing acts to:
   - Restrict tendering procedures to a specific Member State or region.
   - Set buying-in prices per Member State or region based on recorded average market prices, subject to Article 2(1).

4. For cereals such as common wheat, durum wheat, barley, maize, and paddy rice, the buying-in prices established under paragraphs 2 and 3 are adjusted according to main quality criteria. The Commission adopts implementing acts to determine these price adjustments.

5. The implementing acts mentioned in paragraphs 2, 3, and 4 are adopted following the examination procedure outlined in Article 15(2).

6. The Commission also adopts implementing acts without applying the examination procedure to:
   - Ensure compliance with the intervention quantity limits set in paragraph 1.
   - Apply the tendering procedure for common wheat, butter, and skimmed milk powder when quantities exceed the limits in paragraph 1.

The production refund for products in the sugar sector, as outlined in Article 129 of Regulation (EU) No 1308/2013, is determined by the European Commission through implementing acts. These acts set the refund amount based on two key factors: (a) the costs that the sugar industry would incur if it had to source sugar from the world market, reflecting the expenses related to using imported sugar; and (b) the price of surplus sugar available within the Union market. In cases where no surplus sugar is available on the Union market, the refund is based on the reference threshold price for sugar specified in point (c) of Article 7(1) of Regulation (EU) No 1308/2013. The adoption of these implementing acts follows the examination procedure described in Article 15(2) of the same Regulation, ensuring a structured and transparent decision-making process.

The rules establishing common marketing standards continue to apply as set out in various Council and Commission Regulations. Specifically, the provisions laid down in Council Regulation (EEC) No 2136/89, Council Regulation (EEC) No 1536/92, and Council Regulation (EC) No 2406/96 remain in force, along with other related rules such as those in Commission Regulation (EEC) No 3703/85. These regulations collectively govern the common marketing standards to ensure consistency across the market. Furthermore, when minimum conservation reference sizes are established for certain products, these sizes automatically become the minimum marketing sizes, ensuring that only products meeting these size criteria can be marketed. This approach helps maintain product quality and sustainability within the market framework.

A multiannual plan shall include several key components to ensure sustainable fisheries management. Firstly, it must define the scope, specifying the stocks, fisheries, and geographic areas to which the plan applies. It should set objectives aligned with the overarching goals outlined in Article 2 and relevant provisions in Articles 6 and 9. The plan must establish quantifiable targets, such as fishing mortality rates and spawning stock biomass, accompanied by clear time-frames for achieving these targets. Conservation reference points consistent with the objectives in Article 2 are also required.

Additionally, the plan should outline objectives for conservation and technical measures aimed at meeting the targets set out in Article 15, including actions to avoid and reduce unwanted catches as much as possible. Safeguards must be included to ensure that quantifiable targets are met, along with remedial actions to address situations where data quality deteriorates or is unavailable, potentially threatening stock sustainability.

Beyond these mandatory elements, a multiannual plan may incorporate other conservation measures, particularly those aimed at gradually eliminating discards and minimizing the negative impacts of fishing on the ecosystem, guided by the best available scientific advice and in accordance with Article 18 where appropriate. It may also include quantifiable indicators for periodic monitoring and assessment of progress, as well as specific objectives related to the freshwater phases of anadromous and catadromous species’ life cycles.

Finally, the plan must provide for its revision following an initial ex-post evaluation, especially to incorporate changes in scientific advice, ensuring adaptive and responsive management over time.

The landing obligation, as established under the Common Fisheries Policy (CFP), requires that all catches of species subject to catch limits—and in the Mediterranean, also species subject to minimum sizes as defined in Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 1967/2006—caught in Union waters or by Union fishing vessels outside Union waters (in areas not under third-country sovereignty or jurisdiction) must be brought and retained on board, recorded, landed, and counted against quotas where applicable. Exceptions apply only when catches are used as live bait.

The implementation of the landing obligation has been phased in according to fishery types and geographical areas, with key deadlines as follows:

- From 1 January 2015, the obligation applies to small pelagic fisheries (e.g., mackerel, herring, sardine), large pelagic fisheries (e.g., bluefin tuna, swordfish), fisheries for industrial purposes (e.g., capelin, sandeel), and salmon fisheries in the Baltic Sea.

- Also from 1 January 2015 for species defining fisheries in the Baltic Sea, and by 1 January 2017 for all other species subject to catch limits in that area.

- From 1 January 2016 for species defining fisheries, and by 1 January 2019 for other species in the North Sea, North Western waters, South Western waters, and other fisheries subject to catch limits. These include fisheries for cod, haddock, whiting, saithe, Norway lobster, common sole, plaice, hake, Northern prawn, among others.

- From 1 January 2017 for species defining fisheries, and by 1 January 2019 for other species in the Mediterranean, Black Sea, other Union waters, and non-Union waters not under third-country jurisdiction.

The landing obligation respects the Union’s international obligations, and the European Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts to implement these, including possible derogations.

Member States with direct management interests in a fishery may jointly recommend extending the landing obligation to additional species beyond those listed, subject to Commission approval through delegated acts.

Certain exemptions to the landing obligation exist, including:

- Species for which fishing is prohibited by Union law.

- Species with scientific evidence of high survival rates after discard, considering gear, practices, and ecosystem.

- De minimis exemptions allowing up to 5% of total annual catches of species subject to the landing obligation, under specific conditions such as difficulty in increasing selectivity or disproportionate handling costs.

- Fish damaged by predators.

Article 18 outlines the framework for regional cooperation among Member States on conservation measures within the Union’s fisheries management. When the Commission is empowered—such as through multiannual plans or specific provisions—to adopt delegated or implementing acts for Union conservation measures in a given geographical area, Member States with a direct management interest in those areas have the opportunity to collaborate. They may submit joint recommendations aimed at achieving the objectives of the relevant conservation measures, multiannual plans, or discard plans within a specified deadline. The Commission must wait until this deadline expires before adopting any such measures.

To facilitate this process, Member States are required to cooperate closely in formulating joint recommendations and consult relevant Advisory Councils. The Commission supports this cooperation, including by ensuring scientific input from appropriate bodies. If joint recommendations are submitted and deemed compatible with the conservation measures and plans, the Commission may proceed to adopt the measures accordingly.

In cases where the conservation measures concern fish stocks shared with third countries and managed through multilateral organizations or agreements, the Union commits to working with these partners to agree on necessary measures to meet conservation objectives.

Joint recommendations must be grounded in the best available scientific advice and meet several criteria: compatibility with the overarching objectives of the conservation measures and multiannual plans, effectiveness in achieving quantifiable targets, and at least equal stringency compared to existing Union law.

Should Member States fail to agree on joint recommendations within the deadline, or if the recommendations do not align with the conservation objectives, the Commission may propose appropriate measures under the Treaty.

Beyond the formal joint recommendations, Member States with direct management interests may also submit joint recommendations on other measures to the Commission. Additionally, as an alternative or supplementary approach, Member States may adopt further detailed measures within a set deadline to specify Union conservation measures, provided they cooperate closely, involve the Commission, and reach unanimous agreement. The Commission retains the right to request amendments or repeal of national measures that do not comply with the relevant conservation conditions.

Overall, Article 18 establishes a structured, cooperative process that balances regional input and scientific advice with Commission oversight to ensure effective and consistent conservation efforts across the Union’s fisheries management areas.

The Common Fisheries Policy (CFP) is designed to ensure that fishing and aquaculture activities are environmentally sustainable over the long term while simultaneously delivering economic, social, and employment benefits and contributing to food supply security. Central to the CFP is the application of the precautionary approach to fisheries management, aiming to restore and maintain fish populations above levels capable of producing the maximum sustainable yield (MSY). The policy sets clear targets to achieve MSY exploitation rates by 2015 where possible, and progressively by 2020 for all stocks, thereby promoting the recovery and sustainable use of marine biological resources.

To minimize the negative impacts of fishing on marine ecosystems, the CFP implements an ecosystem-based approach, striving to avoid environmental degradation from both fisheries and aquaculture activities. It also emphasizes the importance of scientific data collection to inform management decisions. Key measures include the gradual elimination of discards by reducing unwanted catches and ensuring catches are landed, making the best use of unwanted catches without encouraging markets for undersized fish, and adjusting fishing fleet capacity to align with sustainable fishing opportunities.

The CFP supports the economic viability and competitiveness of the fishing and processing industries, promotes sustainable aquaculture development to enhance food security and employment, and seeks to ensure a fair standard of living for those dependent on fishing, particularly in coastal communities. It also fosters an efficient and transparent internal market for fisheries and aquaculture products, balancing the interests of consumers and producers. Finally, the CFP is designed to be coherent with broader Union environmental legislation, notably aiming to achieve good environmental status by 2020, and aligns with other Union policies to ensure integrated and sustainable management of marine resources.

Promoting sustainable aquaculture is a key objective aimed at enhancing food security, supporting economic growth, and creating employment opportunities within the European Union. To achieve this, the Commission is tasked with establishing non-binding Union strategic guidelines that outline common priorities and targets for sustainable aquaculture development. These guidelines are designed to consider the diverse starting points and circumstances across Member States and serve as a foundation for multiannual national strategic plans.

The strategic guidelines focus on several core aims: improving the competitiveness of the aquaculture industry through development and innovation; reducing administrative burdens to streamline the implementation of Union law; encouraging economic activity; fostering diversification and enhancing the quality of life in coastal and inland areas; and integrating aquaculture into maritime, coastal, and inland spatial planning.

By 30 June 2014, each Member State is required to develop a multiannual national strategic plan detailing their objectives, measures, and timelines for aquaculture development. These plans emphasize administrative simplification, particularly in evaluations, impact studies, and licensing processes, and aim to provide aquaculture operators with reasonable certainty regarding access to waters and space. They also include indicators to monitor environmental, economic, and social sustainability, assess potential cross-border effects on marine resources and ecosystems, and promote synergies between national research programs and industry-science collaboration.

Furthermore, the plans seek to enhance the competitive advantage of sustainable, high-quality aquaculture products and encourage practices and research that maximize positive environmental impacts while minimizing negative ones. This includes efforts to reduce pressure on fish stocks used for feed and to improve resource efficiency.

To support these objectives, Member States are encouraged to exchange information and best practices through an open method of coordination, with the Commission facilitating this exchange and the coordination of national measures. This collaborative approach aims to foster a sustainable, innovative, and competitive aquaculture sector across the Union.

The Regulation will enter into force on the day after its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union. However, its provisions will apply starting from 1 January 2014. Once in force, the Regulation is binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States, ensuring uniform implementation across the European Union.

Conservation measures for the sustainable exploitation of marine biological resources encompass a variety of strategies aimed at preserving fish stocks and minimizing the environmental impact of fishing activities. Seven key types of conservation measures include:

1. **Multiannual Plans**: These are long-term management plans designed to regulate fishing activities over several years, ensuring sustainable exploitation of fish stocks and compliance with conservation objectives.

2. **Stock Conservation Targets and Environmental Impact Minimization**: Setting specific targets for the conservation and sustainable use of fish stocks, alongside measures to reduce the negative effects of fishing on marine ecosystems.

3. **Fishing Capacity Adaptation**: Adjusting the fishing capacity of vessels to align with available fishing opportunities, preventing overfishing and promoting resource sustainability.

4. **Incentives for Selective and Low-Impact Fishing**: Economic and other incentives encourage fishers to adopt selective fishing methods that reduce unwanted catches and minimize harm to marine ecosystems.

5. **Allocation and Fixing of Fishing Opportunities**: Establishing rules for the distribution of fishing quotas and opportunities to ensure fair and sustainable use of marine resources.

6. **Minimum Conservation Reference Sizes**: Implementing size limits for catches to protect juvenile fish and allow populations to replenish.

7. **Technical Measures**: These include regulations on fishing gear characteristics and usage, such as modifications to improve selectivity, reduce bycatch of endangered species, restrictions on gear types or fishing in certain areas or periods, and temporary closures to protect vulnerable species during critical times like spawning.

Together, these measures form a comprehensive framework to promote the conservation and sustainable exploitation of marine biological resources, balancing ecological protection with the economic needs of fishing communities.

The Commission has the authority to review the suspensions for the products listed in Annex I under two circumstances: first, on its own initiative, and second, upon a request from Member States. Additionally, the Commission is required to conduct a review of these suspensions in the specific year indicated in Annex I. This ensures that the status of the suspensions is regularly evaluated either proactively by the Commission or reactively based on Member States' concerns, maintaining an up-to-date and responsive regulatory framework.

When a declaration for release for free circulation is submitted for products classified under the CN codes or TARIC codes specified in Annex II, it is mandatory to enter the supplementary unit indicated in that Annex into the appropriate field of the declaration. This ensures that the customs authorities receive complete and accurate information regarding the quantity measurement of the goods, facilitating proper processing and compliance with regulatory requirements. The supplementary unit complements the primary unit of measurement and is essential for correctly assessing duties, taxes, and statistical data related to the products.

The resolution authority is responsible for drawing up a resolution plan for each institution that is not part of a group subject to consolidated supervision under Articles 111 and 112 of Directive 2013/36/EU. This process involves consultation with the competent authority and, where relevant, with resolution authorities of jurisdictions hosting significant branches. The resolution plan outlines the resolution actions the authority may take if the institution meets the conditions for resolution, and key information must be disclosed to the institution concerned.

When preparing the resolution plan, the authority must identify any material impediments to resolvability and, if necessary and proportionate, propose actions to address these impediments in line with Chapter II of the Title. The plan must consider various scenarios, including idiosyncratic failures and broader financial or systemic crises, without assuming extraordinary public financial support beyond established financing arrangements, nor central bank emergency or non-standard liquidity assistance.

The plan should analyze how and when the institution might access central bank facilities under the conditions addressed, identifying assets likely to qualify as collateral. Institutions may be required to assist in drafting and updating the plans. Resolution plans must be reviewed and updated at least annually or following material changes to the institution’s legal, organizational, business, or financial situation that could affect the plan’s effectiveness. Institutions and competent authorities must promptly communicate any such changes to the resolution authority.

The resolution plan must set out options for applying resolution tools and powers, including quantified summaries where appropriate. It should cover key elements such as material changes since the last plan, legal and economic separation of critical functions and core business lines to ensure continuity, estimated timeframes for execution, detailed resolvability assessments, and measures to address impediments. The plan must describe processes for valuing critical functions and assets, arrangements for maintaining up-to-date information, and explanations of how resolution options could be financed without extraordinary public or central bank support.

Additionally, the plan should detail different resolution strategies for various scenarios and timelines, critical interdependencies, options for preserving access to payment and clearing services, portability of client positions, and the impact on employees including consultation procedures. It must include a communication plan for media and public engagement, minimum requirements for own funds and eligible liabilities with deadlines, descriptions of essential operations and systems, and any opinions expressed by the institution regarding the plan.
