Directive 2001/24/EC has been amended to extend its scope and clarify its interaction with other EU financial regulations, particularly concerning investment firms and resolution frameworks. Specifically, new paragraphs (3) to (6) have been added to Article 1:

- Paragraph 3 establishes that the Directive now also applies to investment firms as defined in point (2) of Article 4(1) of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013, including their branches located in Member States other than where their head offices are situated. This broadens the Directive’s applicability beyond traditional credit institutions to include investment firms under the prudential requirements regulation.

- Paragraph 4 states that when resolution tools and powers under Directive 2014/59/EU (the Bank Recovery and Resolution Directive) are applied, Directive 2001/24/EC also applies to the financial institutions, firms, and parent undertakings within the scope of Directive 2014/59/EU. This ensures consistency and coordination between the resolution framework and the Directive on the reorganization and winding up of credit institutions.

- Paragraphs 5 and 6 provide that certain provisions of Directive 2001/24/EC—specifically Articles 4 and 7, and Article 33—do not apply where corresponding provisions in Directive 2014/59/EU (Articles 83 and 84, respectively) are applicable. This avoids overlapping or conflicting rules between the two Directives in the context of resolution proceedings.

These amendments integrate Directive 2001/24/EC more closely with the prudential regulation of investment firms and the EU’s recovery and resolution framework, reflecting developments in the EU’s financial regulatory architecture aimed at enhancing financial stability and the orderly resolution of financial institutions.

The 120th Amendment to Directive 2005/56/EC introduces a new paragraph 4 to Article 3, specifying an important exclusion. According to this amendment, Member States are required to ensure that Directive 2005/56/EC does not apply to companies that are subject to the use of resolution tools, powers, and mechanisms outlined in Title IV of Directive 2014/59/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council. This means that companies undergoing resolution procedures under the framework established by Directive 2014/59/EU—commonly known as the Bank Recovery and Resolution Directive (BRRD)—are exempt from the provisions of Directive 2005/56/EC, which primarily governs cross-border mergers of limited liability companies. The amendment aims to prevent conflicts between the rules governing company mergers and those designed to manage the resolution of failing financial institutions, thereby ensuring legal clarity and regulatory coherence within the EU framework.

Directive 2007/36/EC has been amended to clarify its relationship with the resolution framework established under Directive 2014/59/EU. Specifically:

1. A new paragraph 4 has been added to Article 1, stipulating that Member States must ensure that Directive 2007/36/EC does not apply when resolution tools, powers, and mechanisms under Title IV of Directive 2014/59/EU are used. This ensures that the recovery and resolution framework for credit institutions and investment firms takes precedence in such situations.

2. Article 5 has been supplemented with paragraphs 5 and 6 to facilitate certain procedural flexibilities in the context of Directive 2014/59/EU. Paragraph 5 allows the general meeting, by a two-thirds majority of votes cast, to convene or modify the statutes to allow convening a general meeting on shorter notice than normally required, specifically to decide on a capital increase. This shorter notice is permitted provided the meeting is held at least ten calendar days after convocation, the conditions in Articles 27 or 29 of Directive 2014/59/EU are met, and the capital increase is necessary to prevent resolution conditions under Articles 32 and 33 of that Directive.

Paragraph 6 exempts such meetings from certain procedural requirements in Directive 2007/36/EC, namely the obligation to set a single deadline for convening (Article 6(3)), the timely availability of a revised agenda (Article 6(4)), and the setting of a single record date (Article 7(3)).

Together, these amendments ensure that shareholder rights and meeting procedures under Directive 2007/36/EC are adapted to accommodate the urgent and exceptional measures required under the EU’s bank recovery and resolution framework.

The conditions for resolution concerning financial institutions and holding companies are established to ensure effective intervention by resolution authorities within Member States. Firstly, resolution authorities are empowered to take resolution actions regarding a financial institution as defined in point (b) of Article 1(1) only when the conditions specified in Article 32(1) are satisfied both for the financial institution itself and its parent undertaking under consolidated supervision. This dual requirement ensures that both the individual institution and its overarching parent entity meet the criteria for resolution.

Secondly, for entities referred to in points (c) or (d) of Article 1(1), resolution actions may be initiated when the conditions in Article 32(1) apply to both the entity itself and one or more of its subsidiaries that are institutions. In cases where a subsidiary is located outside the Union, resolution can proceed if the relevant third-country authority confirms that the subsidiary meets the resolution conditions under its local law.

Thirdly, in situations involving mixed-activity holding companies whose subsidiary institutions are held through an intermediate financial holding company, resolution actions aimed at group resolution must be directed at the intermediate financial holding company rather than the mixed-activity holding company. This approach centralizes resolution efforts at the appropriate level within the corporate structure.

Lastly, even if an entity under points (c) or (d) of Article 1(1) does not itself meet the resolution conditions of Article 32(1), resolution authorities may still act if one or more of its subsidiary institutions do meet these conditions (including those in paragraphs (4) and (5) of Article 32), and if the failure of these subsidiaries poses a threat to the institution, the group as a whole, or if insolvency laws require group-wide treatment. In such cases, resolution action concerning the parent entity is necessary to effectively resolve the subsidiaries or the entire group. When assessing whether subsidiaries meet the resolution conditions, resolution authorities of both the subsidiaries and the parent entity may jointly agree to disregard intra-group capital or loss transfers, including the use of write-down or conversion powers, to ensure an accurate evaluation of the financial situation.

Together, these provisions establish a comprehensive framework that allows resolution authorities to act decisively and cohesively across different levels of financial groups, ensuring stability and minimizing systemic risk within the financial sector.

Article 52 outlines the requirements and procedures for preparing, submitting, assessing, and implementing a business reorganisation plan following the application of the bail-in tool to certain financial institutions or entities within the EU.

1. **Submission Deadline and Responsibility:** Member States must ensure that within one month after the bail-in tool is applied to an institution or entity (as defined in Article 1(1) points (b), (c), or (d)), the management body or appointed persons (per Article 72(1)) prepare and submit a business reorganisation plan to the resolution authority. If the Union State aid framework applies, the plan must be compatible with the restructuring plan submitted to the European Commission under that framework.

2. **Group Entities:** If the bail-in tool is applied to multiple group entities, the Union parent institution must prepare a consolidated business reorganisation plan covering all group institutions. This plan is submitted to the group-level resolution authority, which then shares it with other relevant resolution authorities and the European Banking Authority (EBA).

3. **Extension of Deadline:** In exceptional cases, the resolution authority may extend the one-month deadline for submitting the plan up to two months after the bail-in application. If the Union State aid framework applies, the extension cannot exceed the earlier of two months or the framework’s deadline.

4. **Content and Assumptions:** The business reorganisation plan must outline measures to restore the long-term viability of the institution or entity within a reasonable timeframe. These measures should be based on realistic economic and financial market assumptions, considering best- and worst-case scenarios and identifying the institution’s main vulnerabilities. Assumptions must be benchmarked against sector-wide data.

5. **Required Elements:** The plan must include:
   - A detailed diagnosis of the causes and circumstances leading to the institution’s failure or likely failure.
   - A description of the measures intended to restore long-term viability.
   - A timetable for implementing these measures.

6. **Possible Measures:** Measures to restore viability may involve:
   - Reorganising activities.
   - Changing operational systems and infrastructure.
   - Withdrawing from loss-making activities.
   - Restructuring competitive activities.
   - Selling assets or business lines.

7. **Assessment and Approval:** Within one month of submission, the resolution authority, in agreement with the competent authority, assesses whether the plan is likely to restore long-term viability. If satisfied, the plan is approved.

8. **Amendments:** If the plan is deemed insufficient, the resolution authority notifies the management body or appointed persons

Article 61 outlines the authorities responsible for making the determinations referred to in Article 59(3) of the Directive. Member States are required to ensure that these authorities are those specified in this Article. Each Member State must designate, through national law, the appropriate authority responsible for such determinations, which may be either the competent authority or the resolution authority as defined under Article 32.

When relevant capital instruments are recognized for meeting own funds requirements on an individual basis pursuant to Article 92 of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013, the authority responsible for the determination under Article 59(3) shall be the appropriate authority of the Member State where the institution or entity (as defined in points (b), (c), or (d) of Article 1(1)) is authorized according to Title III of Directive 2013/36/EU.

In cases where relevant capital instruments are issued by a subsidiary institution or entity and are recognized for own funds requirements both individually and on a consolidated basis, the responsibility for making the determinations under Article 59(3) is divided as follows:

- The appropriate authority of the Member State where the issuing institution or entity is established shall make the determinations referred to in point (b) of Article 59(3).

- The appropriate authority of the consolidating supervisor’s Member State, together with the authority of the Member State where the issuing institution or entity is established, shall jointly make the determination referred to in point (c) of Article 59(3), taking the form of a joint decision.

This framework ensures clarity and coordination between national authorities in supervising and regulating capital instruments within the EU banking and financial system.

Article 63 outlines the general powers granted to resolution authorities to effectively apply resolution tools to financial institutions and certain related entities that meet the conditions for resolution. Member States are required to ensure that resolution authorities possess all necessary powers, which they may exercise individually or in combination, to manage and resolve institutions in distress.

Key powers include the authority to:

- Request any information needed to prepare and decide on resolution actions, including through on-site inspections.
- Take control of an institution under resolution, exercising all rights and powers of shareholders, owners, and management.
- Transfer shares or ownership instruments of the institution.
- Transfer rights, assets, or liabilities to another entity with that entity’s consent.
- Reduce or write down eligible liabilities, including reducing them to zero.
- Convert eligible liabilities into ordinary shares or other ownership instruments of the institution or related entities.
- Cancel debt instruments, except secured liabilities as specified.
- Reduce or cancel shares or ownership instruments.
- Require the institution or its parent to issue new shares or capital instruments.
- Amend the maturity or interest terms of debt instruments, including temporarily suspending payments, except for secured liabilities.
- Close out and terminate financial or derivatives contracts as necessary.
- Remove or replace the management body and senior management.
- Require timely assessment of buyers of qualifying holdings, overriding usual procedural time limits.

Furthermore, Member States must ensure that resolution authorities can exercise these powers without needing approval or consent from any public or private parties, including shareholders or creditors, and without prior procedural notifications or filings that would otherwise be required under national law or contracts. This ensures swift and effective resolution actions.

If certain powers are not applicable to an entity due to its legal form, Member States must provide resolution authorities with similar powers that achieve comparable effects. Additionally, safeguards equivalent to those in the Directive must be applied to affected persons, such as shareholders, creditors, and counterparties, to protect their rights during the exercise of these powers.

In summary, Article 63 empowers resolution authorities with comprehensive tools to manage the resolution of financial institutions efficiently, while ensuring necessary legal safeguards and minimizing procedural obstacles.

The Directive establishes specific exclusions regarding the treatment of certain contractual terms in the context of early intervention and resolution measures applied to entities. Specifically, any crisis prevention or crisis management measure taken under this Directive, including any event directly linked to such measures, shall not automatically be considered an enforcement event under Directive 2002/47/EC (which governs financial collateral arrangements) or as insolvency proceedings under Directive 98/26/EC (which relates to settlement finality), provided that the substantive contractual obligations—such as payment, delivery, and collateral provision—continue to be fulfilled.

This exclusion applies not only to contracts entered into by the entity subject to the measure but also extends to contracts involving subsidiaries whose obligations are guaranteed or supported by the parent or other group entities, as well as to any group entity contracts containing cross-default provisions. In other words, the mere application of a crisis prevention or management measure does not trigger enforcement rights, insolvency proceedings, or cross-default clauses by itself.

Furthermore, when third-country resolution proceedings are recognized under Article 94 or when a resolution authority designates such proceedings as crisis management measures, these proceedings are also covered by the same exclusion.

Importantly, as long as the substantive obligations continue to be performed, no party may, solely due to the crisis measure or related events, exercise rights such as termination, suspension, modification, netting, or set-off; take possession or control of property; enforce security interests; or otherwise affect contractual rights related to the entity or its group companies under contracts with cross-default provisions.

However, this Article does not prevent parties from exercising such rights if they arise from events unrelated to the crisis prevention or management measures. Additionally, any suspension or restriction imposed under Articles 69, 70, or 71 shall not be considered a failure to perform contractual obligations for the purposes of these exclusions.

Finally, the provisions of this Article are deemed overriding mandatory provisions under Article 9 of Regulation (EC) No 593/2008, meaning they take precedence over conflicting contractual or legal provisions within the EU. This ensures that crisis prevention and resolution measures can be implemented effectively without triggering automatic contractual enforcement or insolvency consequences that could undermine financial stability.

Article 16 sets out the organisational requirements that investment firms must comply with, as mandated by their home Member State. These requirements ensure that firms operate with adequate internal controls, risk management, and client protection measures.

Firstly, investment firms must establish comprehensive policies and procedures to guarantee compliance with the Directive, covering all personnel including managers, employees, and tied agents. This includes rules on personal transactions to prevent conflicts of interest.

Firms are required to maintain effective organisational and administrative arrangements to prevent conflicts of interest from harming client interests. For firms that manufacture financial instruments, a robust product approval process must be in place before marketing or distribution. This process should identify the target market, assess relevant risks, and ensure the distribution strategy aligns with the target market. Regular reviews of financial instruments are also mandated to confirm ongoing suitability and appropriateness. When offering or recommending instruments not manufactured by the firm, adequate arrangements must be made to understand the product characteristics and target market.

To ensure service continuity and regularity, firms must employ appropriate systems, resources, and procedures. When outsourcing critical operational functions, firms must take reasonable steps to avoid additional operational risks and ensure that outsourcing does not impair internal controls or supervisory oversight.

Investment firms must have sound administrative, accounting, and internal control procedures, including effective risk assessment and information security measures. These security mechanisms must protect data confidentiality, prevent unauthorized access, and ensure secure information transfer.

Record-keeping obligations require firms to maintain comprehensive records of all services, activities, and transactions to enable competent authorities to supervise and enforce compliance. This includes recording telephone conversations and electronic communications related to client orders and transactions, with appropriate client notification and consent. Records must be retained for at least five years, extendable to seven years upon request.

When holding client financial instruments or funds, firms must safeguard client ownership rights and prevent unauthorized use of these assets for the firm’s own account, except with explicit client consent. Title transfer financial collateral arrangements with retail clients are prohibited.

For branches of investment firms, the local competent authority enforces record-keeping obligations, while home Member State authorities retain supervisory access. Member States may impose additional safeguarding requirements on client assets if objectively justified and proportionate, notifying the Commission in advance. The Commission reviews and publicly communicates such additional requirements.

Finally, the Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts to specify detailed organisational requirements tailored to different types of investment services, activities, and ancillary services performed by investment firms and branches of third-country firms.

In summary, Article 16 ensures that investment firms operate with robust organisational structures, risk controls, transparency, and client

The specific requirements for Multilateral Trading Facilities (MTFs) set out several obligations for investment firms and market operators operating such platforms. Firstly, in addition to complying with the general requirements in Articles 16 and 18, they must establish and implement non-discretionary rules for the execution of orders within the MTF system. Access rules to the MTF must also comply with the conditions specified in Article 53(3).

Furthermore, these firms and operators are required to have robust arrangements to manage operational risks effectively. This includes being adequately equipped to identify and mitigate significant risks, ensuring efficient and timely finalisation of transactions, and maintaining sufficient financial resources at all times to support the orderly functioning of the MTF, considering the nature and extent of transactions and associated risks.

Certain provisions, specifically Articles 24, 25, 27(1), (2), (4) to (10), and 28, do not apply to transactions concluded under MTF rules between members or participants or between the MTF and its members or participants regarding the use of the MTF. However, when members or participants execute orders on behalf of clients through the MTF, they must comply with the obligations in these Articles concerning their clients.

Lastly, Member States must prohibit investment firms or market operators running an MTF from executing client orders against their own proprietary capital or engaging in matched principal trading, ensuring a clear separation between client orders and the firm’s own trading activities.

The Directive sets out specific exemptions under which its provisions do not apply. These exemptions include a variety of entities and activities, summarized as follows:

1. **Insurance and Reinsurance Undertakings**: Insurance companies and those engaged in reinsurance and retrocession activities as defined in Directive 2009/138/EC are exempt when performing those activities.

2. **Intra-Group Investment Services**: Persons providing investment services exclusively to their parent companies, subsidiaries, or other subsidiaries within the same group are exempt.

3. **Incidental Investment Services in Regulated Professions**: Professionals who provide investment services incidentally during their regulated professional activities, governed by legal or ethical codes that do not prohibit such services, are exempt.

4. **Persons Dealing on Own Account in Certain Financial Instruments**: Those dealing on their own account in financial instruments other than commodity derivatives or emission allowances (or their derivatives) and not providing other investment services or activities are exempt unless they are market makers, members or participants of regulated markets or multilateral trading facilities (MTFs), have direct electronic access to trading venues, use high-frequency algorithmic trading, or deal on own account when executing client orders. Persons exempt under insurance or certain other points do not need to meet these conditions.

5. **Operators under Emission Trading Schemes**: Operators subject to Directive 2003/87/EC who deal in emission allowances on own account without executing client orders and do not use high-frequency algorithmic trading are exempt.

6. **Employee-Participation Scheme Administrators**: Persons providing investment services solely related to the administration of employee-participation schemes, or combined with intra-group investment services, are exempt.

7. **Public and International Financial Institutions**: Members of the European System of Central Banks (ESCB), national bodies managing public debt, and international financial institutions established by multiple Member States to provide financial assistance are exempt.

8. **Collective Investment Undertakings and Pension Funds**: These entities, along with their depositaries and managers, are exempt.

9. **Persons Dealing in Commodity Derivatives or Emission Allowances**: Those dealing on own account (including market makers) or providing investment services related to commodity derivatives or emission allowances to customers or suppliers of their main business are exempt if these activities are ancillary to their main business, do not involve high-frequency algorithmic trading, and they notify the competent authority annually.

The Directive allows Member States to optionally exempt certain persons from its application, provided specific conditions are met. These optional exemptions apply to persons for whom the Member State is the home Member State, and whose activities are authorised and regulated at the national level. The exemptions are subject to the following key criteria:

1. **Scope of Activities and Restrictions**  
   - The exempt persons **must not hold client funds or client securities**, and therefore cannot place themselves in debit with their clients at any time.  
   - They are **only permitted to provide limited investment services**, specifically:  
     - Reception and transmission of orders in transferable securities and units in collective investment undertakings, and/or  
     - Provision of investment advice related to such financial instruments.  
   - When transmitting orders, these persons may only transmit to:  
     - Investment firms authorised under the Directive;  
     - Credit institutions authorised under Directive 2013/36/EU;  
     - Branches of investment firms or credit institutions authorised in third countries that comply with prudential rules deemed equivalent to those in the Directive or related EU regulations;  
     - Collective investment undertakings authorised to market units to the public and their managers; or  
     - Investment companies with fixed capital whose securities are listed or traded on a regulated market in a Member State.

2. **Specialized Exemptions for Hedging Services**  
   - Persons providing investment services exclusively in commodities, emission allowances, and/or derivatives thereof for hedging commercial risks of clients who are exclusively local electricity or natural gas undertakings (as defined in relevant EU energy directives), provided these clients jointly hold 100% of the capital or voting rights and exercise joint control, and are themselves exempt if they provide such services.  
   - Persons providing investment services exclusively in emission allowances and/or derivatives thereof for hedging commercial risks of clients who are exclusively operators under Directive 2003/87/EC, under similar ownership and control conditions as above.

3. **National Regulatory Requirements**  
   Member States must ensure that persons exempted under these provisions are subject to national requirements that are at least analogous to certain key provisions of the Directive, including:  
   - Authorisation and ongoing supervision procedures;  
   - Conduct of business obligations;  
   - Organisational requirements.  
   Additionally, exempt persons must be covered by an investor-compensation scheme recognized under Directive 97/9/EC, or alternatively, hold professional indemnity insurance that provides equivalent client protection, considering their size, risk profile, and legal nature.

Member States are required to ensure that investment firms and market operators running a Multilateral Trading Facility (MTF) or an Organised Trading Facility (OTF) put in place and maintain effective arrangements and procedures tailored to the specific MTF or OTF. These arrangements must enable the regular monitoring of compliance by members, participants, or users with the platform’s rules. This includes continuous oversight of orders submitted, cancellations, and transactions executed within their systems to detect any breaches of rules, disorderly trading conditions, conduct potentially prohibited under Regulation (EU) No 596/2014 (Market Abuse Regulation), or system disruptions related to financial instruments. Adequate resources must be allocated to ensure that such monitoring is thorough and effective.

Furthermore, investment firms and market operators are obligated to promptly notify their competent authority of any significant rule infringements, disorderly trading, suspicious conduct under the Market Abuse Regulation, or system disruptions. Upon receiving such information, competent authorities must share it with the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) and the competent authorities of other Member States. However, in cases involving conduct that may constitute market abuse, notification to other Member States and ESMA should only occur once the competent authority is convinced that such behavior has taken place or is ongoing.

In addition, Member States must require these firms and operators to provide, without undue delay, the relevant information to authorities responsible for investigating and prosecuting market abuse, and to fully cooperate with them in such investigations and prosecutions.

Finally, the European Commission holds the power to adopt delegated acts, pursuant to Article 89, to specify the circumstances that trigger the obligation to provide information as described above.

For the purposes of this Directive, several key definitions are established to clarify the scope and application of its provisions:

1. **Investment Firm**: An investment firm is any legal person whose regular occupation or business involves providing one or more investment services to third parties and/or performing one or more investment activities on a professional basis. Member States may also include undertakings that are not legal persons as investment firms, provided that their legal status offers a level of protection for third parties equivalent to that of legal persons and that they are subject to equivalent prudential supervision appropriate to their legal form. Additionally, a natural person holding third-party funds or transferable securities may be considered an investment firm under this Directive and Regulation (EU) No 600/2014 only if certain conditions are met, including safeguarding third-party ownership rights, solvency monitoring, audited annual accounts, and provisions for investor protection in case of the proprietor’s death or incapacity.

2. **Investment Services and Activities**: These encompass any services and activities listed in Section A of Annex I related to the instruments specified in Section C of Annex I. The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts to specify particular derivative contracts, including wholesale energy products requiring physical settlement and other derivative financial instruments, considering factors such as trading venues.

3. **Ancillary Services**: Ancillary services refer to any of the services listed in Section B of Annex I, which support or complement investment services.

4. **Investment Advice**: This is defined as the provision of personal recommendations to a client, either upon the client’s request or at the initiative of the investment firm, concerning one or more transactions related to financial instruments.

These definitions form the foundation for understanding the entities, services, and activities regulated under the Directive, ensuring clarity and consistency in its application across Member States. The Commission retains the authority to update and refine these definitions through delegated acts to reflect market and technological developments and to maintain uniform application.

Article 50 addresses the synchronisation of business clocks within trading venues and their members or participants. It mandates that Member States require all such entities to synchronise the business clocks they use to record the date and time of any reportable event. To ensure uniformity and precision, the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) is tasked with developing draft regulatory technical standards that specify the required level of accuracy for clock synchronisation, aligning with international standards. ESMA was to submit these draft standards to the European Commission by 3 July 2015. Furthermore, the Commission is granted delegated power to adopt these regulatory technical standards in accordance with Articles 10 to 14 of Regulation (EU) No 1095/2010. This framework aims to enhance the reliability and consistency of time-stamping in financial reporting across the EU.

Article 71 of the Directive sets out detailed requirements for the publication of decisions imposing administrative sanctions or measures related to infringements of Regulation (EU) No 600/2014 or corresponding national provisions. Member States must ensure that competent authorities publish such decisions on their official websites without undue delay after informing the sanctioned person. The published information must include at least the type and nature of the infringement and the identity of the responsible persons. However, this obligation excludes decisions imposing investigatory measures.

If publishing the identity of legal or natural persons is deemed disproportionate after a case-by-case assessment, or if publication could jeopardize financial market stability or ongoing investigations, competent authorities have three options: (a) defer publication until the reasons for non-publication no longer apply; (b) publish the decision anonymously in compliance with national law to protect personal data; or (c) refrain from publishing the decision if options (a) and (b) are insufficient to protect market stability or ensure proportionality, especially for minor infringements. In cases of anonymous publication, the release of relevant data may be postponed for a reasonable time if the reasons for anonymity are expected to cease.

When a sanction or measure is appealed, competent authorities must immediately publish information about the appeal and its outcome, including any annulment of previous decisions. Published decisions must remain accessible on official websites for at least five years, with personal data retained only as long as necessary under data protection rules.

Competent authorities are required to inform ESMA of all sanctions imposed but not published under the conditions described, including appeals and outcomes. They must also provide ESMA with information and final judgments on criminal sanctions. ESMA maintains a central database of sanctions for information exchange among competent authorities, accessible only to them and updated based on submitted data.

Annually, Member States must provide ESMA with aggregated data on all sanctions and measures imposed, excluding investigatory measures. ESMA publishes this information in an annual report. For criminal sanctions, anonymized and aggregated data must also be submitted and published by ESMA.

When a sanction or criminal sanction is publicly disclosed, the competent authority must report this to ESMA simultaneously. If the sanction concerns entities such as investment firms, market operators, data reporting service providers, credit institutions related to investment services, or branches of third-country firms authorized under the Directive, ESMA will add a reference to the sanction in the relevant register.

Finally, ESMA is tasked with developing draft implementing technical standards on the procedures and forms for submitting information as required by this Article, to be submitted to the Commission by

Article 73 of the Directive mandates that Member States ensure competent authorities implement effective mechanisms for reporting potential or actual infringements of Regulation (EU) No 600/2014 and related national provisions. These mechanisms must include specific procedures for receiving and following up on reports, secure communication channels, and protections for employees who report infringements within financial institutions, safeguarding them against retaliation, discrimination, or unfair treatment. Additionally, the identity of both the whistleblower and the alleged infringer must be protected throughout the process, except where disclosure is required by national law during investigations or legal proceedings. Furthermore, Member States are required to oblige investment firms, market operators, data reporting service providers, credit institutions involved in investment services or activities, ancillary service providers, and branches of third-country firms to establish internal procedures that allow their employees to report potential or actual infringements through a dedicated, independent, and autonomous channel.

The exercise of the delegation of power to adopt delegated acts is governed by specific conditions outlined in this Article. The power to adopt delegated acts is conferred on the European Commission, as specified in various Articles including Article 2(3), Article 4(1)(2), Article 4(2), Article 13(1), and others, for an indeterminate period starting from 2 July 2014.

This delegation of power may be revoked at any time by either the European Parliament or the Council. Such a revocation decision terminates the delegation of power as specified and takes effect the day after its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union or on a later date if specified. Importantly, revocation does not affect the validity of any delegated acts already in force.

Upon adopting a delegated act, the Commission must notify it simultaneously to both the European Parliament and the Council. The delegated act will only enter into force if neither the European Parliament nor the Council objects within a three-month period following notification. This period can be extended by an additional three months if either institution so requests. If both institutions inform the Commission before the expiry of the period that they will not object, the act also enters into force.

These provisions ensure a balance between the Commission’s ability to adopt delegated acts efficiently and the oversight role of the European Parliament and the Council.

Article 93 outlines the transposition requirements for Member States regarding the Directive. Specifically, Member States are required to adopt and publish the necessary laws, regulations, and administrative provisions to comply with the Directive by 3 July 2016. Once adopted, these measures must be communicated promptly to the European Commission. The application of these measures is set to begin from 3 January 2017, except for the provisions transposing Article 65(2), which will apply from 3 September 2018.

When adopting these measures, Member States must include a reference to the Directive or ensure such a reference accompanies the official publication of the measures. The exact manner in which this reference is made is left to the discretion of each Member State. Additionally, Member States must include a statement clarifying that any references in existing laws, regulations, and administrative provisions to directives repealed by this Directive should be interpreted as references to the current Directive. The formulation and method of including this statement are also determined by each Member State.

Furthermore, Member States are required to apply the measures referred to in Article 92 starting from 3 July 2015. Finally, Member States must communicate to both the Commission and the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) the text of the main provisions of national law they adopt in the field covered by this Directive.

This Regulation establishes the obligations and requirements concerning the construction, installation, use, testing, and control of tachographs employed in road transport. Its primary purpose is to ensure the verification of compliance with Regulation (EC) No 561/2006, Directive 2002/15/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council, and Council Directive 92/6/EEC. Accordingly, tachographs must adhere to the specified standards in their design, installation, operation, and testing as outlined in this Regulation. Furthermore, the Regulation defines the conditions and requirements governing the use of information and data recorded, processed, or stored by tachographs—excluding personal data—for purposes beyond verifying compliance with the aforementioned legislative acts.

Digital tachographs and tachograph cards must present information related to vehicle activities and driver or co-driver status in a clear, unambiguous, and ergonomic manner. The displayed data shall include the current time, mode of operation, and driver activity details. Specifically, if the driver is currently driving, the display must show the continuous driving time and cumulative break time. If the driver is engaged in availability, other work, rest, or break, the display should indicate the duration of that current activity since it began, along with the cumulative break time. Additionally, information related to warnings and menu access must be shown. While other supplementary information may be displayed, it must be clearly distinguishable from the mandatory data.

Digital tachographs are required to alert drivers upon detecting any event or fault and provide warnings before and at the moment the maximum allowed continuous driving time is exceeded, helping ensure compliance with relevant regulations. These warnings must be visual and may also include audible signals. They should last at least 30 seconds unless the driver acknowledges them by pressing any key on the tachograph. The specific reason for the warning must be displayed and remain visible until the driver acknowledges it using a designated key or command.

To guarantee uniform compliance with these display and warning requirements, the Commission will adopt detailed implementing acts through the examination procedure outlined in Article 42(3). These acts will provide the necessary provisions for the consistent application of the rules governing digital tachograph displays and warnings.

Article 27 outlines the provisions regarding technical assistance funded by the Fund to support the implementation of the Regulation. 

1. The Fund may finance various measures such as preparation, monitoring, administrative and technical assistance, audit, information, control, and evaluation activities necessary for implementing the Regulation and activities under Article 10. This financing can be initiated either by the Commission or on its behalf, with a maximum limit set at 0.35% of the Fund’s annual allocation.

2. Before utilizing technical assistance funds, the Commission is required to consult with Member States and organizations representing partner organizations at the Union level to ensure coordinated and effective use of resources.

3. Each year, the Commission must present its planned actions related to the technical assistance measures mentioned above through implementing acts, especially when a contribution from the Fund is anticipated.

4. Additionally, Member States may initiate financing for similar technical assistance measures through the operational programme. This financing is subject to a ceiling of 5% of the Fund allocation at the time the operational programme is adopted. The operational programme may also support technical assistance and capacity building specifically aimed at partner organizations.

In summary, technical assistance under this Regulation is carefully regulated with defined ceilings and requires consultation and planning to ensure effective support for implementation and capacity building.

Article 54 outlines the procedure for financial corrections by the Commission concerning Union contributions to operational programmes. The Commission is empowered to implement financial corrections through implementing acts, which involve cancelling all or part of the Union funding allocated to an operational programme and recovering the corresponding amounts from the Member State. This action is taken to exclude expenditure that violates applicable law from Union financing.

A financial correction is applicable only to expenditure that has been declared to the Commission and where a breach of applicable law meets specific conditions. These conditions include: (a) the breach has influenced the selection of an operation by the responsible body for Fund support, or where it is not possible to definitively establish such impact but there is a substantiated risk that the breach affected the selection; or (b) the breach has affected the amount of expenditure declared for reimbursement by the Union budget, or where the financial impact cannot be precisely quantified but there is a substantiated risk of such an effect.

In making financial corrections, the Commission must adhere to the principle of proportionality, considering the nature and seriousness of the breach as well as its financial consequences for the Union budget. Furthermore, the Commission is required to keep both the European Parliament and the Council informed about decisions taken regarding financial corrections.

The total resources available for the Fund for budgetary commitments during the period 2014–2020 amount to EUR 3,395,684,880, calculated in 2011 prices, as detailed in the annual breakdown provided in Annex II. The allocation of these funds to each Member State is specified in Annex III, with a guaranteed minimum allocation of EUR 3,500,000 per Member State for the entire period. For programming purposes and inclusion in the general budget of the Union, the total resources will be indexed at a rate of 2% per year. Additionally, 0.35% of the global resources will be reserved for technical assistance initiatives led by the Commission.

The exception to the decommitment rule allows for a reduction in the amount subject to decommitment under certain conditions. Specifically, the amount concerned by decommitment shall be reduced by amounts corresponding to budget commitments where: (a) operations have been suspended due to a legal proceeding or an administrative appeal with suspensory effect; or (b) it has been impossible to submit a payment request because of force majeure seriously affecting the implementation of all or part of the operational programme. In cases of force majeure, national authorities must demonstrate the direct impact of such circumstances on the programme’s implementation.

Regarding the duration of these exceptions, the reduction can be requested once if the suspension or force majeure lasted no longer than one year. If the suspension or force majeure extends beyond one year, reductions may be requested multiple times, corresponding to the duration of the suspension or force majeure or the number of years between the initial suspension decision and the final legal or administrative decision.

Furthermore, by 31 January each year, the Member State is required to provide the Commission with information on these exceptions (both legal suspensions and force majeure) for the amounts to be declared by the end of the previous year. This ensures transparency and proper accounting of exceptions to the decommitment process.

The process for validation, assessment, and decision regarding a substantial modification of an aspect covered by Part II of the assessment report is clearly defined to ensure timely and transparent handling by the Member State concerned.

1. **Initial Notification (within 6 days):** Upon submission of the application dossier, the Member State must notify the sponsor via the EU portal whether the substantial modification pertains to an aspect covered by Part II of the assessment report and whether the dossier is complete according to Annex II. If no notification is provided within this timeframe, the modification is automatically considered to concern Part II aspects, and the dossier is deemed complete.

2. **Incomplete or Non-Part II Modifications:** If the Member State determines that the modification does not concern Part II or that the dossier is incomplete, it must inform the sponsor and allow up to 10 days for comments or completion of the dossier. After receiving the sponsor’s response, the Member State has 5 days to confirm compliance. Failure to notify within these periods results in the modification being deemed to concern Part II and the dossier complete. If the sponsor does not respond within the 10-day period, the application lapses.

3. **Validation Date:** The validation date is the date the sponsor is notified under the initial or follow-up communications. If no notification is sent, the validation date defaults to the last day of the respective notification periods.

4. **Assessment and Decision (within 38 days):** The Member State assesses the application and communicates the Part II assessment report, including its conclusion and decision on authorisation, through the EU portal within 38 days from the validation date. The decision can be to authorise, authorise with conditions (limited to those that cannot be fulfilled at the time of authorisation), or refuse authorisation.

5. **Request for Additional Information:** If needed, the Member State may request additional information with justified reasons, extending the assessment period by up to 31 days. The sponsor must provide the requested information within a maximum of 12 days. Upon receipt, the Member State has 19 days to complete the assessment. Failure by the sponsor to provide information within the set timeframe results in the application lapsing. All communications occur via the EU portal.

6. **Refusal and Appeal:** A Member State must refuse authorisation if the Part II aspects are not met or if a valid negative ethics committee opinion exists. The Member State must provide an appeal procedure for such refusals.

The application dossier for the authorisation of a clinical trial must include all necessary documentation and information required for validation and assessment as outlined in Chapter II. This encompasses details related to the conduct of the clinical trial, including its scientific context and organizational arrangements; information about the sponsor, investigators, potential subjects, enrolled subjects, and clinical trial sites; comprehensive data on the investigational medicinal products and, if applicable, auxiliary medicinal products, focusing on their properties, labelling, manufacturing, and control; measures implemented to protect subjects; and, when applicable, a justification for classifying the trial as a low-intervention clinical trial. The specific list of required documentation and information is detailed in Annex I.

For the authorisation of a substantial modification to a clinical trial, the application dossier must contain all documentation and information necessary for validation and assessment as specified in Chapter III. This includes a reference to the clinical trial(s) being modified using the EU trial number; a clear description of the substantial modification, including its nature and rationale; supporting data and additional information where necessary; and a clear explanation of the consequences of the modification on subjects’ rights and safety, as well as on the reliability and robustness of the trial data. The detailed list of required documentation and information for substantial modifications is provided in Annex II.

Non-clinical information submitted must be based on studies conducted in compliance with Union law principles of good laboratory practice applicable at the time of the studies. Any clinical trial data referenced in the dossier must originate from trials conducted in accordance with this Regulation or, if prior to the relevant date in Article 99, in accordance with Directive 2001/20/EC. For trials conducted outside the Union, the data must come from studies adhering to principles equivalent to those of this Regulation, particularly regarding subject rights and safety and data reliability.

Furthermore, data from clinical trials initiated on or after the date specified in Article 99 may only be submitted if the trial was registered before its start in a public registry recognized by the WHO ICTRP. For trials started before that date, data may be submitted only if the trial is registered in such a registry or if results have been published in an independent peer-reviewed scientific journal.

Any data submitted that do not comply with these requirements—covering good laboratory practice, trial conduct standards, and registration or publication criteria—will not be considered during the assessment of an application for clinical trial authorisation or for a substantial modification.

A clinical trial involving minors may only be conducted if, in addition to meeting the general conditions outlined in Article 28, several specific requirements are fulfilled to ensure the protection and rights of the minor participants. First, informed consent must be obtained from the minor’s legally designated representative. Additionally, the minors themselves must receive information about the trial in a manner appropriate to their age and mental maturity, delivered by investigators or team members experienced in working with children. Importantly, if a minor is capable of forming an opinion and understanding the information provided, their explicit wish to refuse participation or to withdraw from the trial at any time must be respected by the investigator.

No incentives or financial inducements may be offered to the minor or their representative, except for compensation covering expenses and loss of earnings directly related to participation. The clinical trial must be designed to investigate treatments for medical conditions that occur only in minors or be essential for validating data obtained from adults or other research methods. Furthermore, the trial must either directly relate to a medical condition affecting the minor or be of such a nature that it can only be conducted on minors.

There must be scientific justification that participation will either provide a direct benefit to the minor that outweighs the risks and burdens involved or offer some benefit to the population represented by the minor, while posing only minimal risk and burden compared to standard treatment. Throughout the process, minors should be involved in the informed consent procedure in a way suited to their age and maturity. If a minor reaches the age at which they can legally provide informed consent during the trial, their explicit consent must be obtained before they continue participation. These safeguards ensure that clinical trials involving minors are conducted ethically, respecting their rights and well-being.

Authorised investigational medicinal products and authorised auxiliary medicinal products must be labelled either in accordance with Article 66(1) or in accordance with Title V of Directive 2001/83/EC. However, if the specific circumstances of a clinical trial, as outlined in the trial protocol, require it to ensure the safety of the subject or to maintain the reliability and robustness of the data generated, additional information related to the identification of the clinical trial and the contact person must be included on both the outer and immediate packaging of authorised investigational medicinal products. The exact list of these additional particulars is detailed in section C of Annex VI.

The assessment report under Part II requires each Member State concerned to evaluate the application within its own territory based on several key aspects. These include: (a) verifying compliance with the informed consent requirements as detailed in Chapter V; (b) ensuring that arrangements for rewarding or compensating subjects and investigators meet the standards set out in Chapter V; (c) assessing the recruitment procedures for subjects against the criteria in Chapter V; (d) confirming adherence to Directive 95/46/EC; (e) compliance with Article 49; (f) compliance with Article 50; (g) compliance with Article 76; and (h) compliance with applicable rules regarding the collection, storage, and future use of biological samples from subjects. This comprehensive evaluation forms Part II of the assessment report.

Each Member State must complete its assessment within 45 days from the validation date and submit Part II of the assessment report, including its conclusions, to the sponsor via the EU portal. If necessary, the Member State may request additional information from the sponsor concerning the specified aspects, but only within this 45-day period and with justified reasons.

To facilitate the review of any additional information, the Member State may extend the initial 45-day assessment period by up to 31 days. The sponsor is required to provide the requested information within a timeframe set by the Member State, which cannot exceed 12 days from receipt of the request. After receiving the additional information, the Member State must finalize its assessment within 19 days. Failure by the sponsor to submit the requested information within the specified period results in the application being deemed to have lapsed in that Member State. All requests for additional information and the corresponding responses must be submitted through the EU portal.

The prohibitions outlined in Articles 14 and 15 of this Regulation do not apply to trading in own shares conducted under buy-back programmes or stabilisation activities, provided certain conditions are met.

For buy-back programmes, the exemption applies when the full details of the programme are disclosed before trading begins, trades are reported to the competent authority of the trading venue and subsequently made public, and adequate price and volume limits are observed. Additionally, the buy-back must be carried out in line with specific objectives, namely: (a) reducing the issuer’s capital; (b) fulfilling obligations arising from debt instruments exchangeable into equity; or (c) meeting obligations related to share option programmes or other share allocations to employees or members of the issuer’s administrative, management, or supervisory bodies, or those of an associate company. Each transaction under the buy-back programme must be reported to the competent authority with detailed information as specified in Regulation (EU) No 600/2014.

Regarding stabilisation activities, the exemption applies when stabilisation is conducted for a limited period, relevant information is disclosed and notified to the competent authority, price limits are respected, and the trading complies with conditions set out in regulatory technical standards. Details of all stabilisation transactions must be notified to the competent authority no later than the end of the seventh daily market session following the transaction date.

To ensure harmonised application, ESMA is tasked with developing draft regulatory technical standards specifying the conditions for buy-back programmes and stabilisation measures, including trading conditions, time and volume restrictions, disclosure and reporting obligations, and price conditions. These standards were to be submitted to the Commission by 3 July 2015, which holds delegated power to adopt them in accordance with Regulation (EU) No 1095/2010.

Inside information, as defined under this Regulation, encompasses several specific types of information that share common characteristics. Primarily, inside information refers to information of a precise nature that has not been made public and relates directly or indirectly to one or more issuers, financial instruments, commodity derivatives, emission allowances, or related contracts. Such information, if disclosed publicly, would likely have a significant effect on the prices of the relevant financial instruments, derivative financial instruments, spot commodity contracts, or auctioned products based on emission allowances.

More specifically:

1. **General Financial Instruments:** Inside information includes precise, non-public information concerning issuers or financial instruments that could significantly influence their market prices.

2. **Commodity Derivatives:** It also covers precise, non-public information related to commodity derivatives or the associated spot commodity contracts, especially when such information is reasonably expected or legally required to be disclosed under Union or national laws, market rules, contracts, or customary practices on relevant commodity markets.

3. **Emission Allowances:** Information of a precise nature about emission allowances or auctioned products based on them, which is not public and could significantly affect their prices or those of related derivatives, is also considered inside information.

4. **Client Orders:** For persons executing orders on financial instruments, inside information includes precise, non-public information conveyed by clients about their pending orders that could impact the prices of financial instruments, spot commodity contracts, or related derivatives.

Information is deemed of a precise nature if it indicates existing or reasonably expected circumstances or events specific enough to allow conclusions about their potential price impact. This includes intermediate steps in a protracted process aimed at bringing about particular circumstances or events, provided those steps themselves meet the criteria for inside information.

Furthermore, information likely to have a significant effect on prices is defined from the perspective of a reasonable investor who would consider such information important for investment decisions. However, for emission allowance market participants with emissions or thermal input below certain thresholds, information about their physical operations is not considered to have a significant price effect.

Finally, the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) is tasked with issuing guidelines that provide a non-exhaustive indicative list of information expected or required to be disclosed in commodity derivatives markets, taking into account the specific characteristics of those markets.

The competent authorities have a set of important obligations to ensure the proper functioning and integrity of financial markets. Among these, they must verify that investment firms regularly update the bid and offer prices they publish, as required under Article 14. This means that the prices provided by these firms should be current and accurately reflect the prevailing market conditions at all times. Additionally, competent authorities are responsible for ensuring that investment firms adhere to the conditions for price improvement specified in Article 15(2). This involves checking that any price improvements offered by the firms meet the regulatory standards designed to protect investors and promote fair trading practices. Through these checks, competent authorities help maintain transparency, fairness, and efficiency in the market.

Article 25 outlines the obligation of investment firms and trading venue operators to maintain records related to orders and transactions in financial instruments. 

1. Investment firms are required to keep, for a period of five years, all relevant data concerning every order and transaction they have executed, whether on their own account or on behalf of clients. For client transactions, these records must include comprehensive information about the client’s identity and the details mandated by Directive 2005/60/EC. These records must be made available to the competent authority upon request. Additionally, the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) may request access to this information following the procedures established in Article 35 of Regulation (EU) No 1095/2010.

2. Operators of trading venues must also retain, for at least five years, all relevant data related to orders advertised through their systems. These records should capture the essential characteristics of each order, including links between orders and any resulting executed transactions, as specified in Article 26(1) and (3). ESMA plays a facilitation and coordination role to ensure competent authorities can access this information efficiently.

3. To further specify the details of the order data that must be maintained by trading venues, ESMA is tasked with developing draft regulatory technical standards. These standards will cover data elements not already detailed in Article 26, such as the identification codes of the member or participant transmitting the order, the order identification code, timestamps, order characteristics (type, limit price, validity period, special instructions), and details of any modifications, cancellations, or executions. ESMA was required to submit these draft standards to the European Commission by 3 July 2015. The Commission holds delegated powers to adopt these standards in accordance with the relevant provisions of Regulation (EU) No 1095/2010.

In summary, Article 25 ensures transparency and traceability in financial markets by mandating comprehensive record-keeping by investment firms and trading venues, facilitating regulatory oversight and market integrity.

Article 46 outlines the general provisions governing the ability of third-country firms to provide investment services or perform investment activities within the European Union without establishing a branch. Specifically, a third-country firm may offer such services to eligible counterparties and professional clients, as defined in Section I of Annex II to Directive 2014/65/EU, across the Union if it is registered in the ESMA register of third-country firms pursuant to Article 47.

ESMA will register a third-country firm only if certain conditions are met: (a) the European Commission has adopted a decision confirming the equivalence of the third country’s legal and supervisory framework; (b) the firm is authorized and effectively supervised in its home jurisdiction to provide the relevant investment services or activities; and (c) cooperation arrangements between ESMA and the third country’s competent authorities are in place.

Once registered, Member States cannot impose additional requirements on the third-country firm beyond those established by this Regulation or Directive 2014/65/EU, nor can they treat third-country firms more favorably than Union firms. The application process requires the third-country firm to submit all necessary information to ESMA after the Commission’s equivalence decision. ESMA will assess the completeness of the application within 30 working days and make a registration decision within 180 working days of receiving a complete application.

In the absence of a Commission equivalence decision or if such decision ceases to be effective, Member States may still allow third-country firms to provide investment services or activities under their national regimes. However, third-country firms must inform their Union-based clients in writing, prominently, that they are only permitted to serve eligible counterparties and professional clients, are not subject to EU supervision, and provide the contact details of their home country’s supervisory authority.

Furthermore, if an eligible counterparty or professional client in the Union initiates the provision of services with a third-country firm on their own initiative, the restrictions of this Article do not apply to that relationship, although the firm cannot market new investment products or services to that client.

Before providing any service or activity to a Union client, third-country firms must offer to submit disputes to the jurisdiction of a court or arbitral tribunal in a Member State. Lastly, ESMA is tasked with developing draft regulatory technical standards specifying the information required for registration applications and client disclosures, to be submitted to the Commission by 3 July 2015, with the Commission empowered to adopt these standards.

When advising on or selling a Packaged Retail and Insurance-based Investment Product (PRIIP), the person responsible must provide the Key Information Document (KID) to retail investors free of charge. The KID should be delivered in one of three ways:

1. **On paper** – This is the default method, especially when the PRIIP is offered face-to-face, unless the retail investor requests a different format.

2. **Using a durable medium other than paper** – This is allowed if it is appropriate for the business context and the retail investor has been given a choice between paper and the durable medium, selecting the latter in a verifiable manner.

3. **By means of a website** – This option is permissible if several conditions are met: the website provision is appropriate for the business context; the retail investor has chosen this option over paper in a way that can be evidenced; the retail investor has been informed electronically or in writing of the website address and the exact location of the KID; and the KID remains accessible on the website for as long as the retail investor needs, with the ability to download and store it in a durable medium. Additionally, if the KID is updated, previous versions must be available upon request.

If the KID is provided via a durable medium other than paper or through a website, the retail investor must be informed of their right to request a free paper copy, which must be supplied upon request without charge.

Furthermore, the use of durable media other than paper or websites is considered appropriate if there is evidence that the retail investor has regular internet access. Providing an email address for the business relationship is regarded as such evidence.

In summary, the delivery of the KID must be free, transparent, and tailored to the retail investor’s preferences and circumstances, ensuring accessibility and the option to receive a paper copy at any time.

Article 9(5) of Regulation (EU) No 1094/2010 empowers the European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority (EIOPA) to temporarily prohibit or restrict, within the Union, either the marketing, distribution, or sale of certain insurance-based investment products (IBIPs) or specific features thereof, or particular types of financial activities or practices carried out by insurance or reinsurance undertakings. Such prohibitions or restrictions may be tailored to specific circumstances or include exceptions as determined by EIOPA.

EIOPA may only take such action if three cumulative conditions are met: (a) the proposed measure addresses a significant investor protection concern or a threat to the orderly functioning and integrity of financial markets or to the stability of the financial system in the Union; (b) existing Union regulatory requirements applicable to the relevant IBIP or activity do not sufficiently mitigate the identified threat; and (c) competent authorities have either not acted or their actions are inadequate to address the threat. Importantly, EIOPA may impose these measures on a precautionary basis even before the IBIP is marketed or sold.

When exercising this power, EIOPA must ensure that its actions do not disproportionately harm market efficiency or investors relative to the benefits achieved, nor create risks of regulatory arbitrage. If competent authorities have already taken measures under Article 17, EIOPA may proceed without issuing the opinion required under Article 18.

Prior to implementing any prohibition or restriction, EIOPA is required to notify the relevant competent authorities. Furthermore, it must publish a notice on its website detailing the decision, including the nature of the prohibition or restriction and the date from which it takes effect. The measures apply only to actions taken after this effective date.

EIOPA is also mandated to review any imposed prohibition or restriction at least every three months, with the measure expiring if not renewed. Actions taken by EIOPA under this Article override any previous measures by competent authorities.

Finally, the European Commission is tasked with adopting delegated acts specifying criteria and factors to guide EIOPA in determining when significant investor protection concerns or threats to market integrity or financial stability exist. These criteria include the complexity of the IBIP relative to the target investor, the size or notional value of the product, the degree of innovation involved, and the leverage provided by the product or practice.

This Regulation applies to PRIIP manufacturers as well as to persons advising on or selling PRIIPs. However, it explicitly excludes certain products from its scope. These exemptions include non-life insurance products listed in Annex I to Directive 2009/138/EC, and life insurance contracts where benefits are payable solely on death or due to incapacity caused by injury, sickness, or infirmity. Additionally, the Regulation does not apply to deposits except for structured deposits as defined in Directive 2014/65/EU. Certain securities specified in Directive 2003/71/EC are also excluded. Pension-related products are exempted as well, including those recognized under national law primarily to provide retirement income, officially recognized occupational pension schemes under Directive 2003/41/EC or Directive 2009/138/EC, and individual pension products mandated by national law requiring employer contributions where neither employer nor employee can choose the pension product or provider.

Article 28 outlines the obligations of competent authorities and Member States regarding the establishment of mechanisms for reporting actual or potential infringements of the Regulation. Firstly, competent authorities are required to set up effective mechanisms that allow individuals to report such infringements to them. These mechanisms must include specific procedures for receiving reports and ensuring their proper follow-up. Additionally, they must provide appropriate protections for employees who report infringements within their employer’s organization, safeguarding them against retaliation, discrimination, and other forms of unfair treatment. The mechanisms must also ensure the confidentiality of the identity of both the whistleblower and the person allegedly responsible for the infringement throughout all stages of the procedure, except where disclosure is mandated by national law for further investigation or judicial proceedings.

Furthermore, Member States have the discretion to authorize competent authorities to establish additional reporting mechanisms under national law. They may also require employers, particularly those operating in sectors regulated for financial services purposes, to implement internal procedures that enable employees to report actual or potential infringements through a specific, independent, and autonomous channel. This framework aims to promote transparency, protect whistleblowers, and ensure effective enforcement of the Regulation.

The key information document (KID) serves as essential pre-contractual information for retail investors and must be accurate, fair, clear, and not misleading. It provides the key details about the PRIIP and must align consistently with any binding contractual documents, relevant offer documents, and the PRIIP’s terms and conditions.

The KID is a stand-alone document, distinctly separate from marketing materials, and must not include cross-references to such marketing content. However, it may reference other documents, such as a prospectus, but only when these references relate directly to information required by the regulation.

In cases where a PRIIP offers multiple investment options and it is not feasible to include all required information about each option within a single concise document, the KID should at least provide a generic description of the underlying investment options. It must also clearly indicate where and how more detailed pre-contractual information about these options can be accessed.

The KID is designed to be a short, concise document, limited to a maximum of three A4 pages when printed, to facilitate comparability. It should be presented in an easy-to-read format with readable font sizes, focus strictly on the key information retail investors need, and be written in clear, succinct, and comprehensible language that aids understanding.

If colors are used in the KID, they must not reduce the document’s clarity or comprehensibility when printed or photocopied in black and white. Additionally, any corporate branding or logos included must not distract from the information or obscure the text, ensuring the investor’s focus remains on the content.

Directive 2003/87/EC has been amended to update the provisions related to the auctioning and issuance of emission allowances. Specifically, Article 10 has been revised as follows:

1. Paragraph 1 of Article 10 is replaced to mandate that, starting from 2019, Member States must auction all emission allowances that are not allocated free of charge under Articles 10a and 10c, and that are not placed in the market stability reserve established by Decision (EU) 2015/1814 of the European Parliament and of the Council.

2. A new paragraph is inserted after paragraph 1 to clarify the issuance of allowances in relation to cancelled allowances. In Article 13(2), the second subparagraph is replaced to state that Member States shall issue allowances to entities for the current period to replace any allowances they held which have been cancelled. Likewise, allowances held in the market stability reserve that are no longer valid must be replaced by valid allowances for the current period.

These amendments ensure a clear framework for the auctioning process and the replacement of cancelled or invalid allowances, thereby maintaining the integrity and functionality of the EU Emissions Trading System.

Member States are required to implement measures that protect individuals—such as employees and representatives of obliged entities—who report suspicions of money laundering or terrorist financing either internally or to the Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU). These protections must ensure that whistleblowers are not subjected to threats, hostile actions, or any form of retaliation. Specifically, safeguards should prevent adverse or discriminatory employment actions against these individuals, thereby fostering a secure environment that encourages the reporting of suspicious activities without fear of negative consequences. This approach is essential to maintaining the integrity of anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing efforts.

Member States are required to ensure that Financial Intelligence Units (FIUs) exchange information relevant to the analysis or processing of cases related to money laundering or terrorist financing. This exchange can occur spontaneously or upon request and must include details about the natural or legal persons involved, even if the specific predicate offences are not yet identified. Requests for information must include relevant facts, background, reasons for the request, and intended use of the information. FIUs may use different agreed-upon mechanisms for exchanging information, such as FIU.net or its successor platforms. When an FIU receives a report concerning another Member State, it must promptly forward it to the appropriate FIU of that Member State.

Furthermore, the FIU receiving a request must employ the full range of its domestic powers for receiving and analyzing information when responding, and it must do so in a timely manner.
