If an FIU needs additional information from an obliged entity located in another Member State but operating within its territory, the request must be directed to the FIU of the Member State where the obliged entity is established, which will then promptly transfer requests and responses.

An FIU may refuse to exchange information only in exceptional cases where such exchange would conflict with fundamental principles of its national law. These exceptions must be clearly defined to prevent misuse or undue restrictions on the free exchange of information for analytical purposes.

By 26 June 2019, the Commission is required to prepare a comprehensive report on the implementation of this Directive. This report must be submitted to both the European Parliament and the Council. The purpose of the report is to evaluate how effectively the Directive has been applied across member states, identify any challenges encountered during its implementation, and assess whether the objectives of the Directive have been met. The findings will provide a basis for any necessary adjustments or future legislative actions to improve the Directive’s impact.

The management of operational and security risks in payment services is governed by a comprehensive regulatory framework to ensure robust risk mitigation and control. Member States are required to ensure that payment service providers (PSPs) establish frameworks incorporating appropriate measures and control mechanisms to manage operational and security risks related to their services. This includes the implementation and maintenance of effective incident management procedures, which cover the detection and classification of major operational and security incidents.

Furthermore, PSPs must provide competent authorities with updated and comprehensive assessments of these risks and the adequacy of their mitigation measures on an annual basis or more frequently if requested. This ongoing reporting ensures continuous oversight and responsiveness to emerging threats.

The European Banking Authority (EBA), in collaboration with the European Central Bank (ECB) and after consulting relevant stakeholders, is tasked with issuing guidelines on the establishment, implementation, and monitoring of security measures, including certification processes where applicable. These guidelines, first issued by 13 July 2017, are reviewed regularly, at least every two years, to incorporate practical experience and evolving security challenges.

Additionally, the EBA may develop draft regulatory technical standards on the criteria and conditions for establishing and monitoring security measures upon request by the European Commission. The Commission holds delegated powers to adopt these standards in accordance with relevant EU regulations.

To enhance the effectiveness of operational and security risk management, the EBA also promotes cooperation and information sharing among competent authorities, the ECB, and, where relevant, the European Union Agency for Network and Information Security. This collaborative approach supports a coordinated response to risks across the payment services sector within the EU.

The European Banking Authority (EBA) was tasked with submitting the draft regulatory technical standards (RTS) on authentication and communication to the European Commission by 13 January 2017, as stipulated in paragraph 1 of the relevant regulation. Following this submission, the Commission holds the delegated power to formally adopt these RTS in accordance with Articles 10 to 14 of Regulation (EU) No 1093/2010. Furthermore, pursuant to Article 10 of the same regulation, the EBA is required to regularly review and, where necessary, update these regulatory technical standards. This ongoing review process ensures that the RTS remain current and effective by incorporating innovations and technological advancements in the field.

Under the provisions governing their financing and investment operations, the European Investment Bank (EIB), the European Investment Fund (EIF), and all associated financial intermediaries are strictly prohibited from supporting any activities conducted for illegal purposes. These prohibited activities include money laundering, terrorist financing, organized crime, tax fraud and evasion, corruption, and fraud that undermines the financial interests of the European Union. Specifically, the EIB is barred from participating in any financing or investment operations involving vehicles located in non-cooperative jurisdictions. This restriction aligns with the EIB’s policy on weakly regulated or non-cooperative jurisdictions, which is based on the standards and policies established by the European Union, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), and the Financial Action Task Force (FATF).

Furthermore, the EIB must adhere to the principles and standards set forth in Union law aimed at preventing the misuse of the financial system for money laundering and terrorist financing. This includes compliance with Regulation (EU) 2015/847 and Directive (EU) 2015/849 of the European Parliament and Council. A key requirement under these rules is that the EIB conditions both direct funding and funding through intermediaries on the disclosure of beneficial ownership information, ensuring transparency and accountability in all its financing and investment operations covered by this Regulation.

Additionality, as defined in this Regulation, refers to the support provided by the European Fund for Strategic Investments (EFSI) to projects that address market failures or sub-optimal investment situations and that could not have been implemented, or not to the same extent, by the European Investment Bank (EIB), the European Investment Fund (EIF), or through existing Union financial instruments without EFSI backing during the period when the EU guarantee is available. Typically, projects supported by the EFSI carry a higher risk profile compared to those financed under the EIB’s normal operations, resulting in an overall EFSI portfolio that is riskier than the EIB’s pre-Regulation investment portfolio. For projects to be considered additional, they must generally involve risks aligned with EIB special activities, as outlined in Article 16 of the EIB Statute and the EIB’s credit risk policy guidelines. However, projects with risks below the minimum threshold for EIB special activities may also qualify for EFSI support if the EU guarantee is necessary to ensure additionality.

Furthermore, the Steering Board is responsible for adjusting the project mix by sector and country, based on continuous monitoring of market conditions and investment environments across Member States. This adjustment aims to address market failures and sub-optimal investment situations, including those caused by financial fragmentation, while avoiding unnecessarily high risk. When higher risk levels are justified, the use of EIB special activities under this Regulation will be expanded beyond previous levels, particularly in Member States where such activities were rarely or never used before. This approach facilitates the implementation of additional projects and financing by the EIB, national promotional banks, institutions, or investment platforms, thereby enhancing the overall additionality effect of the EFSI.

The use of the EU guarantee under the European Fund for Strategic Investments (EFSI) is subject to nine key requirements:

1. **Entry into Force of the EFSI Agreement:** The EU guarantee can only be granted once the EFSI Agreement has entered into force.

2. **Scope of Operations Covered:** The guarantee applies to financing and investment operations approved by the Investment Committee, either directly by the European Investment Bank (EIB) or through funding or guarantees to the European Investment Fund (EIF). These operations must align with Union policies and support general objectives such as:
   - Research, development, and innovation, including projects aligned with Horizon 2020, research infrastructures, demonstration projects, academia-industry collaboration, and knowledge transfer.
   - Development of the energy sector in line with Energy Union priorities and climate frameworks, focusing on renewable energy, energy efficiency, and modernizing energy infrastructure.
   - Development of transport infrastructure and innovative transport technologies, including projects under relevant EU regulations, sustainable urban mobility, and connections to TEN-T networks.
   - Financial support to entities with up to 3,000 employees, especially SMEs and small mid-cap companies, through working capital, investment, and risk financing from seed to expansion stages.
   - Development and deployment of information and communication technologies, such as digital content, services, high-speed telecommunications, and broadband networks.
   - Environment and resource efficiency projects, including environmental protection, ecosystem services, sustainable development, and climate action.
   - Human capital, culture, and health initiatives, covering education, cultural industries, innovative health solutions, new medicines, social infrastructure, and tourism.

3. **Initial Investment Period:** The EU guarantee may be granted for operations contracted by 30 June 2020, with the investment period lasting until 5 July 2019 for both EIB and EIF operations.

4. **Extension of Investment Period:** A new investment period may be established following the procedure outlined in Article 18.

5. **Use of the Guarantee for Eligible Vehicles:** The EIB may use the guarantee to support investment platforms, funds, and national promotional banks or institutions investing in eligible operations, subject to approval by the Investment Committee and policies set by the Steering Board. The Investment Committee evaluates and approves conformity and may retain rights to approve new projects within these vehicles.

6. **Cost Recovery and Use of Guarantee for Expenses:** According to Article 17 of the EIB Statute, all EFSI-related expenses must be borne by the beneficiaries of the financing operations. No administrative or other fees for these operations

According to the provisions on refusal of entry, a third-country national who does not meet all the entry conditions specified in Article 6(1) and who is not included among the exceptions listed in Article 6(5) must be refused entry to the territories of the Member States. This refusal is without prejudice to special rules related to the right of asylum, international protection, or the issuance of long-stay visas.

Entry refusal must be based on a substantiated decision that clearly states the precise reasons for the refusal. This decision must be made by an authority empowered under national law and takes effect immediately. The refusal must be communicated to the individual using a standard form (as detailed in Annex V, Part B), which the authority completes and the third-country national acknowledges receiving.

Persons refused entry have the right to appeal the decision, with appeals conducted according to national law. They must also be provided with written information about contact points that can assist them with legal representation. However, lodging an appeal does not suspend the immediate effect of the refusal decision. If an appeal finds the refusal unjustified, the individual is entitled to have any entry stamps or related cancellations corrected by the Member State that refused entry, and may be eligible for compensation under national law.

Border guards are responsible for ensuring that individuals refused entry do not enter the Member State’s territory. Additionally, Member States are required to collect and submit annual statistics to the European Commission (Eurostat) on the number of refusals, reasons for refusal, nationality of refused persons, and the type of border where refusal occurred (land, air, or sea), in line with Regulation (EC) No 862/2007.

Further detailed rules on refusal of entry are provided in Part A of Annex V.

The specific rules for checks on certain categories of persons are detailed in Annex VII and apply to the following groups: (a) Heads of State and members of their delegations; (b) pilots of aircraft and other crew members; (c) seamen; (d) holders of diplomatic, official, or service passports as well as members of international organizations; (e) cross-border workers; (f) minors; (g) personnel involved in rescue services, police, fire brigades, and border guards; and (h) offshore workers. These specific rules may include derogations from the provisions set out in Articles 5 and 6 and Articles 8 to 14, allowing for tailored procedures in these cases. Additionally, Member States are required to notify the European Commission of the model identity cards issued by their Ministries of Foreign Affairs to accredited members of diplomatic missions, consular representations, and their family members, as stipulated in Article 39. This ensures standardized recognition and facilitates the application of the specific rules during checks on these categories of persons.

Member States are required to notify the European Commission of several key pieces of information related to border control and residence permits. Specifically, they must provide: (a) a list of residence permits, clearly distinguishing between those covered by Article 2(16)(a) and those under Article 2(16)(b), including specimens for the latter; residence cards issued under Directive 2004/38/EC must be clearly identified, and specimens provided for any cards not issued in the uniform format established by Regulation (EC) No 1030/2002; (b) a list of their border crossing points; (c) the reference amounts set annually by national authorities that are required for crossing their external borders; (d) a list of national services responsible for border control; (e) specimens of model cards issued by Foreign Ministries; (f) any exceptions to the rules on crossing external borders as outlined in Article 5(2)(a); and (g) statistics as referred to in Article 11(3). The Commission, in turn, is tasked with making this information available to Member States and the public by publishing it in the Official Journal of the European Union, C Series, and through other appropriate channels.

The crossing of external borders is generally permitted only at designated border crossing points and during their fixed opening hours. These hours must be clearly displayed at crossing points that do not operate 24 hours a day. Member States are required to notify the European Commission of their list of border crossing points in accordance with Article 39.

However, exceptions to this rule may be granted under certain conditions. These include cases where individuals or groups need to cross the border outside of official points or hours due to special circumstances, provided they hold the necessary permits under national law and that such crossings do not threaten public order or internal security. Member States may also establish specific arrangements through bilateral agreements, which must be communicated to the Commission. Additionally, exceptions apply in unforeseen emergency situations and as specified by particular rules outlined in Articles 19 and 20 along with Annexes VI and VII.

Despite these exceptions and obligations related to international protection, Member States must enforce penalties for unauthorized border crossings outside designated points or times. These penalties, established under national law, must be effective, proportionate, and serve as a deterrent.

The relaxation of border checks at external borders may occur only under exceptional and unforeseen circumstances. These circumstances are defined as unforeseeable events that cause traffic volumes so intense that waiting times at border crossing points become excessive, despite the full deployment of available staff, facilities, and organizational resources. When such a situation arises, the border guard in command at the crossing point has the authority to decide to relax border checks. This relaxation must be temporary, tailored to the specific conditions causing the delay, and implemented gradually to ensure proper management.

In cases where checks are relaxed, priority should generally be given to border checks on entry movements over those on exit movements. Importantly, even when checks are eased, border guards are still required to stamp the travel documents of third-country nationals upon both entry and exit, in line with Article 11. To maintain oversight and transparency, each Member State is obligated to submit an annual report on the application of these provisions to the European Parliament and the Commission.

Article 23 establishes the framework for mandatory contributions to critical benchmarks, particularly those based on input data submitted predominantly by supervised entities. It applies to critical benchmarks where most contributors are supervised entities and sets out detailed procedures and powers for administrators and competent authorities to ensure the benchmark’s integrity and representativeness.

Key provisions include:

1. **Biennial Assessment:** Administrators of critical benchmarks must submit every two years an assessment to their competent authority regarding the benchmark’s ability to accurately measure the underlying market or economic reality.

2. **Notification of Cessation:** If a supervised contributor intends to stop providing input data, it must promptly notify the benchmark administrator in writing. The administrator then informs its competent authority, which in turn notifies the competent authority of the contributor if located in another Member State. The administrator must assess and report on the impact of this cessation on the benchmark’s capability within 14 days.

3. **Competent Authority’s Role:** Upon receiving assessments, the competent authority evaluates the benchmark’s representativeness and informs ESMA and, if applicable, the relevant supervisory college. It considers the administrator’s cessation procedures in its assessment.

4. **Power to Require Continued Contribution:** From notification of cessation until the competent authority completes its assessment, it may require the contributor(s) to continue providing input data for up to four weeks, without obliging them to trade or commit to trade.

5. **Mandatory Contribution Measures:** If the competent authority determines the benchmark’s representativeness is at risk after this period, it can:
   - Require selected supervised entities, including new contributors, to provide input data according to the benchmark’s methodology and code of conduct, for up to 12 months.
   - Extend mandatory contribution for an additional period not exceeding 12 months, with a total maximum of 24 months.
   - Specify the form and timing of input data contributions without forcing trading commitments.
   - Require changes to the benchmark’s methodology, code of conduct, or other rules.

6. **Selection of Contributors:** The competent authority selects supervised entities required to contribute based on their actual and potential market participation, coordinating with other competent authorities as needed.

7. **Enforcement Cooperation:** Competent authorities of contributors required to contribute must cooperate with the administrator’s competent authority to enforce these measures.

8. **Review and Revocation:** At the end of the initial mandatory contribution period, the competent authority reviews the measures and may revoke them if it finds that contributors are likely to continue voluntarily, the benchmark can continue without mandated contributors, a suitable substitute benchmark exists, or

Article 45 of the Regulation sets out the rules for the publication of decisions imposing administrative sanctions or other administrative measures related to infringements of the Regulation. 

1. Generally, a competent authority must publish any such decision on its official website immediately after informing the person subject to the decision. The published information must include at least the type and nature of the infringement and the identity of the persons subject to the decision. However, this requirement does not apply to decisions imposing investigatory measures.

2. The competent authority may limit or defer publication if it considers that publishing the identity of a legal person or personal data of a natural person would be disproportionate, or if publication could jeopardize financial market stability or ongoing investigations. In such cases, the authority may:  
   (a) defer publication until the reasons for deferral no longer exist;  
   (b) publish the decision anonymously, in line with national law, ensuring effective protection of personal data; or  
   (c) decide not to publish the decision at all if deferral or anonymous publication would still risk market stability or if the measure is minor.  
If anonymous publication is chosen, the authority may postpone publication for a reasonable time if the reasons for anonymity are expected to cease.

3. If the decision is appealed before a national judicial, administrative, or other authority, the competent authority must immediately publish information about the appeal and any subsequent outcome. Any decision annulling a previous sanction or measure must also be published.

4. Published decisions must remain accessible on the official website for at least five years. Personal data included in the publication should only be kept for as long as necessary under applicable data protection rules.

5. Member States are required to annually provide ESMA with aggregated information on all administrative sanctions and measures imposed under Article 42, excluding investigatory measures. ESMA publishes this information in an annual report. If Member States have criminal sanctions for infringements under Article 42, their competent authorities must also provide ESMA with anonymised and aggregated data on criminal investigations and sanctions, which ESMA includes in its annual report.

A robust complaints-handling mechanism is essential for administrators overseeing benchmark determination processes. Administrators must establish and publicly disclose clear procedures for receiving, investigating, and retaining records of complaints, including those related to the benchmark determination process itself. This mechanism should ensure that the complaints-handling policy is readily accessible, allowing stakeholders to submit complaints regarding whether a specific benchmark determination accurately reflects market value, proposed changes to the benchmark determination process, the application of the methodology to a particular benchmark, and other related decisions.

Furthermore, complaints must be investigated promptly and fairly, with the results communicated to the complainant within a reasonable timeframe. Exceptions to this communication may occur only if disclosure conflicts with public policy objectives or specific regulatory requirements, such as those outlined in Regulation (EU) No 596/2014. Importantly, the investigation must be conducted independently, free from involvement by any personnel who are or have been connected to the subject matter of the complaint, thereby ensuring impartiality and maintaining the integrity of the complaints-handling process.

The duration, review, and refund provisions for anti-dumping measures are designed to ensure that such measures remain in force only as long as necessary to counteract dumping causing injury, and to provide mechanisms for their timely review and possible adjustment.

1. **Duration of Measures:** An anti-dumping measure remains effective only as long as it is necessary to offset dumping causing injury. Definitive measures automatically expire five years after imposition or five years after the conclusion of the most recent review covering dumping and injury, unless a review determines that expiry would likely lead to continuation or recurrence of dumping and injury.

2. **Expiry Reviews:** These reviews are initiated by the Commission or upon request by Union producers, provided sufficient evidence indicates that expiry would likely result in continued or recurring dumping and injury. Evidence may include ongoing dumping, injury removal due to existing measures, or exporter and market conditions suggesting further injurious dumping. During the review, all parties—including exporters, importers, exporting country representatives, and Union producers—can present evidence and comments. A notice of impending expiry is published in the Official Journal of the European Union during the final year of the measure’s application, and Union producers may request a review no later than three months before expiry. A notice of actual expiry is also published.

3. **Interim Reviews:** These may be initiated by the Commission, a Member State, or, after at least one year since imposition, by exporters, importers, or Union producers with sufficient evidence. Interim reviews assess whether the measure is still necessary, whether injury would continue or recur if removed or varied, or whether the measure is insufficient to counteract dumping. The Commission considers changes in dumping and injury circumstances and the effectiveness of existing measures, taking all relevant evidence into account.

4. **Reviews for New Exporters:** Reviews can determine individual dumping margins for new exporters not involved during the original investigation period. Such reviews are initiated if the new exporter proves independence from existing exporters subject to measures and actual or contractual exports to the Union. These reviews are conducted on an accelerated basis, with Union producers given an opportunity to comment. During the review, duties on the new exporter are repealed and imports registered to allow retroactive duties if dumping is found. This does not apply where duties were imposed under Article 9(6).

5. **Procedural Rules and Time Limits:** The procedural rules for investigations apply to all reviews, excluding time limits. Expiry and interim reviews are normally concluded within 12 months, and in any case within 15 months of initiation. Reviews for new

**Determination of Dumping**

**A. Normal Value**

1. The normal value is generally based on prices paid or payable by independent customers in the exporting country in the ordinary course of trade. If the exporter does not produce or sell the like product, prices from other sellers or producers may be used. Prices between associated parties or those with compensatory arrangements may be excluded unless proven unaffected by the relationship. Association is assessed with reference to definitions such as those in Article 127 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2015/2447.

2. Domestic sales of the like product are normally used to determine normal value if they constitute at least 5% of the sales volume of the product exported to the Union. Lower volumes may be accepted if prices are representative of the market.

3. If there are no or insufficient domestic sales, or if the market situation is distorted (e.g., artificially low prices, significant barter trade, or non-commercial processing), normal value is calculated based on the cost of production plus reasonable selling, general and administrative costs and profits, or on export prices to an appropriate third country, provided these prices are representative.

4. Sales below unit production cost plus selling and administrative costs may be disregarded if made over an extended period (normally at least six months, usually one year), in substantial quantities (e.g., at least 20% of sales volume), and prices do not allow cost recovery within a reasonable time. Prices below cost at the time of sale but above weighted average costs for the investigation period are considered to allow cost recovery.

5. Costs are normally calculated from the party’s accounting records, provided they comply with generally accepted accounting principles and reasonably reflect production and sales costs. If not, costs are adjusted or established based on other producers’ data or other reasonable bases. Cost allocations should be historically consistent, preferably based on turnover, and adjusted for non-recurring costs benefiting current or future production. Start-up phase costs related to new production facilities and low capacity utilization are treated specially, with average costs at the end of the start-up phase used for the relevant period.

6. Selling, general and administrative costs and profits are based on actual data from the exporter or producer. If unavailable, these may be derived from weighted averages of other investigated exporters or producers, from similar product categories, or by other reasonable methods, ensuring profit does not exceed normal levels in the domestic market.

7. For imports from non-market-economy countries, normal value is determined based on prices or constructed values in a market economy third country

Article 25 – Entry into Force

This Regulation shall enter into force on the twentieth day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union. This means that the provisions set out in the Regulation will become legally binding and applicable starting from that date, allowing sufficient time for Member States and relevant stakeholders to prepare for its implementation.

A subsidy is defined as a financial contribution by a government in the country of origin or export that confers a benefit. Specifically, a subsidy exists if:

1. (a) There is a government practice involving a financial contribution, which can take several forms:
   (i) A direct transfer of funds, such as grants, loans, or equity infusions, or potential direct transfers like loan guarantees.
   (ii) Forgone or uncollected government revenue, for example through fiscal incentives like tax credits. However, exemptions of exported products from duties or taxes that apply to similar domestic products, or remission of such duties or taxes up to the amount accrued, are not considered subsidies if granted according to specific regulatory provisions.
   (iii) Provision of goods or services by the government other than general infrastructure, or government purchases of goods.
   (iv) Payments made by the government to a funding mechanism, or the entrusting or directing of a private body to perform functions normally carried out by the government, provided these practices do not substantially differ from normal government practices.

(b) Alternatively, any form of income or price support as defined under Article XVI of the GATT 1994 also constitutes a subsidy.

2. In all cases, the financial contribution or support must confer a benefit to the recipient for it to be deemed a subsidy.

The Regulation will become effective on the twentieth day after its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union. This means that once the Regulation is officially published, there is a waiting period of twenty days before its provisions are legally binding and must be complied with. This entry into force clause ensures a clear and predictable timeline for the implementation of the Regulation across all member states.

The general provisions for EU type-approval of engines under this Regulation establish clear criteria and procedures to ensure compliance and harmonisation across Member States. Approval authorities must grant EU type-approval to all engine types or families that meet the particulars specified in the information folder, comply with the Regulation’s requirements, and particularly adhere to conformity of production arrangements as outlined in Article 26. Once an engine satisfies these conditions, no additional EU type-approval requirements related to exhaust emissions may be imposed by approval authorities for non-road mobile machinery using that engine.

After the deadlines specified in Annex III for each engine sub-category, approval authorities are prohibited from granting EU type-approval to any engine type or family that does not meet the Regulation’s requirements. EU type-approval certificates must be numbered according to a harmonised system established by the Commission.

To facilitate transparency and cooperation, approval authorities are required to use the Internal Market Information system (IMI) to share information with other Member States. Within one month of issuing or extending an EU type-approval certificate, they must provide a list of such approvals. They must also promptly share lists of refusals or withdrawals of approvals, including reasons for these decisions. Upon request, they must supply copies of the EU type-approval certificates and the associated information packages to other Member States.

The information package compiled by the approval authority includes the information folder, test reports, and any additional documents added during the approval process. This package must be clearly indexed and maintained for at least 25 years after the EU type-approval expires, ensuring a comprehensive record of the approval’s management and any revisions.

Finally, the Commission is empowered to adopt implementing acts by 31 December 2016 to define the harmonised numbering system for certificates and the templates and data structures for data exchange, following the examination procedure in Article 56(2). These measures aim to standardise and streamline the EU type-approval process across the Union.

The EU type-approval certificate must include specific provisions to ensure clarity and compliance. Firstly, it shall contain certain attachments: the information package and, where applicable, the names and specimen signatures of the persons authorized to sign statements of conformity as outlined in Article 31, along with an indication of their position within the company. The European Commission is responsible for establishing a standardized template for the EU type-approval certificate to maintain uniformity across approvals.

For each approved engine type or engine family, the approval authority has several duties. It must complete all relevant sections of the certificate, attach the corresponding test report, compile an index to the information package, and promptly issue the finalized certificate and its attachments to the applicant. If the EU type-approval is subject to any restrictions on its validity or if certain regulatory requirements have been exempted for the engine type or family, these conditions must be clearly specified on the certificate.

Furthermore, the Commission holds the power to adopt implementing acts that define the template for the EU type-approval certificate as mentioned above. These acts are to be adopted by 31 December 2016, following the examination procedure set out in Article 56(2), ensuring a formal and transparent process for establishing the certificate format.

The conduct of measurements and tests for EU type-approval of engines under this Regulation involves several key procedures and requirements to ensure compliance with exhaust emission limits.

1. **Calculation of Final Emission Test Results:**  
   The final exhaust emission results must be derived from laboratory test data by applying:  
   - Emissions of crankcase gases, if required and not already included in the measurements.  
   - Adjustment factors for engines equipped with regenerating exhaust after-treatment systems, where applicable.  
   - Deterioration factors corresponding to the emission durability periods specified in Annex V, applicable to all engines.

2. **Reference Fuels for Testing:**  
   Testing to verify compliance with emission limits must be conducted using appropriate reference fuels, including:  
   - Diesel  
   - Petrol  
   - Petrol/oil mixtures for two-stroke spark-ignition engines  
   - Natural gas or biomethane  
   - Liquid petroleum gas (LPG)  
   - Ethanol  
   Additionally, engines must meet emission limits for any other specified fuels, mixtures, or emulsions included by the manufacturer in the type-approval application and documented in the information folder.

3. **Technical Requirements for Measurements and Tests:**  
   The Regulation mandates compliance with technical requirements covering:  
   - Apparatus and procedures for conducting tests and for emission measurement and sampling.  
   - Methods for data evaluation, calculations, and establishing deterioration factors.  
   - Specific methods for engines in certain categories (NRE, NRG, IWP, IWA, RLR, NRS, NRSh, SMB, ATS) complying with Stage V limits, including accounting for crankcase gas emissions and exhaust after-treatment system regenerations.  
   - For electronically controlled engines in specified categories complying with Stage V limits, requirements include documentation and demonstration of emission control strategies, NOx control measures, defining control areas within the steady-state test cycle where emissions may exceed limits, and selection of additional measurement points during bench tests.

4. **Delegated Acts by the Commission:**  
   The Commission is authorized to adopt delegated acts to supplement the Regulation by specifying:  
   - Methodologies for applying deterioration factors to laboratory test results.  
   - Technical characteristics of reference fuels and requirements for describing other specified fuels.  
   - Detailed technical requirements for conducting measurements and tests.  
   - Methods for measuring particle number (PN) emissions, aligned with UNECE Regulation No. 49.  
   - Technical requirements for testing dual-fuel and gaseous-fuelled single-fuel engines

For the purposes of this Regulation, the following definitions apply:

1. **Non-road mobile machinery**: Any mobile machine, transportable equipment, or vehicle, with or without bodywork or wheels, not intended for transporting passengers or goods on roads. This also includes machinery installed on the chassis of vehicles intended for road transport of passengers or goods.

2. **EU type-approval**: The procedure by which an approval authority certifies that an engine type or engine family meets the relevant administrative provisions and technical requirements set out in this Regulation.

3. **Gaseous pollutants**: Pollutants emitted by an engine in gaseous form, specifically carbon monoxide (CO), total hydrocarbons (HC), and oxides of nitrogen (NOₓ). NOₓ includes nitric oxide (NO) and nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), expressed as NO₂ equivalent.

The manufacturer, as the holder of an engine type or engine family EU type-approval, is required to provide a statement of conformity when placing engines on the market under certain exemptions or transitional provisions specified in the relevant Articles (Article 34(2), (4), (5), (6), (7), (8), Article 35(4), and Article 58(9), (10), (11)). This statement of conformity must detail the specific features and restrictions applicable to the engine and must be delivered free of charge along with the engine. When applicable, it should also accompany the non-road mobile machine into which the engine is installed. Importantly, the delivery of this statement cannot be contingent upon an explicit request or the submission of additional information by the recipient. The statement may be provided as a secure electronic file.

Manufacturers are obligated to retain the ability to issue duplicates of the statement of conformity for up to 10 years after the engine’s production date, upon request by the end-user, with a fee not exceeding the cost of issuance. Any duplicate must be clearly marked as such.

The statement must be prepared in at least one of the official languages of the European Union institutions. However, any Member State may request a translation into its own official language(s).

Only authorized personnel within the manufacturer’s organization, who have been duly empowered by management to assume full legal responsibility for the engine’s design, construction, or production conformity, may sign the statement of conformity.

The statement must be fully completed and may not include any usage restrictions beyond those established by the Regulation.

Finally, the European Commission is empowered to adopt implementing acts to establish a standardized template for the statement of conformity. These acts will include security features to prevent forgery and enable verification of secure electronic files. Such implementing acts were to be adopted by 31 December 2016, following the examination procedure outlined in Article 56(2).

The statutory marking of engines is a mandatory requirement for manufacturers producing engines that conform to an approved type. According to the regulations, each engine must bear a statutory marking affixed by the manufacturer. This marking serves as an official identifier confirming the engine’s compliance with the approved standards.

For certain categories of engines, the statutory marking must also include supplementary information indicating that the engine is subject to specific exemptions or transitional provisions. These categories include:

- Engines manufactured for export to third countries as specified in Article 34(1), whether produced inside or outside the Union and later installed in non-road mobile machinery within the Union.
- Engines placed on the market under the conditions outlined in Article 34(2), (5), (6), or (8).
- Engines temporarily placed on the market pursuant to Article 34(4).
- Transition engines placed on the market according to Article 58(5).
- Replacement engines placed on the market in line with Article 34(7) or Article 58(10) or (11).

Furthermore, the European Commission holds the authority to adopt implementing acts that establish the template for the statutory marking. These acts will specify the mandatory essential information that must be included when the engine leaves the production line and before it is placed on the market. They will also define the supplementary information required for engines subject to exemptions or transitional provisions as described above. Such implementing acts were to be adopted by 31 December 2016, following the examination procedure set out in Article 56(2).

For the purposes of this Regulation, engines are classified into several categories based on their intended use, power rating, and application. Four key engine categories include:

1. **Category NRE**: This category covers engines for non-road mobile machinery that are designed and suited to move, or be moved, by road or other means, provided they are not excluded under Article 2(2) and do not fall into other specified categories. It also includes engines with a reference power below 560 kW used as substitutes for Stage V engines in categories IWP (inland waterway propulsion), IWA (inland waterway auxiliary), RLL (locomotive propulsion), or RLR (railcar propulsion).

2. **Category NRG**: Engines in this category have a reference power greater than 560 kW and are exclusively used in generating sets. Generating set engines that do not meet these criteria are classified under NRE or NRS depending on their characteristics.

3. **Category NRSh**: This category is for hand-held spark-ignition (SI) engines with a reference power less than 19 kW, intended solely for use in hand-held machinery.

4. **Category NRS**: This includes spark-ignition engines with a reference power less than 56 kW that are not part of the NRSh category.

Additional categories exist for engines used in specific transport modes such as inland waterways (IWP and IWA), railways (RLL and RLR), snowmobiles (SMB), and all-terrain vehicles (ATS), each with their own definitions and power thresholds. Variable-speed engines may replace constant-speed engines within the same category, subject to additional compliance requirements. Auxiliary railway engines are generally included in the NRE or NRS categories based on their characteristics.

The Union may recognize the equivalence of engine type-approvals granted under international or third-country regulations with those established by EU law, within the framework of multilateral or bilateral agreements. Specifically, type-approvals and statutory markings that comply with UNECE regulations—provided the Union has supported or acceded to these regulations as listed in delegated acts—are considered equivalent to EU type-approvals under this Regulation. Similarly, EU type-approvals issued based on certain Union acts, also identified in delegated acts, are recognized as equivalent to those granted under this Regulation. To facilitate this process, the Commission is authorized to adopt delegated acts that specify (a) the UNECE regulations and amendments applicable to EU type-approval of engine types and families for non-road mobile machinery, and (b) the Union acts under which EU type-approvals are granted, including relevant application requirements. These delegated acts were to be adopted by 31 December 2016.

The designation of technical services is governed by specific categories of activities aligned with their areas of expertise. Approval authorities are responsible for designating technical services under one or more of the following categories:

- **Category A:** Conducting tests specified in the Regulation within the technical service’s own facilities.
- **Category B:** Supervising tests outlined in the Regulation when these are carried out in the facilities of a manufacturer or a third party.
- **Category C:** Regularly assessing and monitoring the manufacturer’s procedures to ensure production conformity.
- **Category D:** Supervising or performing tests or inspections to verify conformity of production.

An approval authority itself may also serve as a technical service for any of these categories. Additionally, technical services based in third countries that are not designated under this Article may be notified under Article 50, provided there is a bilateral agreement between the Union and the third country recognizing such services. Furthermore, a technical service established under Article 45(2) is permitted to set up subsidiaries in third countries, on the condition that these subsidiaries remain under the direct management and control of the original technical service.

Member States have several key obligations under this Regulation to ensure the proper approval, market surveillance, and placement of engines and non-road mobile machinery within the EU market. First, they must establish or appoint approval authorities and market surveillance authorities responsible for overseeing compliance with the Regulation. Once these authorities are designated, Member States are required to notify the European Commission, providing details such as their names, postal and electronic addresses, and specific areas of responsibility. The Commission, in turn, publishes a list of these approval authorities on its website for transparency.

Furthermore, Member States are obligated to allow only those engines that have a valid EU type-approval, granted in accordance with the Regulation, to be placed on the market. This applies both to engines sold separately and those already installed in non-road mobile machinery. Similarly, non-road mobile machinery containing such approved engines may also be placed on the market.

In addition, Member States must not prohibit, restrict, or impede the marketing of engines or non-road mobile machinery on grounds related to the construction, functioning, or emissions aspects covered by the Regulation, provided these products meet the Regulation’s requirements. Finally, Member States are responsible for organizing and conducting market surveillance and control activities for engines available on the market, in line with the provisions set out in Chapter III of Regulation (EC) No 765/2008. These measures collectively ensure that only compliant products circulate within the EU, safeguarding environmental and technical standards.

Each Member State is required to develop and maintain up-to-date contingency plans for each priority pest that could potentially enter and establish itself within its territory or parts thereof. These contingency plans must detail the decision-making processes, procedures, protocols, and minimum resources necessary to respond effectively to an officially confirmed or suspected presence of the pest. Additionally, procedures for mobilizing further resources must be included. The development and updating of these plans should involve consultation with all relevant stakeholders at appropriate stages. However, contingency plans are not required for pests that are conclusively determined to be unable to establish or spread in the Member State due to unsuitable ecoclimatic conditions or absence of host species.

Each contingency plan must comprehensively cover several key elements:

- The roles and responsibilities of all bodies involved in executing the plan, including the chain of command and coordination procedures among competent authorities, public authorities, delegated bodies, laboratories, professional operators, and, where relevant, coordination with neighboring Member States and third countries.

- Access rights for competent authorities to premises of professional operators, other relevant operators, and natural persons.

- Access to laboratories, equipment, personnel, external expertise, and other resources necessary for rapid and effective eradication or containment of the pest.

- Measures for providing information to the European Commission, other Member States, professional operators, and the public regarding the pest’s presence and control measures once confirmed or suspected.

- Arrangements for recording findings related to the pest’s presence.

- Available pest risk assessments and any additional assessments conducted by the Member State concerning the pest’s risk to its territory.

- Risk management measures aligned with regulatory requirements and the procedures to be followed.

- Principles for defining geographical demarcation areas.

- Protocols for visual examinations, sampling, and laboratory testing methods.

- Training principles for personnel of competent authorities and, where appropriate, other involved bodies, laboratories, professional operators, and persons.

Where suitable, items such as information provision, recording arrangements, risk assessments, risk management, demarcation principles, testing protocols, and training may be presented as instruction manuals.

Contingency plans may be consolidated for multiple priority pests that share similar biology and host ranges. In such cases, the plan should include a general section applicable to all pests covered and specific sections for each individual pest.

Member States must establish contingency plans for all priority pests within four years of the list’s establishment. For any pest added subsequently to the priority list, a contingency plan must be developed within one year of its inclusion. These plans should be regularly reviewed and updated as necessary.

Upon request, Member States

Under specific derogations from Article 5(1), Member States within the Union may temporarily authorize the introduction, movement, holding, and multiplication of Union quarantine pests or pests subject to measures under Article 30(1) for purposes such as official testing, scientific or educational research, trials, varietal selections, or breeding. Such authorizations are granted only when adequate restrictions are imposed to prevent the establishment or spread of these pests within the Union territory. These restrictions take into account the pest’s identity, biology, dispersal methods, the nature of the activity, environmental interactions, and other relevant risk factors.

Authorizations must include several mandatory conditions: the pest must be kept in locations and under conditions deemed appropriate by competent authorities and specified in the authorization; activities involving the pest must occur within designated quarantine stations or confinement facilities; personnel conducting these activities must possess the necessary scientific and technical competence and be named in the authorization; and the pest must always be accompanied by the authorization during introduction, movement, holding, or multiplication within the Union.

Furthermore, authorizations are limited in terms of the quantity of pest material allowed and the duration of the authorized activity, ensuring these limits do not exceed the capacity of the designated facilities. Restrictions must be sufficient to eliminate the risk of pest establishment and spread. Competent authorities are responsible for monitoring compliance with all conditions and limitations, and they must take necessary actions, including revoking authorizations if non-compliance occurs.

The European Commission holds the power to adopt delegated acts to supplement these regulations by establishing detailed rules on information exchange between Member States and the Commission, procedures and conditions for granting authorizations, and monitoring and enforcement measures related to compliance.

Article 161 of the Directive specifies that any processing of personal data conducted within the scope of this Directive must comply with the provisions set out in Directive 95/46/EC. This means that the handling, storage, and use of personal data are governed by the data protection principles established in Directive 95/46/EC, ensuring the protection of individuals' privacy rights. The alignment with Directive 95/46/EC guarantees that personal data is processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently, with appropriate safeguards against misuse or unauthorized access.

Member States are required to ensure that up-to-date information is made available regarding the provisions of their national law that govern the rights of third parties to rely on particulars and each type of document referred to in Article 14. This obligation is established in accordance with Article 16(5), (6), and (7), which set out the conditions under which third parties may invoke such documents. To facilitate accessibility and transparency, Member States must provide the necessary information for publication on the European e-Justice portal, adhering to the portal’s specific rules and technical requirements. Subsequently, the European Commission is responsible for publishing this information on the portal in all official languages of the European Union, ensuring broad and multilingual dissemination across Member States. This framework aims to promote legal certainty and ease of access to relevant national law provisions for third parties throughout the Union.

Article 84 outlines specific derogations that Member States may apply concerning certain provisions related to employee participation and company share structures. Firstly, Member States are permitted to derogate from the first paragraph of Article 48, the first sentence of Article 60(1)(a), and Articles 68, 69, and 72 when such derogations are necessary to implement measures encouraging employees or other groups defined by national law to participate in the capital of undertakings. This flexibility aims to promote employee involvement in company ownership.

Secondly, Member States may choose not to apply the first sentence of Article 60(1)(a) and Articles 73, 74, and 79 to 82 to companies established under special laws that issue both capital shares and workers' shares. In these companies, workers' shares are allocated collectively to employees, who are represented at general shareholders' meetings by delegates with voting rights, thereby recognizing a distinct form of employee representation.

Finally, Member States must ensure that certain provisions—specifically Article 49, Articles 58(1), 68(1), (2), and (3), the first subparagraph of Article 70(2), Articles 72 to 75, and Articles 79 to 81—do not apply when resolution tools, powers, and mechanisms under Title IV of Directive 2014/59/EU are used. This ensures that the special rules governing the resolution of financial institutions take precedence over the standard company law provisions in these contexts.

Article 12 outlines the requirements and procedures for issuing and validating specific authorisations for boatmasters within Member States. Firstly, applicants must provide satisfactory documentary evidence proving their identity, compliance with minimum age, competence, administrative, and navigation time requirements as specified in Annex I, and possession of a valid Union certificate of qualification as a boatmaster or an equivalent certificate recognized under Article 10(2) and (3), or demonstrate that they meet the minimum standards for Union certificates of qualification.

A derogation applies for authorisations related to navigation on inland waterways with specific risks (as per point (b) of Article 6). In these cases, applicants must submit evidence of identity, competence for the specific risks associated with the waterway stretch (as established under Article 20), and hold the relevant Union certificate or meet its minimum requirements.

Member States are responsible for verifying the authenticity and validity of all submitted documents before issuing the specific authorisations. Furthermore, the competent authority issuing Union certificates of qualification must explicitly indicate any specific authorisations granted pursuant to Article 6 on the certificate, following the model set out in Article 11(3). The validity of these specific authorisations is tied to the validity period of the Union certificate of qualification.

An exception exists for the specific authorisation mentioned in point (d) of Article 6, which concerns liquefied natural gas expertise. This authorisation is issued as a Union certificate of qualification in its own right, following the model in Article 11(3), with its validity period determined according to Article 11(6).

Upon the expiry of a Union certificate of qualification, Member States are required to renew the certificate and any relevant specific authorisations included within it, provided that certain conditions are met. Specifically:

(a) For Union certificates of qualification issued to deck crew members, as well as for specific authorisations other than the one mentioned in point (d) of Article 6, renewal will be granted only if satisfactory documentary evidence, as outlined in points (a) and (c) of Article 11(1), has been submitted.

(b) For Union certificates of qualification related to specific operations, renewal depends on the submission of satisfactory documentary evidence referred to in points (a) and (b) of Article 11(1).

In summary, the renewal process hinges on the timely submission of the appropriate documentary evidence specified in Article 11(1), ensuring that boatmasters maintain the necessary qualifications and authorisations to operate safely and legally.

Article 17 of the Directive addresses the assessment of competences required for certain maritime qualifications and authorisations. It establishes that the Commission shall adopt delegated acts, pursuant to Article 31, to define the standards for competences, including the necessary knowledge and skills, in line with the essential requirements outlined in Annex II.

Member States are responsible for ensuring that applicants for documents specified in Articles 4, 5, and 6 demonstrate compliance with these competence standards. This demonstration must be done, where applicable, by passing an examination organized either under the authority of an administrative body as per Article 18 or as part of a training programme approved under Article 19.

The competence assessment includes a practical examination for obtaining specific qualifications and authorisations, namely: (a) a Union certificate of qualification as a boatmaster; (b) a specific authorisation for sailing with radar assistance; (c) a Union certificate of qualification as a liquefied natural gas (LNG) expert; and (d) a Union certificate of qualification as a passenger navigation expert. For the first two categories, practical exams may be conducted on board a craft or using a simulator compliant with Article 21. For the LNG and passenger navigation experts, practical exams may take place either on board a craft or at a suitable onshore facility.

Furthermore, the Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts to supplement the Directive by specifying the standards for these practical examinations. These acts will detail the specific competences and conditions to be tested, as well as set minimum requirements for the craft used during the practical assessments.

When adopting the implementing acts referred to in Articles 11(3), 18(3), and 22(4), the Commission is required to make reference to standards established by CESNI and set the date of application, provided certain conditions are met. These conditions include that the CESNI standards must be available and up-to-date, must comply with any applicable requirements set out in the Annexes, and that Union interests are not compromised by any changes in CESNI’s decision-making process. If these conditions are not fulfilled, the Commission may instead provide or refer to other standards. Furthermore, when implementing acts under this Directive refer to standards, the Commission must include the entire text of those standards within the implementing acts themselves.

The transitional provisions outlined in Article 38 address the validity and replacement of boatmasters’ certificates, Rhine navigation licences, and crew members’ qualifications issued prior to 18 January 2022, ensuring a smooth transition to the new certification framework established by the Directive.

1. **Validity of Existing Certificates:**  
Boatmasters’ certificates issued under Directive 96/50/EC, including those referred to in Articles 1(5) and 1(6) of that Directive, as well as Rhine navigation licences issued before 18 January 2022, remain valid on the Union inland waterways where they were originally recognized for up to 10 years after that date, i.e., until 18 January 2032.

2. **Issuance of Union Certificates:**  
Before 18 January 2032, Member States must, upon request and subject to satisfactory documentary evidence (as specified in Article 11(1)(a) and (c)), issue to holders of these older certificates a Union certificate of qualification or a certificate as per Article 10(2), following the model prescribed by the new Directive. When doing so, Member States should preserve previously granted entitlements, especially specific authorizations mentioned in Article 6.

3. **Crew Members’ Certificates:**  
Crew members (other than boatmasters) holding certificates issued before 18 January 2022 or qualifications recognized in one or more Member States may continue to rely on these for up to 10 years after that date. During this period, recognition under Directive 2005/36/EC remains applicable. Before this period expires, crew members may apply for a Union certificate of qualification or a certificate under Article 10(2), again subject to providing satisfactory evidence.

   When issuing new certificates to replace older ones, Member States must ensure that the competence requirements are similar to or lower than those of the replaced certificate. Certificates with higher requirements may only be issued if the applicant meets specific navigation time criteria:

   - **Boatman:** 540 days total navigation, including at least 180 days inland  
   - **Able Boatman:** 900 days total navigation, including at least 540 days inland  
   - **Helmsman:** 1,080 days total navigation, including at least 720 days inland  

   Navigation experience must be proven via service record books, logbooks, or equivalent documentation. These minimum durations may be reduced by up to 360 days if the applicant holds a recognized diploma confirming specialized inland navigation training, but the reduction cannot exceed the training duration.
